div.head: NATION'S GREATEST ASSET A CONTENTED PEOPLE.
div.p: NATION'S GREATEST ASSET A CONTENTED PEOPLE.
BISHOP PRAISES THE CITIZENS GUILD
OF HELP.

"We want to give every man, woman and child a chance," declared the Bishop of Liverpool in his address to the Warrington Citizens Guild of help at the annual meeting held in tbe Co-operative 11,111 on Tuesday even- ing. His Lordship spoke in terms of warm commenda- tion of the work of the Guild and said every clergyman ought to hail it with delight. There was a good attend- ance, the Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph) presiding. Amongst those present were :—The Mayoress (Mrs A yield), the Revs Canon Morley Stevenson, W Brace- camp, E E Peters, end W Reid, Mr and Mrs F A Frost, Mr C E Parker, Mr and Mrs J A Ransome, Nlr Wll Stansfleld, Colonel J D Fairclough, Mrs Crosileld (Colwyn Bay), Captain G H Croslield, Mr James Ball, Miss R Macadam (lecturer, School of Social Science, Liverpool University), and Mr Wilfred J Rowland (secretary of the Guild). The MAYOR referred to the interest of the Guild in health matters—particularly in the lessening of infantile mortality and consumption. It might seem •on the surface that the Guild was not satisfied with the efforts made by the Health Committee to ward off the attacks of disease. He took it, however, that there were different aspects of the question—sanitary, social, religious and educational. Ho would not ask the members of the Guild not to condemn the Health Com- mittee, but at the same time he did not think there was any committee, either in Warrington or anywhere else, which worked more consistently, practically and earnestly to fulfil its duties. The members vied with each othsr to try and obtain as much knowledge as possible, and aided and guided by an able, efficient and earnest Medical Officer of Health, and an acute and well read legal adviser, they did their work to the utmost of their ability. (Hear, hoar, and applause.) The question of health, especially in the slums, was of such enormous magnitude that they wanted all the help they could get ; end there was no more efficient outside help than the Citizens' Guild of Help. He thought that poverty combined with ignor ance was far more dangerous than poverty alone. Having referred to the different classes of people with which the Guild had to deal and to the apparent hope- lessness of the task of reforming slum dwellers, who, suffering from the evil effects of heredity and bad environment, were almost in a state of paralysis, the Mayor said that if they could not reclaim those who were now in the midst of the mire—a quagmire they could not get out of—they could, at all events, thanks to improved education, hope to relieve the children of those people from the dreadful legacy they had from their parents. (Applause). THE WORK OF THE YEAR.

The second annual report gain a very encouraging record of work. The year had been marked ny steady progress and numbers of families were thankful for the help and advice given by the band of voluntary helpers. There were 364 cases disposed of during the year, and a large number of cases were brought forward from 1910. Not until there had been close contact with the work of a guild was it possible to realize the amount of personal service rendered. It was gratifying to find that many who received a helping hand two years ago were standing to-day as independent citieens ; still more encouraging was it to see that some who formerly received assistance were now trying to repay the com- munity. There had been a diminution in the number of cases classified ander the beading " False Addresses " (45 in 1911, as compared with 74 in 1910.1 That indi- cated a reduction of door-to-door begging, as the direct result of the Guild's work ; indeed, the Guild was effective just in proportion as it was made use of in SAVING THE PUBLIC FROM MISDIRECTED PHILANTHROPY. Early in 1911 the Guild sent deputations to the Health Committee on the subject of infantile mortality, and, eventually, with their approval, a Mothers and Babies' Welcome was opened. Such work could not have been accomplished but for the practical helpfulness of the Medical Officer and his staff. During the year the Guild had also devoted attention to consumption. Being in touch with many tuberculous patients, the Guild had taken a deep interest in the progressive work of the Town Council. The executive looked forward to an extension of the sanatorium accommoda- tion already provided. The Guild continued to co-operate with all agencies working for the good of the town. It was only part of a larger movement that was steadily extending over the country. The local societ3 had joined the National Association of Guilds of Help. There was an adverse bank balance on January Ist 1912, of £45 ls. sd.

div.head: MATERIAL ASSISTANCE.
div.p: MATERIAL ASSISTANCE.

The following table, though not complete, sets forth some of the material help given directly by the Guild. The figures, of course, do not include the large amount of help procured through the instrumentality of the Guild from co-operating charities including parochial and other funds :—Boots and clogs' 14; other clothing and bedding, 46; necessary food, 51; milk, 12; nourish- ment for invalids, IS; convalescent homes and sanatoria, 5; railway fares, 5; financial help in loans, debts, S;c., 24; surgical or medical aid, 3; hawkers' licences, 2; work found, 32. MOTTIF.RS AND BABIES' 'WELCOME. The report of the Mothers and Babies' Welcome,which was started by the Guild after consultation with the Health Committee of the Town Council, states that no fewer than 70 mothers visited the welcome during the first seven months. Many cannot make a habit of attend. log, but some who have come regularly have learned a good deal of mothercraft. The average attendance of mothers has been twelve, and the ladies of the com- mittee have undertaken to visit those who might attend more often. A club for baby clothing has recently been started and is much appreciated. Mrs. Hibbert, Barricane, Latchford, is the honorary treasurer of the Ladies' Committee, and Miss M. Broadbent,of the Hollies,Latchford,honorary secretary THE BISHOP ON ENGLAND'S GREAT ASSET, The BISHOP OF LIVERPOOL, who moved the adoption of the report, said the Guild was part of a great move- ment which was going on all over the country to cope with the suffering and poverty in our great industrial centres and to do it on sane, scientific and truly Christkn lines. That Guild and others were reducing the old district visiting to a fine art, and yet without any loss of sympathy or of that personal touch which did so much for district visitors in times past. Their great object, he took it, was not so much to get money as to get men—(hear, hear)—not so much to raise sub- scriptions as to obtain workers, not so much to encourage alms giving as alms doing. It was a society for promoting friends for the poor. The Archbishop of Canterbury had recently put his imprimatur upon the old saying that in two generations, if England would only wake up, there need be none of the grinding poverty and shameful Equalor which at present disfigured our great cities. The Guild was seeking to bring about that GOLDEN AND LONGED-FOR AGE. . . . .

It was educating its workers and giving them experi- ence in carefully investigating cases. it was also teaching what the report happily termed " mother- craft," and he was sure the Mayor would bear him out when he said that one of the most important points from a health point of view was that the mothers of England should know how to bring up their children on the right lines. The Guild was doing a really national work In that direction. It was also educating the poor to help themselves, which was the best help it could give them. Those who had worked, as he had for twenty }ears. among the poor, knew that the truest cases of poverty hid themselves, that the true poor were too self-respecting to make their poverty known. It was not the blatant beggar who was the deserving one. It was the man who never let his poverty be known, who sought in the direst hour of distress to look respectable, and to go about his ordinary life as if nothing extraordinary were behind it. The Guild was seeking out those deserving cases end putting it in their power to be relieved. Every clergyman ought to hail with delight such a society as that. During his parochial work One of his great difficulties was to deal with new comers who asked for help and he would have given worlds to have been able to go to a society like that for information. NO CLERGYMAN OUGHT TO STAND ASIDE from such a movement but should throw himself heart and soul into a work so Christ-like and so useful. (Applause) Already their work was beginning to make itself felt. He saw from their first annual report that 74 gave false addresses, whereas in the present report, there were only 45 who had given false addresses. They Were becoming a terror to the evil doer. He hoped that little by little they would rid Warrington of those imposters who preyed upon the credulity of kind-hearted End benevolent people. Be ventured to say that if the clergy looked to the Guild—as they ought—for help, the Guild wculd not
MIME

div.head: GREATEST ASSET Or A NATION WAS A CONTENTED
div.p: GREATEST ASSET Or A NATION WAS A CONTENTED
PEOPLE.

They could not all be equal in this world, and those who talked about equality were making a very great mistake and conjuring up a false vision. If they were all equal to-day they would be unequal again in ten years. God had given them unequal gifts, and many a man lost through his character what another man gained through his good character. There must be inequality to the world's end. But what they wanted to do was to give every man, woman, and child a chance—(applause)—and that Guild was giving to many a depressed man and woman and many a sick child a chance which they would not otherw,se have had. They were helping to bring together the classes of England, and in these days of unrest and discontent they were doing their best to make the English people happy, contented, and united. (Applause). Mr. J. BALL, in seconding, said the Guild sought to bring existing, agencies ot helpfulness in touch with actual need. With regard to relief, many poor people had contributed to the poor rate in their rent and were entitled in time of distress to ask for the necessary assistance to tide them over an awkward and desperate period. (Applause'. Mr. RANSOME presented the financial statement and said that most of last year's subscribers had renewed and in many cases increased their stiscriptions. The Guild had no condemnation for the Health Committee; their cbject was to work with it and to help people to help themselves. (Applause). WHY CHARITIES HAVE FAILED.

Miss MACADAM, in moving the adoption of the balance sheet, said voluntary cha.ities had often failed in the past, and one reason was because their standard had been to) low—it had been too much taken for granted that anyone with a kind heart could do social work. We were outgrowing that state of affairs and beginning to realisa that social work was very complicated and difficult, that organisations were difficult to understand, that modern legislation was every day becoming more complicated and puzzling, and that therefore we must have social workers who were well trained. In the reports of the Poor Law Commission some organization like the Guild of Help was recommended for every town. The Guild should unite citizens of all creeds, politics and classes. It was important that such bodies should not be societies of the well-to-do to help tha poor. They must draw in the intelligent and thinking workingmen and women. Many of the difficulties of a town might be solved by such an organization which could do con- structive, preventive work—preventing people becoming pauperised, being obliged to give up their homes or to apply for out-relief. (Applause). Canon STEVENSON seconded. Ile said that anything that would put an end to the indiscriminate giving of money to persons who did not deserve it would be a great step in the right direction. He had personally, in more than one instance, found the very great help of being able to send cases to the office of the Guild, with the assurance that they would receive fair and candid investigation. Captain CRosrIELD proposed a vote of thanks to the Mayor and the speakers. Mr. W. H. STANSFIELD seconded. He said the Guild endeavoured to put courage into the hearts of moral cos ards and make them " buck up" and do their duty in life. The vote was heartily passed.

div.head: 2M-BUK SAVED HER LEG!
div.p: 2M-BUK SAVED HER LEG!
Like Raw Meat from Knee to Ankle.
MAnvELLous HEALING AmAzEi NEIGHBOUR

No more convincing proof of Zam-Buk's wonderful healing powers could surely be revealed than the cure of Mrs. Davies's bad leg. When the" Denbigh Free Press " reporter visited her at her home, 13, Garden Place, Mold, N. Wales, he found Mrs. Davies cheerfully doing her housework without any trace of pain. " I have had an awful time, though," Mrs. Davies said. "My leg used to itch a lot, and one day when scratching it I broke the skin. Some dirt must have got into the leg, for it swelled and began to thiob. Little eruptions kept breaking out, too, leaving the skin like raw meat. The pain was terrible—a burning, smarting sensation, besides the constant itching and throbbing. The festering worked up my leg, eating the skin away from ankle to knee. I was so helpless I had to be carried up and down stairs.

"Besides wasting pounds on cheap ointments, I was attended by two doctors, and a nurse came every day for three months to dress my leg. My case com- pletely baffled them, however, and they all strongly advised me to go into hospital. My leg was then in such a shocking state that I was afraid the hospital surgeons would want to cut it off, so I refused to go. "Just at this time my soldier brother came home from India, and at once advised Zam-Buk, which, he said, was used very extensively in the army for heal- ing wounds and sores. I put Zam-Buk to the test at once, and was astonished at its effect. The soothing sensation was something quite new, the pain getting less acute after each dressing. Zam-Buk gradually dried up the sticky discharge, too. As the cure progressed all pain vanished and the use returned to my leg. "Over the whole limb, between knee and ankle, Zam-Buk drew out the badness and inflammation and grew new healthy skin until there wasn't a sign of the old sores. lam convinced that Zam-Buk saved my leg, which is thoroughly sound and healthy again. My friends are amazed at what they call a marvellous Zam-Buk cure."
No cheap ointment or crude home-made salve conld possibly have healed Mrs. Davies's leg. Zam-Buk (sold only in sealed boxes at is. 11d., 2s. 9d. and Is. GI) alone possesses the power.

APPLETON RIFLE CLUB v. DARESBURY CLUB A match between these clubs took place on Friday evening last, on the miniature range at the Drill Hall. The conditions were :—Ten shots and two sighting shots, at a decimal target, at 25 yards ; possible score per man, 100 ; eleven men aside, the best ten scores to count. The match was an even one and proved very exciting. One of the Appleton team, John L Shepherd, was late in arriving, and it was necessary for him to make a score of 93 points to win the match for his side. div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
LICENSING REFORMS DISCUSSED.

The members of the Warrington Debating Society met on Tuesday evening to discuss a Bill to amend and supplement the Licensing Laws which was intro- duced by the Rev. H. Ogden (President of the Board of Education), and contained the following among other provisions :- 1. Full powers of granting, renewing or refusing licenses of all (including the registration of clubs) shall be vested in the Local Magisrrates, the Local Governing Bodies and ratepayers of respective districts in the manner set forth herein. 2. On the expiretion of seven years after the passing of this Act, the refusal to renew any license shall not involve compensation on account of such refusal. Licenses being granted for one year only, every renewal shall be subject to public conveni- ence as interpreted by the aforesaid authorities. 3. Any license shall be granted or refused by the magistrate OD petition from two-thirds of the ratepayers of the Ward, or Polling District in which the premises in question are situated. 6. The hours of sale on licensed premises shall be :—On week-days, from 8.30 a.m. t 3 10 p.m.; anckon Sundays, from 12 noon to 1 o'clock, and 7 to 9in the evening. Total Sunday closing shall be observed in any town or district on petition of two-thirds of the ratepayers of such district. 7. That no woman or person under 16 years of age shall be served with intoxicating liquor for consumption either "on " or " off " the premises before 12 noon. 8. The basis for Excise Duty shall be the quantity of intoxicants sold. The rev, gentleman claimed that the Bill was of a generous nature, more generous than perhaps others might have dreamt. (Hear, hear.) It should therefore commend itself t 3 the judgment of members of both sides of the House. In regard to the first clause he thought it was useless to ask the members opposite to discuss that. On the second clause he knew he carried his own side of the House with him if n)t those opposite, when he said that whenev-r the nation resumed the right to licenses for 12 months only, it was only just commencing to undo Mr. Balfour's Act. (Hear, hear.) If that Bill became law the nation would resume the right it. had prior to the Act of Mr. Balfour. They were all agreed that that Act had done something in regard to the reduction of licensed houses—(hear, hear)—but the compensation clause in that very Act had been the means of retarding what ought to have proceeded with much greater facility The seven years in wh;ch the compensation period should continue was as generous as the provision as set forth by the Commission of which Lard Pell was chair- man which suggested seven years as the limit. In the third clause, he thought that surely a district which kept the public-houses should have the right to any whether they should he continued or not. The clause was not local veto but local option. Where the people were the poorest and where there was the greatest need for thrift, public-houses were erected. There was a temptation on every poor man's doorstep and it was nothing less than tragic to hear them say that if they had only the opportunity to thrust the temptation away they would do it willingly. That clause gave the district that opportunity. (Applause.) Then in the next clause it was only right and fair that something should be done for the protection of the publican. In the past the public-house had been blamed for the work of the clubs. The club was a temptation for those who were exceedingly young. Young men of respectable homes who would not like to cross the door of a public house went and drank in the clubs. He thought it was only just and fair that those clubs should come under direct magisterial control. He was of the opinion that they could have nothing against the next clause which meant that all traders in drink should be under the same law and control as the public-house. (Hear, hear.) How many working men were there who had thought they were paying for tea when they had been paying for drink ? The answer and the reasons were plain. In regard to Sunday closing the rev, gentle- man said he felt they would agree that if the public-house was closed from sunrise to sunset they would see fewer of th deplorable sights that one saw in the streets of Warrington. In all his experi- ences in other towns he had not seen so much drunkenness in the public streets on Sunday afternoons as in Warrington. The facilities fcr drinking on a Sunday would be curtailed. Then in regard to the week-day closing. The employer Was now feeling the result of the public house being opened at 6 o 'clock in the morning. One regretted that a working man had so little will control that he must needs have a drink as soon as the public houses opened. The sooner the temptation was removed from him all the better for the worker and the employer. (Hear, hear.) He thought it was admirable that they should not be opened until 8.30 in the morning. Whatever their friends might think about the drink trade and about the licensing methods of the country, he thought that every member of that Howe was agreed that one of the most deplorable and disreputable spectacles was to see a woman drunk in the public streets,which could be seen in any Lancashire town. After a man had been working hard all morning he went home and expected his noontide meal provided for him, and there on the hearth was the woman be had taken for better or worse—drank. Why was all this ?—Because the woman had free access to the public-house and off- licence from 6 o'clock in the morning. How much brighter would the home be if that were done away with? (Applause). Mr. J. A. HEYWOOD (L., Limehouse) in seconding the Bill, said it had his full approval. There was just one point he would like to emphasise, and that was that when magistrates were appointed to sit upon any licensing bench, he was of the opinion that they should be equally divided. Representatives of various oblates should be on, not all men of one mind, and then they would arrive at a proper method of either refusing or granting a licence. (Rear, hear.) He thought the publican should have the same compensation in propor- tion as the brewer. So far as his knowledge of clubs was concerned, be lid not see much of which he could

seziously complain. He agreed that men some- times sit in the public-house and then feeling that they would like to go to the club had proceeded there "and finished the job." He approved of the Bill in its entirety except for the clause in regard to women. So far as women were concerned he could not see that there was very much difference in a drunken man and a drunken woman." (Hear, bear, and a Voice : " Shame") He had always been in favour of women having their rights. (Applause). Mr. C. PLINSTON (C., Darlington) moved that the Bill be read that day six months. The measure was like all the others that had been introduced by the Liberals— (laughter)—it was faalty in construction. (Hear, hear, and a VOICE : " Always the case."). (Laughter.) Beyond that he would say it was opposed to sound democracy. The Liberal party instead of truiting the
I that had

peopf.o were be;:iing them round wah all sorts of checks and devices to prevent them doing this, that and the other. They were talone away from them the liberty of movement and almost of will. During the last twenty years there had been a charge in the habits of tha people. Men and women of the present time were learning that it was not only foolish and injurious but morally wrong to take liquor in excess. The change that had come about in the country had not been caused by restrictions in public hous::,s or in the hours of sale but it was by education and the raising of 013 m oral tone. Let the temperance advocate go on as his forefathers had done, bel'eving in the gospel he wt s preaching. It was because tney were losing faith that they we re losing ground. One of the greatest causes for the reduction of drunkenness was the great multiplication of places of amuserneat in their midst. Those had more to do with the reduction than any restriction they had put on the sale of drink. Unfortunately and largely owing to their Cobdenite policy—(Oh !)—and its cursed cheapness, they had created dismal streets of slum dwellings. (Oh.) The poor people who resided in them had bad to seek their amusement elsewhere, and small blame to them. If they would do all in their power to remove the slum dwellings then they would help on their temperance CHISO far more than by restrictions. (Hear, hear.) All he could say was that the Bill was absolutely absurd and unworthy of the consideration of the House. :Applause). Mr. L. WArtuctsToN formally seconded the proposal. Mr. P. O'BRIEN (L., St. Pancras) said he did not believe Warrington was one of the worst towns in the United Kingdom in regard to the drinkinequestion. One person had remarked to him that he was glad to see the order which prevailed in Warrington on Satur- days and Sundays. He bad not seen it so good in any other town in Great Britain. (Hear, hear.) They could always rely on it that a man's character had been investigated betore he was granted a licence. Grocers he contended, should keep to their own trade and off-licences he had no particular love for. He agreed with the Bill and said it was not altogether a temper- ance question but a question for all citizens. Mr. BRISCOE (C., Hereford City), said the first past of the Bill had been taken out of the dead Licensing Act and the second half had been taken from the recom- mendation of the Liverpool magistrates. For the brewer the Bill was an excellent one and would allow him to sell considerably more beer at about one-half the cost. Was a man going to carry on a business on a clean basis when he had only a guarantee of one year's license ? Mr. C. DUKES (Socialist, West Ham), in opposing the Bill said the idea of making the people sober by Act of Parliament was an absolute fallacy. Factory dis- cipline in itself had done more to make workingmen sober than all the legislature which had come from the House of Commons. Great stress had been laid on the drunkenness of the poor. They heard nothing of the middle-class who got drunk and could go home in motor cars and so forth. It was the poor class who had to walk through the streets publicly, when they were drunk and people only saw them. All the endeavours to convert the individual by restrictions and the delivery of temperance tracts were not (going to make one iota of difference. If they wanted lthe worker to become more sober they should provide better housing conditions and better conditions of labour and he would not fly to that cheap rubbish. the public-house was Many a time more attractive than the hovels some people lived in. If they wanted to reform the individual they should commence by reforming the economic conditions of the working man. They were not going to effect the drink question by coercive measures. (Applause). The discussion was adjourned until the next sitting, which will be on the 27th, next Tuesday being the date fixed for the whist drive.

div.head: CHILD IN CUPBOARD.
div.p: CHILD IN CUPBOARD.
£2O Damages Against School Teacher.

His Honour Judge Reginald Brown delivered his written judgment on Wednesday, in the action of Joseph Astbury, for his infant daughter Barbara, against the managers of Castle Northwich Girls' National School and Miss Robina Wotherspoon, the teacher, now of Warrington. The jury had found that the teacher had administered excessive punishment by placing the child in a school cupboard, St. Vitus's dance and fits developing in consequence. Judgment is given for the plaintiff. with £2O damages and costs on the higher scale, against Miss Wother- spoon. Judgment, however, is given for the managers, with costs. The first £lO out of the damages is to be lodged in court for Barbara Astbury'

div.head: CHICKEN MANAGEMENT.
div.p: CHICKEN MANAGEMENT.

It is now time that we dealt with the subject of chicken management. I expect that quite a number of the" downy ones " will be putting in their appear- ance during the month and onwards. The all important item in connection with this branch cf the work is that of
FEEDING THE CHICKENS.

Newly hatched chickens require no food whatever for the first twenty-four hours at least. For this period nature has provided for them. Before a chicken leaves the shell, it absorbs sufficient nutriment from the yolk of the egg to last it for the period named. The first feed should consist of bard-boiled egg chopped very fine and mixed with stale bread crumbs ; this should be given every two hours for the first two days. Then gradually bring them on to ether foods, in the form of boiled rice and oatmeal, eatmeal and milk and bread and milk. When giving the two first named diets let it be in the crumbly state. Keep them on this food for the first two weeks then at night you may gise them a feed of dry chick , food.
GREEN FOOD.

Green food for chickens is just as essential as it is for adults. If they are reared on a grass run this will prove sufficient.On the other hand you must supply it in some form. Young lettuce and chicken-weed are good when obtainable. When this cannot be got give them a nice green sod to pick, it will be much appreciated by the youngster; and also form good exercise in scrat•hing and picking off the young grass.
GRIT. At even so early an age grit is needed. If you can get a supply of sharp sea-sand so much better, if not then you can purchase chicken grit from any reliable corn merchant. .

When the chicks are a month old you can reduce the number of meals to five times a day. But always let the last meal be as late as possible. This meal should consist of good sound grain, such as small wheat, or cracked wheat. At about six or seven weeks the chickens are able to leave the hen. Care should be taken at this period to supply them with warm coops,and with the floors well covered with dry chaff ; Remember that they now have to generate their own heat. If the floor is thus well covered they will not require a perch, you should never encourage them to perch too early. If you do, then look out for twisted toes, and crooked breast bones, and whether thf y be for exhibition or utility purposes, they deteriorate in value as a result of this deformity. (To be continued).
OLD ENGLISH GAME.

Nearly every one can tell a Gate Fowl at sight. Once seen and once described, one never forgets the King ' of the poultry yard. If we borrow from one of Landseer's titles and apply it to the Old English Game it proves very apt. For surely we can say that the Old English Game Cock is indeed " Monarch of all he surveys." They are very striking birds in more senses than one. Beautiful in colour, wonderfully clear and defined in symmetry, and with their strong beaks and fiery red eyes they at once suggest war. So in olden times they were bred and reared chiefly for fighting. Happily this state of affairs is fast dying out—for it is a cruel business. They are now bred chiefly for their exhibition and utility qualities. As a table bird the Game Fowl ranks in the very first front, and when bred,solely for utility purposes the hens are good layers, especially on a free range. The colours are very numerous, the chief and meat popular of which, are Black Red; Duckwing ; Spangled ; Brown Red ; Black • and Pile. Game are nearly always dubbed. The practice of dubbing is looked upon by some people as being very cruel. Of course opinions vary, but knowing well the pugnacious tendancy of the game fowl—even when not bred for fighting—it is always found that to dub them is better. Because with fighting so much, their ccmla3 and wattles are constantly being damaged. Thus you will observe, that it is better for them to endure the pain of dubbing once, than to be constantly subject to pain through torn combs and wattles. And whilst I personally deplore anything in the nature of giving pain either to animals or birds, I do think—all points c nsidered -it is the beat plan to adopt with this breed of fowls. Still further if one might look at the most selfish side, they certainly look much smarter for it. I can hardly imagine on exhibition game cock with his comb on. Of course it is only the males that are dubbed. This, at least, may give some comfort to lady fanciers of the game fowl.

QI-ER I ES Constant Reader: Desires further information on mustard for poultry. He says that now the hard weather has gone, it seems useless continuing with mustard. This is an error. Fowls can stand a fair amount of cold providing it is dry. What they cannot stand are these wet, cold days. By all means con- tinue with the mustard and drop one feed of maize and substitute Canadian peas. Mustard will ward off the effects of the wet ground. What do you put your feet in mustard and water for ?

A REVIEW. During the week I have received a copy of the "Feathered World Year Bo " for 1012. The editor and staff are to be highly congratulated on so fine a production. To use a fancier's term, I should say " First special and cup ; stands clean away from anything else in the same class." I have still the same opinion cf last !year's wonderful book, hut I am forced to admit that this one, for 1912, " bangs" all previous efforts. It is wonderful ; it contains a mine of information. It appeals to the scientific as well as to the most practical mind. It is intensely concise and will aid the amateur and guide the older bands. Furthermore it is right up-to-date, for therein I actually find a splendid article on the new " Philo" system. This article, ably written by Mr. George Dent, should prove of immense value to the poultry industry. I strongly recommend all my readers to obtain a copy of the Year Book. If for nought else but to study this wonderful new system of intensive poultry culture. Then again, you are let into some of the scietific systems of breeding fancy stock, by. perusing Mr. W. Arkwright's very clear and convincing article cn " Ifendelism for pou try fancier's." The writer does not believe in keeping secrets up his sleeve, but rather, he gives you candidly of his valuable experience. It is a splendid contribution. So also is that by Mr. E. H. Turrell ou line breeding. It is carefully and studiously com- piled and calculated to be of great assistance to fancier and utilitarian alike. Want of space forces me to simply mention other useful contributions such as "A successful way to start a Poultry Farm," by N. D. Lane; "The Poultry Industry in South Africa" by E. Sheppard. and Helpful Hints to poultry

div.head: NOTES BY " WRIST."
div.p: NOTES BY " WRIST."

After all Warrington will make the long j limey into Yorkshire for the first round of the Cup Com- petition. The INormanton executive politely declined to consider Warrington's suggestion that the match should be played at Wihlerspcol. They prefer to take their chances at home—and thcse chances are not to be sneered at.

Warrington will have to fight hard to secure the victory. Any idea that because Normanton are a junior team they can be treated lightly, must be knocked on the bead at once. The Wakefield suburbanites have one of the strongest junior organisations in Yorkshire and are fully equal to the best "A" teams. They gave convincing evid- ence of their strength a year ago, when they entertained Broughton Rangers in the first round and only succumbed after a keen game by 10 points to 0. It was only superior goal-kicking that pulled the Rangers through. Both teams scored two tries. The fact that the Rangers subsequently won the Cup, is the best omen of the occasion from a Warrington point of view.

The fact has been impressed on the Wirepullers that they have no picnic before them, and every man is prepared to do his best. I have no fear of the result, for there is just a gleam of Warrington's Cup- tie form about their recent performances, and class should tell. The Normanton men have plenty of weight and strength—so a prominent referee says—but they are not great on the passing game. Warrington must rely on pace and combination (not kicking) to bring about the result.

Fortunately the Club is able to put the best side in the field. Woodburn comes in in place of Clare, who has not the fini,lt for senior engagements, and in other respects the team is the same as during the last two matches. So well have the forwards been playing that Arnold cannot get back. He is fist re,ierve and the full selection is : Mclntyre, full back ; Bradshaw, Renwick,Dickenson and Woodburn, threequarters ; Daitatith and Brooks, half-backs; Thomas, Shugars, Chesters, Tranter, Fearnley and Skelhorne, forwards.

A special train has been arranged to convey Warrington supporters to Normanton, leaving Arpley Station at 12 o'clock noon. The fare is only 3s. pd. so that the excursi n should prove attractive to a goodly number of enthusiasts.

Last Saturday Warrington gained their first victory of the New Year in unmistakable fashion at the expense af Runcorn. The Linnets scored a fortu- nate victory over Wariington on New Year's Day, and the locals were keen on revenge. Runcorn opened the scoring iu sensational fashion in the first minute but were afterwards over-played and outpointed to the tune of 18-0. Warrington's play was full of fire,and though Runcorn tackled in the deadliest fashion they could not prevent .their line being crossed on four occasions. Great praise is due to the Warrington for- wards, who held their own in the pack, and were very fast and clever in the loose.

Behind the pack also, Warrington were the superior side. Daintith and Brooks combined well together and give the men behind plenty of passes. Some of the combination was only second rate, but in the centre Penwick and Dickenson were capital. The latter played his finest game of the season, and showed a turn of speed that most people thought he had parted vith long ago. Dickenson and the cup-ties always remind me of the old war-horse and the scent of battle. He will be one of Warrington's best men at Normanton to-day.

The wings were both poor. Clare was out of his class, though he did nothing badly, and Bradshaw never seemed able to get ofl the mark quick enough to beat the defence. He was net at his best, or some of Renwick's openings would have been turned to better account. " Mac " played strongly at full hick, and is gradually overcoming the prejudice aroused in the minds of many supporters when Tilley was super- seded.

Runcorn are still a very active and determined side. Lack of weight all round handicaps them in the struggle for points, but few teams are quicker at snapping up an opening, or tackle with greater vigour and certainty. Padbury, the skipper, is not the forward he was a few years back, and displays too great a fondness for the fringe of the pack. Butterworth wears well, but is very slow, and the best of the younger brigade are the two Hoxworths, White, and Lewis. The latter played on the wing, but he is a half-back of promise and might repay Wairingion for some attention.

The " A" team to-day will entertain Pendleton in a friendly, and opportunity is being taken to give several junior players a trial. The selected thirteen are :—Brown, full back; Vernon, Butterworth (brother of the Runcorn player), Clare and Jackson; Blackburn (Oldham) ad Chester, half backs; Bradshaw, Boardman, Harmer, Critchley, Cooper and Clark, forwards.

div.head: Warrington Avenged on Runcorn.
div.p: Warrington Avenged on Runcorn.

Warrington gained their first victory for 1912 on Saturday, when they avenged the defeat sustained on New Year's Day. Beautiful weather favoured the fixture and there was a fair crowd of about 4,1,00. Both teams were representative and turned out as follows : Warrington—Mclntyre, back ; Bradshaw, Renwick, Dickenson and Clare, threequarter backs; Brooks and Daintith, half hacks; Thomas, Shugars, Chesters, Feanley, Tranter and Skelhorne, forwards. Runcorn—Shaw, back; Lewis, Ilutterworth,Stevenson and J W lloxworth, threequarter backs, J Bosworth and White, half backs; Peacock, Richardson, Inman, Donoghue, Williams and Pad bury, forwards. Referee, Mr J F May, St. Helens. Touch judges. Messrs J It Lawton, Oldham,and A Widdeson,Pendleton The start was sensational, for Warrington replied to Richardson's opening kick with a passing run on the left. Brook's pass to Clare was intercepted by Lewis who made Smart run before parting to Padbury, the latter scoring despite Mclntyre attempt to tackle. The goal-kick failed but the lead Runcorn had obtained was enough to spur Warriugton to their best endeavours. The forwards put in some fine work, and were backed up by Brooks, Dickenson and Clare, who ran and handled finely before the wing man was bowled in touch at the corner. The locals kept up the pressure, and there was great disappointment when Bradshaw failed to pr,fit by an opening made by Brookes. Padbury and White led the way back in smart style, but were cleverly robbed by Dickenson, who dodged through at centre and raced away with Clare in attendance. The lengthy centre ran finely, and near the line bluffed the defence with a sham pass to Clare and grounded for an excellent try. Mclntyre failed at goal. Runcorn now got busy on the attack again, and J W Bosworth ran smartly down touch until grassed by Renwick. The latter eased the pressure by fine football, and eventually gave Warrington the lead w ith a smart penalty goal. Warrington were now all over the Unneta, and after Dickenson had been beaten by an inch after a great effort, tbe ball was forced past Shaw, and Fearnley dribbled over from near half way, Renwick failed at goal, and Warrington crossed over, leading by 8 points to 3. The game had been of a very open nature, with Warrington showing marked ascendancy, and on resuming they again held the advantage. Renwick several times worked the ball across to Bradsbaw'a wing, but the latter was not always always well-placed and failed to escape the keen tackling of the Runcorn backs. Chesters and Shugars wera responsible for a vigorous attack on the left, which Lewis checked, but he was injured for his pains and was absent from the field of play for several minutes, Padbury meanwhile tilling the vacancy. After the visitors had successfully checked Bradshaw near the corner-flag, Daintith responded to an effective clearance by Stevenson, and the ball being worked across to the left, Renwick doubled between Bosworth and White and scored behind the posts, the same player improving upon the try. The game was waged for a long time well inside the R mcorn quarters, but near the close spirited play by the It ncorn forwards harassed Mclntyre, and eventually J. \V. Bosworth dribbled past the custodian to score near the corner. Only a minute now remained for play, but during that time Warring- ton made a hot raid, and following a desperate forward rush Skelhorne scored a try and Thomas added the goal. Result : Warrington, three goals four tries (18 points); Runcorn, two tries (six points).

div.head: EBBW VALE v. WIDNES.
div.p: EBBW VALE v. WIDNES.

- At Ebbw Vale, before a large attendance. Widnes set a hot pace in the first few minutes, and the borne defence was severely taxed. Laws scored for Widnes, and almost immediately afterwards Llewellyn scored an unconverted try for Ebbw Vale. The second half was hotly contested, O'Gara scoring for Widnes. Chick Jenkins (Ebbw Vale) end Johnson (Wienei) were ordered off. Result :—Widnes 2 tries (0 points), Ebbw Vale I try (3polnts).

div.head: AUSTRALASIANS.
div.p: THE AUSTRALASIANS.
THE CLOSE OF THE TOUR.

The Australasian team of Northern Union players left their headquarters at Southport on Sxturday on their return journey, and will spend a week in London before sailing for home. div.head: FREEDOM OF WIDNES.
div.p: FREEDOM OF WIDNES.

At a special meeting of the Widnes Tovn Council on Tuesday, it was unanimously decided to confer the freedom of the borough upon Mr. H. Wade Deacon, of Aigburth, Liverpool, and Major J. W. Wareing, of Mill Brow, Widnes. Mr. H. W. Deacon is the son of the late Mr. Henry Deacon, one of the founders of the chemical industry of South-west Lancashire. In 1892, and again in 1805, he unsuccessfully contested the %Vidnes Parliamentary division in the Liberal interest. Since 1878 be has been prominently associated with the educational affairs of Widne., and was one of the originators of a scheme for closely linking the local industries with technical instruction in the schools, a scheme which has won glowing tributes from prominent educationists. Mr. Deacon is an alderman of the Lancashire County Council and the chairman of the Finance Committee, . . _

Major Wareing retired recently from the position of alderman. He was the senior member of the Widnes Town Council, having been a member for forty years. He was Mayor of the borough in 1596-7-8, and chairman of the Prescot Board of Guardians in 1890.

div.head: SIR HARRY VERNEY.
div.p: SIR HARRY VERNEY.

Sir Harry Verney, who moved the Address in reply to the King's Speech in the Commons, probably owed his selection for the task t) the fact that be is a private secretary to the Chief Secretary for Ireland. Sir Harry is the fourth Baronet, and succeeded his father, Sir Edmund Verney, in 1010. Ile represents the Northern Divisioa of Buckinghamshire—a county with which his family has been connected for centuries.

div.head: TARIFF REFORMERS' INCONSISTENCIES.
div.p: TARIFF REFORMERS' INCONSISTENCIES.
THE DUMPING EXHIBITION. CRITICISMS BY MR, P. M. OLIVER AND COUNCILLOR ROBERTS.

Mr. P. M. Oliver, prospective Liberal candidate for the Knutsford Division, made his first appearance before the electors of Stockton Heath on Monday evening, when a largely-attended meeting vas held in the Hall Cafe. Mr. J. Lonaland presided, and was supported on the plafotin by Councillor H. Roberts, Mr. E. Lloyd-Jones, Mr. H. G. Roberts, Mr. W. H. Sherburn, Mr. J. R. Tomlinson, and Miss Duckworth. The Chairman said it wool I hearten the Liberals of the Division to know that they had a candidate to work for. (Applause.) Judging from the events of the past week or two it was essential that they should be alive in their work for Liberalism. Nhen the enemy tried to prevent freedom of speech—one of the oldest principles for which Liberalism stood—it was time they furbished up their weapons and did their utmost to safeguard those liberties to which all Britons claimed to be entitled. It was no use having clipped the wings of the House of Lords or introducing progressive measures, if they did not also secure the right to voice their opinions upon the measures as they were presented to them, (Applause). Mr. P. M Oliver, who had a good reception, said
AN .A.12-TI-ST-OCHATIC LADY -NIYIIO LIVED IN THE NEIGHBOURHOOD

had given it as her rirte-nTown-t-o-ViCk all Radicals out of Warrington. (Laughter). Perhaps she had not pro- ceeded to Stockton Heath vet-(laughter)-or if she h id,she bad not been successful in her object. (Laughter). Their Conservative friends did not thiak it possible to argue in this part of the country unless they engaged in some sort of whirlwind campaign. Therefore in War- rington they had been favoured with a dumping exhibition in which they were shown all kinds of foreign goods-a sort of conglomerate exhibition or bazaar of Babel. (Laughter). Not only did they dump foreign goods; they seemed to have dumprd t'aeir politicians too, and ALL THE BRIGHTEST STARS IS; THE TARIFF FIRMAMENT

_ had been twinkling in Warrington. (Laughter.) One was inclined to ask wlat was the significance of all that sound and fury? The first fact that struck one was that we in England were the greatest dumpers, by a long way, in the whole world. (Hear, hear). We dumped £100,000,000 worth of manufactured goods more than Germany dumped and .C 200,000,000 more than France dumped. He wished Tariff Reformers would talk a little more of the success of our trade than the success of our competitors' trade. The statistics showed that German trade was insreasing with the various nations which lay immediately at her el)ors,—which was natural in view of the ease with which goods could be transported—but, when she went further afield, it was impossible for her to maintain anything like com- petition with Free Trade England. (Applause). Another interesting fact was that into practically all Protectionist countries more manufactured goods were entering than ever before. There were only two countries which were importing fewer manufactured art'cles than they did ten years ago—ltu:sla and Spain. The whole of CIVILIZED AND SCIENTIFIC PROGRESS had been aimed at the gradual linking together of one country and another. the gradual inclease of foreign trade and the glorification of du-aping which their Protectionist friends were attempting to squash. The more civilized we became and the more cooperative we became. The more we dumped and the better it would be for us. It was in the march of events that nations should draw closer together and trade more and more with one another. If we wanted to go in for a real system of Protectjon the bet thing to do was to scrap all our ships, cut all our cables and dam up the Manchester Ship Canal. (Laughter.) Then we should have a system of absolute and complete Protection and no doubt vr e should be very much happier for it. (Laughter.) Mr. Oliver next pointed out that dumped goods were paid for, not by gold but by exports and services. It was sad that after some five or six years one had to repeat that economic argument but so long as Mr. Harold Smith, Mr. George Wyndham and other tariff stars went on twinkling— (laughter)—it would be necessary to answer them with simple facts. He could not understand whether it was logic or common honesty that those tariff reformers lacked. Not only their tariff reform journals, but their I onn leader Mr. Bonar Low, had been perfectly ready to admit that the economic arguments of Free Traders were sound and incontrovertible—that everything we brought into this country had to be paid for by goods or services. If we prevented imports coming into this country, we inevitably prevented exports going out. The dumping exhibition was about the best argument for Free Trade that anybody could have. The visitors to it must see clearly that, taken as a whole, the goods we made in England were INFINITELY SUPERIOR to those produced abroad. Protection was a set back to civilization, for if we excluded certain cheap goods from abroad—the speaker instanced knives and forks and boots—it did not follow that the poor man would be able to buy them equally cheaply from the home manufacturer and he would therefore have to do with- out them. Although Liberals had •to defend Free Trade—and be was afra:d that for some time to come they would have to defend it,until they finally conquered —they did not blind themselves to the fact that every- thing was not for the best in the test of all possible worlds. What they did maintain was that under Free Trade wages were higher here than they were anywhere else, excepting the United Stater,and food was cheaper. It was a brave thing for Sir Henry Campbell- Bannerman to declare that there were 12.000,000 people in this country on the verge of starvation, because the statement lent itself to abuse and misconception. He meant that if any sickness or accident happened to those people, they would in a few weeks, or less, find themselves starving. It bad been the policy of the Liberal party while maintaining Free Trade gradually to withdraw those 12,000,000 from the verge of hunger. They had been doing it consistently and successfully. They withdrew 1,900,003 of them by the Old Age Pensions Act—(apt.lause)—and now they were withdrawing 8,000,000 or 10,000,000 by the National Insurance Act. (Applause.) He admitted that there were little inequalities and difficulties in the latter measure which time alone would show and remedy. Mr. Oliver then explained several points and said the Act was not merely a measure of insurance but also for the

PREVENTION AND CURE OF SICKNESS. Having enlarged upon the medical clauses, he said that if it were only for the great effort that would be made to stamp out, consumption the Act was worth placing on the statute b-ok. (Applause.) Under the Act there would arise a tremendous sum of money which would have to be invested. That fund, so far as it was made up of the contributions of the employer, was in the bands of the Government for investment, and the first purpose for which it !would be employed was the floating of loans for the better housing of the working classes. (Applause.) The Act would also be a spur and incentive to local authorities to use their power with regard to housing, because if excessive sickness could be traced to their neglect in that direction they would be respons- ible for the insurance benefit. The saille would apply to the employer who, through failing to keep his workshop in proper condition, caused excessive sickness to a workmsnAttiThe Act would do much to arouse interest in health questions. The insurance scheme

div.head: MR. W. G. C. GLADSTONE.
div.p: MR. W. G. C. GLADSTONE.

It is appropriate that Mr. W. G. (3. Gladstone should play a prominent part in the opening of a session which is to see Liberalism's third attempt to settle the Irish problem by means of a Home Rule Bill. He is a grandson of the great stites- man who twice failed to carry Home Rule. Mr. Gladstone only entered Parliament last year at a bye-election, when he held Kirmarnock Burghs fa- the Liberals. He seconded the Address.

had bad that effect in Germany and it would do the same here because it would make health a national question and a national need and show us that we had to defend ourselves not only against the enemy with- out but against the still more dreaded enemy within. (Applause.) Councillor H. Roberts then addressed the meeting. He said the one question in regard to which there had been more misrepresentation and ignorance than any other was the Insurance Act. When the measure was introduced in the House of Commons it was blessed by the Tory party, but it had been cursed up hill and down dale by them every day since. That was the kind of thing the Tory party gave us when they Came into the political arena. As individuals and collectively as citizens, they were very good fellows and very pleasant men to know.but as politicians he would rather not attempt to describe what they were. (Laughter.) The Liberals of the Knutsford division were extremely fortunate in having as their candidate a man who was capable of enunciating Liberal principles in a manner worthy of those principles and a man ,t% ho by his lucidity and eloquence of speech was bound to carry conviction. (Applause.) The

TORIES WERE DOING A GREAT DEAL or CROWING just now. He saw a picture in the " Warrington Observer," the other day of Mr. Boner Law clad in mediteval armour—a very suitable kind of armour for a Conservative—(laughter)—monnted on a horse, also in armour, while a band played " See the conquering hero comes;' There was an old Scriptural injunction "Let him that puttath on the armour boast not as him that putteth it oft " and it would be time enough for the Conservative party to crow about the result of the next election when they had won it. He had yet to be convinced that the working class party of this country—the labour party if they liked to call it that—was composed in the main of such arrant fools as to be prepared to bite off their noses to spite their faces. (Laughter.) They could not bring about the economic and social legisla- tion of the kind they wanted without the aid of the Liberal party. It was no use going to the Tory party for it, and he believed that the commonsense with which every workingman was more or less gifted would prevail and that when the testing time came, Liberalism and Labour would be found again walking shoulder to shoulder to the polls, with a result that would satisfy them all. (Applause). Alluding to the dumping exhibition, Councillor Roberts said the worthy

PRESIDENT OF THE CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION, in a moment of exhilaration at the end of the show, made a statement to the effect that they were going to smash every Free Trader in Warrington. He sincerely hoped that Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall would live long enough to see not only their children's children, but their great grand-children—and if they thought it would be kinder to them, even a generation longer than that. (Laughter.) Liberals had no personal feel- ing but the kindliest towards thos3 very worthy people and they wished them well. But Sir Gilbert and Lady Greensll would have to live a great deal longer than that before they saw the time when Free Traders were all smashed in Warrington. (Laughter and Applause.) He was satisfied that the DUMPING EXHIBITION HAD DONE MORE FOR THE CAUSE OF FREE TRADE

in Warrington and the immediate district than anything which had happened for a considerable time. (Hear hear.) When the promoters had to bang the big drum and have a bugle band,an imitation boys' brigade,some- what soiled Union Jacks—(laughter)—cheap teas and refreshments, and free concerts, it reminded him more of a circus than of an exhibition. (Laughter.) lie did not go to the exhibition—he had no time to spare for a thing like that—but he had heard of sorm of the things that were exhibited. Mr. Oliver'l description was perfectly correct. whey got togethei the very worst specimens of foreign manufactures that they possibly could, forgetting that people might ask: "What is the price paid for making those things ?" and "If we are going to keep them out, so are we going to substitute articles of a similar kind of British manu- facture, and are we going to pay our men the Same wages for making them as the worker abroad r They had

- THE AUDACITY TO SHOW GERMAN WIRE The quantity of German wire that curie into Warring- ton could be put in anyone of their eyes —4laughter)—but would be a bad joh for the wire trade in Warrington if the importation of German rods and other things of German manufacture which were raw material for some of the principal works of the town, were stopped. If they began to dabble with the question of Protection, the difficulty was not only where they were going to begin, but where they were going to end. What was a a man's raw material and what was the finished article? The rod that came from Germany was the raw material of the wiredrawer in Warrington,but it was the finished article of the German. If they put a tax on the German rod, they increased the price of the wire drawn from that rod and thus put the local manufacturer in a more difficult position to compete with the foreign manufac- turer abroad. (Applause).

MR. HAROLD SMITH had told them with emphasis that ho would never be a party to doing anything which would tax the food of the workingman. Neither Mr. Smith nor any member of the Conservative party, once they attempted to put a protective duty on, could help making the food of the workingman dearer for this reason : If they began with Protection, they had to begin with the principal industries of the country. They were not going to have Protection to preserve the little halfpenny concerns that were h trdly worth keeping going at ell. It was the big industries that were to he protected, and which was the greatest industry of the lot ? The agricultural industry—the industry which gave them their food, meat, corn, bread and so forth. That was the industry, above all others which would be powerful and strong enough, to demand Protection. if it were protected to the slightest possible extent, it must be PROTECTED AT THE EXPENSE OE THE FOOD OF THE

PEOPLE of this country. " What strikes me about the tariff reformers " continued Councillor Roberts "is their absolute disloyalty to their own convictions. I guarantee to say that, in regard to every household represented amongst the ladies and gentlemen who took part in that show, that if an expert could see through those households ha would find plenty of evidence that foreign materiil of one kind or another had helped to decorate, to furnish or to make comfortable the houses of those very tariff reformers, (Hear, hear.) If those tariff reformers are really honest and in earnest they could, by passing A SELF-DENYING ORDINANCE, put a tremendous check on the importation of foreign goods. Why don't they say' We will not buy or use a single article of foreign manufacture until things are different ?' They could do a tremendous lot in favour of their policy if they cared to attempt it, or rather it would not be in favour of their pplicy in its results but it would show they were honest in their convictions and meant to carry them out. When we find them

GIVING CLOCKS to get people to came to a place, and prizei at bowling green performances, whist drives and all that kind of thing, the origin of which they would prefer we did not inquire into—(laughter)—is it loot a little inconsistent ? I say I will believe in a tariff reformer when he carries out in his own business and private life, so far as his purchases are concerned, the principles he professes to believe in' and I won't believe in him until he does." (Applause.) Councillor Roberts next alluded to the Conservative party's lack of constructive policy, to Mr. Bonar Law's financial inaccuracies, and to Mr. Lloyd George's method of placing taxation oa the shoulders cf those able to bear it.. Referring to the question of National defence, Councillor Roberts said we had been spending money on ships—he thought too lavishly. The time had come when by some kind of negotiation with the only power of which we seemed to be afraid— Germany—we might at least have arrived at an agree- ment to stop at a clrtain point and not waste any more money on unnecessary armaments. At the same time, Liberals and Tories alike believed that the naval supremacy of this country must be maintained at any

cost. With regard to Home Rule, they had recently had an exhibition in Belfast which was more discredit- able to the leaders of the Unionist party in that city than anything which had happened in the annals of political history, that he could reruember. In a lesser degree, but quite as disgraceful was the attack of the young Tory bloods some years ago on Mr. Gladstone in the House of Commons. The Ulster Unionists had been " top dogs" so long that while they claimed equality of privilege with the rest of the United Kingdom they absolutely denied it to anyone who differed from them. The result of the Belfast incidents bad beers& distinct advance of the question of Home Rule in the minds of thoughtful men, He (the speaker) believed sincerely that if there were an opportunity for the Conservative party to return to power to-morrow, they would be

PERFECTLY WILLING TO CONCEDE HOME RULE and they would not hesitate about it. (Applause.) The question was going to be settled very shortly. (Hear, hear., The country was sick and tired of bearing what it had hoard so often and it was beginning to recognize that it was due to the sentiment of the Irish people that the concession of self-government should be made to them. (Applause.) Mr. IV. H. Sherhurn, in moving a vote of thanks to the speakers, said the Tory party must be in very sore I straits when they had to resort to such tactics as they I had recently indulged in. Some of the better Con- servatives had almost hidden their beads in shame at what had been done in their name during the past few years. Progressives were eagerly looking forward to the promised Electoral Reform Bill which would allow every man one vote and no man fifteen or twenty. (Applause), Mr E. Lloyd Jones seconded and said it was impossible for the Liberals of Stockton Heath to go wrong politically so long as they had Councillor Roberts to lead them. (Applause). The vote was supported by Mr. Tomlinson ard heartily passed.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
"The Bad Girl of the Family."

The sccond visit of the company performing Mr. Frederick Melville's thorough-going melodrama has drawn large audiences during the week, and has shown that "the bad girl " when rightly understood has both a lesson to teach and many admirers of the sterling points of her character. The cast is in capable hands down to the most subordinate character, and with numerous and rapidly accomplished changes of szenery the ploy runs its leagth in busy action and incident in such a way as to keep one continuously interested if not exactly edified. Miss Florrie Kelsey's impersonation of Bess Moore, the bad girl, is a piece of acting worthy of admiration in its truthfulness to life as many of u., alas, know it, while the affliction and misfortunes of Gladys Erskine are finely portrayed by Miss Morie Duncan. The Sally Smithers of Miss Gertrude Jones is by no means an easy part, yet it is well done and the boisterous fun that is got out of it greatly relieves the more serious portions of the play. The dormitory scene in which Bess, Sally and the other shop girls in the employ of Betry and Robertson engage in a mirth-provoking conflict with the police. proved quite a realistic piece of " bu,ioess and greatly amused the audience. Mr. Barnett Lando and Mr. Charles Yorke impersonated the rascally parts of the Cordons—father and son—with great success which is of course measured in an inverse ratio to the acclamation they receive at recalls before the curtain, while the two characters of Lord Erskine and Lieutenant Marsh are in the quite able hands of Mr. Stanley Marsh and Mr. St. John who, by dint of clever acting, get out of their parts all the essential and vital points There are many very striking stage pictures in the play—the marriages in the church and in the prison—the attempted robbery at the hall, and the interior of Dartmoor gaol—involving severe tasks for the stage carpenter and the scenic artist which are overcome in a most praiseworthy manner. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. " FITZ," TIIE PUGILISTIC KANGAROO. Fitz," Australia's Champion Boxing Kangaroo, is to top the bill at the Hippodrome the coming week. After the glowing accounts we have heard from his press representative we have no hesitation in predicting his appearance in Warrington will cause no little sensation. The boxing Kangaroo in ques— tion is now on his first nur through England, though he has been boxing in public for three consecutive seasons at the leading Music Halls of America with immense success. " F,tz " is classified by the variety managers in the U.S.A. as one of the biggest b.-,a-ciffice magnets.
CAME,,L

The kangaroo in question is a fine, noble, usually good-natured animal, and seems to take great delight in displaying his boxing propensities before an audience. He engages in a three-round contest upon each occas'on with Pro!essor Tully, and it never fails to elicit the admiration and applause of all present. The knock-out blow usually comes in the third round, and when " Fitz " is proclaimed the victor, " Australia's " admirers are generally loud in their demonstration. The first Boxing Klngaroo known to the British public appeared in the Royal Aquarium, Westminster, London, in 1892, where for slx consecu- tive months it proved one of the biggest sensations of the period. Fitz must be seen, for his almost hunna cleverness to be believed.

Following on the Royal OH LAW! opening of the new Session of Parliament on Wednesday, and the blaring of trumpets and the splendour of pageantry and the KING'S Speech and the moving of the address to the Throne in both Houses, there was something more extraordinary and astounding than anything else, and that was the speech made by the LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION, Mr. BONAR LAW has in an exceedingly short time climbed to a peculiar distinction. He has not been leading the not very numerous forces that are opposed to the Government for more than a few months; but in that time he has received a more crushing rebuff than it has been necessary for any preceding Leader of the -Opposition to encounter. He had made a speech in the face of the whole country, every statement of which has not only been refuted point by point, but with ignominy. "All the world wondered," says TENNYSON, of the charge of the Light Brigade, All the world has been wondering for some weeks past what Mr. BONAR LAW could possibly have to say about the tremendous smashing that has been given to his speech at the Albert Hall. It now appears that he has nothing to say,and up to this point we admit that his position is quite intelligible. When a person who is not too scrupulous on the point of honour has said things that he cannot sustain his best policy beyond all question is absolute silence on the subject. But Mr. BONAR LAW is, it seems clear,not that sort sort of man at all. He main- tains silence as to the charges that he cannot maintain; but at once proceeds to make more charges of the same kind. In the interests of the more noble part of English public life we protest. Take from his speech one example of its general tone and temper. He said that when the fight in the Cabinet is over the PRIME MINISTER would perhaps tell the House what, etc., etc, He is aware, of course,that there is no fight in the Cabinet. He was placing himself at the back Of impudent and baseless statements made in the newspapers of his party. Mr. ASQUITH asked him to make his charge more specific, and the reply was that no charge had been made. All that is necessary, though it is far from all that it would be possible to say on this, is that a party leader who takes these views of controversies which involve great national interests seriously lowers the reputation of his party. It is satisfactory to be able to say that Mr. ASQUITH paid a very small amount of attention to Mr. BONAR LAW. The bulk of his speech . was devoted to really series affairs. He said words that must put an end alike in this country and on the other side of the North Sea, to any notion that we are seeking for anything but friendly relations with Germany. He spoke in the tones of high statesmanship about the various ques- tions that will confront, the Parliament which has just returned to its work. He was, as always, a serious, wonderfully clear- minded man, confronting serious problems. One question he put to Mr. BONAR LAW very directly, and we ask the country to take note of the answer. He asked whether the Opposition, when it cohles into power, will propose the repeal of the Insur- ance Act. "Certainly," said Mr. BONAR LAW His hasty reply commits the Tory Party to a course of action which they have not the slightest intention of following, and the chorus of dismay from Unionist newspapers the following morning was comically pathetic. The new leader has given them the worst possible lead, and another series of blunders such as he has been guilty of in the past few weeks will result in frantic appeals to Mr. BALFOUR to come back. The latter must be enjoying his daily paper more than his golf these days !
Mr. Autfirey ViThite

MR. AUBREY seems to think it rather WHITE'S HUMOUR. rude of us to dub him a humorist. But if we said he was not a humorist,we do not see that it would help very much to soften the blow to his amour propre. His letter, in another column, indicates a determined effort on his part to , " be funny" ; and as a rule when one tells such a man that he is a humorist he is flattered. Not so Mr. White. When he is funniest to the casual observer he is really meaning to be most serious, which is unfor- tunate for him, and must lead to a lot of misunderstanding. Mr. White thinks we might apologise for calling him a humorist, but we would rather fight a duel in the French st3fle. It would be more in keeping with the circumstances.
On the closing day of LADY GREENALL the Dump Exhibition
AND THE CLOCKS. Lady Greenall threw

out a challenge to Liberals to dispute any of the statements of Tariff Reformers concerning a single article "in this hall." In our issue of the 3rd we asked her Ladyship: If it is a fact, or not, that certain clocks presented as prizes to holders of discs in con- nection with the exhibition were of foreign manufacture ?

So far we have not received any answer to the question, though it was a distinct accept- ance of Lady Greenall's challenge. We are informed on reliable authority—and there seems to be not the slightest doubt of the fact—that the clocks presented as prizes by Lady Greenall herself were foreign clocks. They may have been purchased in Warring- ton, but they were made abroad and, to use the Tariff Reform description, were "dumped" into this country to compete with the products of the English clockmakers. Now it does seem to us a matter requiring some explanation if prizes given by the promoters of an exhibition to illustrate the "evils" of dumping, are "dumped" goods themselves.
Mr. Harold Smith,M.P., THE MEMBER "IN seems to have been in FORM." fine form at the meet-

ing of the Conservative Association on Tuesday evening. He made any number of inaccurate statements—some of them wilfully—and heaped vulgar abuse on the Government in general and Mr. Lloyd / George in particular. The latter, he said, was trying to " jockey " Mr. Asquith out of his seat ; "he had done his best not to advance the interests of our great Empire, but first his own personal interest ; " he had uttered " untruthful misrepresentations " ; his land taxes were "fraudulent," and so on, ad nauseam. It is a great pity that Mr. Harold Smith shouldifall so far short of a gentlemanly standard in his criticisms. His immediate predecessors in the representation of the old borough were always careful to observe the canons of good taste in their controversial methods, and one notes the change to-day with regret. For reasons of expediency alone, Mr. Smith should avoid charging Ministers of the Crown with the uttering of" untruthful misrepresentations," unless he is better prepared than his leader, Mr. Bonar Law, to back up his statement with proof. On several occasions he has stated in Warring- ton that the collection of the land taxes cost over £500,000, and that they brought in only £20,000. He repeated this gross untruth on Tuesday, notwithstanding the fact—with which he must be perfectly familiar—that the Chancellor of the Exchequer gave it a categorical denial at the Albert Hall a fort- night ago. Mr. Bonar Law was then the guilty party, and in reply to the Tory leader, Mr. Lloyd George said : "What did we collect the first year? Not £20,000. We collected the first year £327,ooo—sixteen times more than he said. A trifling error! Cost of collec- tion—not half a million—but £16,000! Another trifling error!" . _

And these" trifling errors" Mr. Smith persists in repeating. If he has any respect for honesty in politics he will either attempt to controvert the Chancellor's state- ment or refrain from uttering deliberately a base perversion of fact.

The Education Corn- EDUCATION RATE mittee's estimates have RisING. come to be regarded as a sort of harbinger of the burdens which the ratepayer will be called upon to bear during the year, for the I extent of this department's demand largely determines whether the borough rates advance or fall. Gloomy forebodings will therefore be awakened by the estimates to be submitted for the approval of the Educa- tion Committee on Monday. The expendi- ture of the committee shows an ever-upward tendency and the new call will be a substantial increase upon that for the year just ending, which amounted to is. 6ld. in the £. The total estimated deficiency comes to £24,571 175., as against £21,756 17s. for 1911-12. Last year the • committee, in order to soften the blow as much as possible, decided to take over £l,OOO from the working balance raised to I meet contingencies, leaving a sum of £20,500 ' to be provided from the borough rate. This year it is considered that £571 is the utmost amount by which the working balance may, with prudence, be depleted, and the demand upon the rates will therefore amount to £24,000. The consequence is a rise in the rate for educational purposes of between 3d. and 4d. in the £, according to the new valuation of the borough. The causes of lie advance are not far to seek. Elementary school teachers' salaries will absorb £32,290 as compared with £31,245 but it should be explained that £6OOl of this will be set aside for the staffing of the new boys' department at the Evelyn- street Council school. The automatic increases in salaries therefore account for only about £4OO. Another heavy item is £3,045 for interest and instalments on loans in respect of the new elementary schools, which last year accounted for £2,056 19s. 6d. The outfit of apparatus &c. for Evelyn-street school will cost £255. There is an entirely new item of £2OO for "professional services in respect of the supervision of school build- ings, &c.,'' but this will probably be a matter of adjustment between various Corporation departments. An additional outlay of £l9O will be entailed by the opening of the dental clinic. Rates and taxes are £344 ahead of last year, this being due to a re-assessment of Council schools. On the receipt side, the annual grants for elementary education are down to the extent of £5O, in consequence of the sickness which made such inroads on the attendance last year. The receipts from customs and excise—familiarly termed "whisky money "—will yield £876 as against £603. Lest temperance reformers should think, at first sight, that this indicates an increased consumption of spirits, it should be explained that the change is occasioned by the placingof the grant upon a fixed basis—a much more satisfactory arrangement than the repeated fluctuations with the changing habits of the community.

The discovery of mares THE LATEST ABOUT nests is a favourite "DUMPING." pursuit of our Pro-

-tectionists. After 5 period of discreet silence over the prosperitY of our trade, they now pretend to have found out that all this prosperity and progress is a delusion! The 1911 trade returns show,theY say, that we imported less raw material and more partly manufactured goods, therebY giving less work to our people and encourag- ing "dumping." It is quite true that ill some small classes of raw material the quan- tities imported in 1911 were less than ill 1910, but it is far from being true generally. Cotton, for instance,is an impor- tant exception. But the diminution is easily accounted for by the fact that, generally speaking, there was a considerable accumulation of stocks 1910, compared with 1909. It is impossible to know how much material is actually used in the country in any one year, for there is no such thing as a national stocktaking. All the evidence proves that there was greater trade activitY in 1911 than in the previous year, or in manY previous years. Indeed, the very fact that we are using less purely 'raw material and importing more partly manufactured goods suggests that labour is being transferred from the less remunerative industrial processes to the more highly remunerative. Lastly, it is in itself sufficient to discredit the false alarms of the Tariff Reformers to say that general unemployment was less ia 1911 than since the war year of 1900, a fact which is not only demonstrable by official statistics, but by even most casual observa- tion of industrial conditions all over the country.
