Crosfield demonstrated a propheb° vision in regard to the visit of Mr. Haldane to Germany that week. He said: "It would be nothing less than deplorable 0 Lord Haldane returned to England without scale progress having been made in the right directiee without the way being cleared towards 14 permanent understanding with Germany, 901 far better feeling between the German nation ay' ourselves, based as it should be on sal° substantial measure of cencurtence in the policie° of the two Governments." How well informed Mr. Crosfield was, 1135 been proved by the nature of the despatcbes from Berlin in the early part of this week. * *

There seems to be an ever-widenini tendency to deprecate or prohibit corpure punishment in the schools, and the Cheshire,' Education Committee has this week adopte,l new regulations with a view, to "reducing forms of punishment to a minimum." are quite unable to bring ourselveg into line with this most modero of educational developments. Human nature' we suppose, is pretty much what it was say, Torn Brown's school-days; boys Ncl be boys, and girls will be girls, which meaUg that one or the other needs strong discir linary measures at times. There i 9; undoubtedly, less possibility of brute' administration now than ever there wag ; the teaching profession stands higher than., ever it did before; and we see little reason f,e' taking the stick out of the hands of te properly-appointed, responsible, and supervised masters. Are we all not danger of becoming too sentimental?

* * Mr. Crosfield sent a striking letter to meeting organised by the Progressive Labow League in support of the National Insurance, Act. He did not confine himself to a defencl' of that measure but rendered another useni service by exposing a glaring inaccurael in Mr. Wyndham's speech at Warringtc° with reference to the extent of unemPlq,„; ment in this country. Quoting from IPt " Labour Gazettes' returns he shows tb% the number of workingmen clamouring It vain for the "lowest form of employmentfr. pitiful wages" was nothing like as high al Wyndham made it out to be, and, as Crosfield says, tariff reformers must indeee be in a desperate plight when they 11131,c, themselves responsible for such exlr-- ordinary mis-statements.

Mr, A. H. Crosfield had a fine reception I from the Junior Liberals on Saturday and in a speech of exceptional interest he referred to the all-important questions of Home Rule and Protection. By telling illustrations from history he showed how tho gloomy Predictions of fearful reactionaries or noisy factions have been repeatedly falsified bY the success of Liberal measures of reform and.he Arisely urged thoughtful politicians In disregard the clamour of those who, by ‘al3Pealing to prejudice and bitterness, would clePrive Ireland still longer of the rights of self-goverment. In a convincing argu- ment against Protection Mr. Crosfield brought forward a most damaging array of quotations from the speeches of eminent 'C, o.nservatives who denounced Mr. Chamber- lain's proposals not only on domestic and IniPerial grounds, but because they would Inevitably lead to that corruption of our IMblic life of which Mr. Bonar Law professes 'such a wholesome dread.

Salvation Army. Brigadier Llewellyn Williams, of London, led impressive and successful services in the Hippodrome on Snnday. He was most enthusiastically supported by the local Salvation Army Band, under Bandmaster Lee, also by the local commanding officers (Adjutant and Mrs. Coutts. These popular services created great local interest, and many townspeople availed them- selves of this opportunity of hearing this renowned Evangelist, who with his wife is announced to deliver three striking subjec.s for this coming Sunday in the Grand Picture Theatre, Bridge Foot, at 11 a.m., 8 p.m., and 630 p.m. The Stockton Heath Wesleyan Prize Choir will render a special musical programmel in this theatre at 8 30 p.m. for church-goers and others, and it is expected that many will avail themselves of these special and attractive services. At the ant.ual meeting of the Library Association (North Western Branch), which was held at Man- chester on the 9th inst., Mr. Charles Madeley (Director of the Warrington Municipal Museum), was elected president for the coming year, in succession to Mr. Sutton (Chief Librarian of the Manchester Public Libraries). —The branch, which includes representa- tives of practically all the public libraries in Lanca- shire and Cheshire, was formed at M. Madeley's suggestion in 1896, and he held the position of honorary secretary for the first eight 3ears of its existence. div.head: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.
div.p: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.

Saturday last was an ideal day for the sport, and conducive to good musters. Rylands W.R.C.H. visited St Helens Rens and took part in a three-cornered race with St. Helens Parish Church, with the following result :—ltylands : Harding, 4 ; Thornley, 5 ; Woods, 6 ; Burton, : Warburton, 10 ; Whitmore. 12-45 points. St. Helens Recs : Swift, 1 ; Marsh, 7 ; Tones, ; Murray, 13 ; Latham, 14 ; Atalie, 19— 65 points. St. Helens P.C. : Atherton, 2 ; Heaton, 3; Fairclough, 9 ; Bright, 15 ; Mach, 16 ; Skidmore, 20-65 points. The trail extended for about eight miles, and the racing in a field of GO runners was keen all the way, with Swift of the home team setting a strong pace and maintaining the lead to the finish. Rylands showed improved form and won hand- somely by 20 points from the others who tied for second place. Harding earned useful points in the competition, and J Thornily won the medal for the first novice home of the "Royal Blues," who are now seeking fresh fields to conquer. Porhaps they will find an opportunity in the novice team race of the St. Helens C.C.A. in a few week's time. Warrington A.C. had a nice muster for a grand run over about 91 miles and H Holbrook, C Vote, W Bolton, A Siddall, W Antrobus. J Parsonage and H K Jepson moved in good style. The junior section covered about six miles with J Livesey and W Walters showing up well all the way. The West Lancashire C.C.A. decided on Thursday evening that Warrington A.C. and Ravenhead be joint champions, that medals of equal value be awarded and that the clubs hold the " Courier " and Express Trophy for six monts each so that the tie made at Knowsley Park a fortnight ago in the Junior Championship will not be "run oft" in the Northern to-diy as was at one time considered likely.o Thompson of Liverpool Boundary was cautioned to exercise greater care in future races as his inadvertent action of passing the judg.s in the closing stages of the Junior race had caused his name before the error was rectified to be published in the press reports as having finished in the sixth position, this correction permits A Gardner, Lancaster Park to take part in to-days race. Warrington A.C. leave Bank Quay Station at 10.40 turn to-day for Wakefield and are very hopeful of making a good show in both of the Northerd Championship races, Hallamshire are booked a certainty but West Lanca- shire runners will make them move.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH LICENSING SESSIONS.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH LICENSING SESSIONS.

The licensing sessions for the Daresbury Division were held on Tuesday at Stockton Heath, the magis- trates present being Messrs J Charlton Parr (in the chair), J Hepherd, Roger C Parr, H Roberts, G Dakin, F W Monks, W Fletcher and A H Talbot.—Superin- tendent Ennion, in his annual report, stated that there were 23 licensed houses in the district, giving an average of 500 for each licence. He had been directed ,by the Chief Constable to draw the attention of the Licenslnz Justices to Section 12 of the Licensing Consolidation Act, 1910, and respectfully request that the Licensing Justices would consider the advisability of requiring plans of on-licensed houses to be deposited with their Clerk, such plans to show the whole of the premises. If such plans were available for ready reference there was no doubt considerable inconvenience would be avoided, especiallywhen applications for alterations or additions to licensed preunses were made.—The Chairman said the fact that no licensees had been proceeded against was a satisfactory feature of thefl report.— The 'Magistrates Clerk said that in most of the other divisions in Cheshire, the same recommendations had been considered by the licensing benches and in most of the cases they had decided there was no necessity to put the owner to the expense of plans for anylhouse but that if application was made for alterations or additions in the future the l plans should be then deposited.—The Bench agreed to the Clerk's suggestion. —All the existing licences were renewed.

div.head: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
The Headmastership of Evelyn-street School.

The Education Committee will meet on Monday. The minutes of the Sites and Buildings Committee contain the following :—lt having been reported that the Education Committee at their last meeting had not approved the resolution of this Committee with reference to the appointment of a headmaster of the boys' department of the Evelsn-street Council school, it was, after some discussion, resolved that applications be invited from male certificated teachers who have served or are now serving Ecbools within the County Borough of Warrington for the post of Head Master of the Boys' department of the Evelyn-street Council school, the commencing salary for the position to be at the rate of £250 per annum up to the 31st March, 1913, and to be increased or reduced after that date, in accordance with the Com- mittee's scale of salaries, upon the average attendance of the department during that period; that all appli- cants be warned that canvassing members of the Education Committee, either directly or through friends or third persons, will be considered a dicqualification ; and that the appointment be made by this Committee. POST OF CARETAKER. The applications which had been received for the post of caretaker of the Evelyn-street Council school were referred to a Sub-committee, comisting of Alderman D. Tinnion, Councillors T. Birtles and J. Wilkinson and the Chairman of the committee (Hr. Alfred J. Jolley). TRACKERS' SALARIES. The School Management Committee have reaffirmed their resolution that the salaries for teachers in the public elementary schools in the Borough, which was adopted by the committee at the meeting on the 24th May, 1906, be amended as follows, viz. :—The portion of condition 4 on page sof the scele which deals with the annual increments for teachers serving in classes C and F to be so altered as to provide for the rate of increase to be £5 per annum, and, after 9 increases, £lO per annum, instead of £5 per annum throughout as at resent.

div.head: WARRINGTON CHURCH SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON CHURCH SOCIETY.
The Rector on Disestablishment and
Christian Unity.

There was a large attendance at the anneal cm• versazione in connection with the Warrington Church Society which was held in St. Paul's School,liendrick- street. on Teursday evening. The Rector (Rev. Canon Willis), president of the S3ciety, was in the chair and amongst others present were Mr C A Littler (treasurer) and the Rev G Vale Owen (hon. secretary). The RECTOR, after commenting upon the work of the Society during the past year patsed on to the question of Welsh Disestablis"ament, and s tid they were told that the valu3 of the fabrics of the Welsh Church was about £1,000,000 and the income was £273,000 a year. Under the contemplated Bill it was proposed to taly3 away £253,000 and leave the Church £20,000 per annum, or Is Gd in the £. Ile wanted to ask three questions :—(l) Why was the line drawn at the year 102 ? The answer was : In order to secure Nonconformist endowments. (2) Are the tithes not to be ttken from the laity who hold them as well as from the clergy ? Tne answer" was : No, because of the opposition that would be caused if it were proposed to take laymen's property?. (3) Why was it not proposed to take away the fabrics? Because they belonged to the laity, as well as to the clergy, and hostile feeling would be aroused. The audience would see the mockery of it all and he advised them to think earnestly about the question and to remember what a loss it would be to have Disestablish- ' ment of the Church of England, to have no Bishops in the House of Lords to speak out boldly for what they believed to be right,and no-one to crown the Sovereign. They must also think of the need for the money. Though it was hot money they ought to think about so much in itself, they knew that their work could not be done without it. How could the clergy live and do their duty if they had not funds? He now wanted to speak about three great concentric circles. The first was the smaller one of the , Warrington Church Society, the object of which was to draw them all together, to break down miserable parochialism and create a larger and wider feeling. The second was the Church of England Men's Society. Teat was a wider circle but for men only and the object wig exactly the same—to create a feeling of sympathy with the work of others. Finally he took a still wider circle the Church Catholic. Having impressed upon his hearers the importance of caring for unity, the Rector touched upon the succession of Bishops from the Apostolic age, and said that anxious as he was to draw near to Nonconformists, he corgi never give up the historic episcopate. He prayed for the re-union of East and West, and of Rome and England, without any compromise of truth, and for the maintenance of the unity between the Church of England and the Church in Wales, so that they might help to realise Our Lord's prayer that they might all be one. (Applause). The principal feature of the proceedings was a lecture by the Rev. W. Bracecarop on his recent visit to Egypt and Palestine. It was illustrated by a splendid collec- tion of lantern slides, many of the photogiapks having been taken by the lecturer. The lantern was manipu- lated by Mr. Malcolm. The following musical items were rendered :—" The Holy City," the Rev. .1. H. Bankes ; " Father Eternal," Miss Hewitt ; " Under the desert star," Mr. E. H. Pearce. Mr. E Wilkes was an efficient accompanist. During an interval refresh- ments were served. A hearty vote of thanks was passed to the lecturer and lanternist on the proposition of Mr. J. H. !Smethurst.

div.head: IRISH AFFAIRS. 1 NOTES FOR IRISH READERS.
div.p: IRISH AFFAIRS. 1 NOTES FOR IRISH READERS.

WHAT 130NAR LAW HAS ASKED FOR. The leader of the Unionist Party can no longer complain that leading Home Rulers are avoiding the subject. Since Mr. Law included that statement in the mass of inaccuracies composing the speech with which he opened his Anti- tiome Rule campaign, speeches on Irish self-government have been delivered by Mr. Churchill—in that most memorable gathering of Ulster- men in Belfast—Mr. Redmond, Mr. Dillon, Mr. Devlin and the Master of Elibank ; while this week is published the introduction which Sir Edward Grey has provided for Mr. Harold Spender's book, presenting, we may add, the fruits of the observation and reflection of an experienced journalist on the question. Mr. Law scented disagreements,! and, if he had been right in his conclusion, trouble should have accummulated the nearer grew the date for the opening of the session. That fable—along with many others of which Mr. Lloyd George took such destructive notice—has disappeared. As the days pass, the members of the Liberal Government and Party are speaking more and more often on a question which Mr. Law thought was too thorny to be touched. But the Unionist thirst for information still remains unsatisfied. Although within the next few weeks everybody will be acquainted with the Government's proposal. Mr. Law's supporters in the press grow more and more impatient. They are not comforted even by their own cold conclusions as to Mr. Churchill's speech—namely, that it foretells disaster for the cause of Irish Self-Government.

div.head: SIR EDWARD GREY'S TRIBUTE.
div.p: SIR EDWARD GREY'S TRIBUTE.

His clear and reasoned speech at Sunder- land last month prepared the public for the views which Sir Edward Grey expresses this week over his own signature. At Sunder- land, it will be recalled, Sir Edward declared that Home Rule had become more urgent than ever. That judgment he repeats in his introduction to Mr. Spender's instructive book, while careful to express no opinion as to some principles and conclusions put for- ward by that writer. But he heartily agrees with the author that if the Imperial Parlia- ment is to ba free to meet the obligations of the business of the Empire, and the United Kingdom considered as a whole, Ireland must be entrusted with the management of her own affairs. The Foreign Secretary recalls that when he and other Gladstonian Home Rulers associated themselves with the

Irish cause, they entered it—in his own phrase—from the Irish side. The growing burden of the work 01 the Imperial Parlia- ment has now compelled them to regard Home Rule as essential in the purely British interest. The Unionists, we all clearly remember to-day, thought in 1910 some such solution of the problem of congestion was totally necessary, but that at present is no longer a settled item of Unionist policy. The rank and file are asked to choose from the views of Mr. Law, who paralysed comment by asking "What good can Home Rule do," of Mr. Chamberlain who recommends devolution, a modified form, as some define that hazy word, of Home Rule, and of Mr. Walter Long who urges that if Home Rule is to come it ought to be a full measure allow- ink the Irish people to work out their own destinies. In that declaration Mr. Long repeated the expressed intention of the Government as proclaimed by the Prime Minister on the eve of the general election of 1910. Mr. Asquith—though the Unionists try hard conveniently to forget that supremely important statement—announced then that if his party were returned to power they would proceed to frame a measure con- ferring "full self-government " on Ireland. That speech was, it is relevant to mention in view of current Unionist criticism, a Cabinet statement and delivered before there was any balance of power in the Commons resting in Mr. Redmond's hands. As the Master of Elibank pointed out in his recent address to the Midlothian Liberal Association, that declaration was endorsed by Mr. Asquith's colleagues and by every Liberal candidate throughout Great Britain. Nor were the Unionist electors allowed to have any doubts as to the certain effects of the passing of the Parliament Bill. They were told, time and time again, from a hundred platforms that by the passing of the Bill the sole obstacle to the granting of Home Rule to Ireland would be removed. In the stirring speech in which he claimed that all his political life he had been "up to the neck in Home Rule " the Chief Liberal Whip merely reviewed the salient and indisputable facts of the political history of the past two years. The task would be wholly unneces- sary but for the feeble pretence of Mr. Law and many of his supporters that the ques- tion has been "sprung" upon them. Even on Monday last the "Morning Post" was found inquiring" why the Liberals have been at such pains to deprive the electors of any opportunity of expressing an opinion upon it?"

div.head: TITLED LAW BREAKERS.
div.p: TITLED LAW BREAKERS.

Lord Londorderry, Sir Edward Carson i and the whole mob of titled law- breakers have their defenders in quarters where one would look to see a restraining ! influence exerted. The "Times" could not justify their plot "as a matter of political ethics," but it argues that Unionists ought to be grateful to the noblemen and Privy Councillors for proclaiming the hostility of 1" Ulster " to a Home Rule Government. The Master of Elibank indicated some of the possible consequences of the unchecked law- lessness of the Belfast faction. The Unionist example, depend upon it, will be remembered in the trying times when armies of workers set out to seek reforms. But an immediate consequence of the action of the organisers of disorder is that England knows that opposition to Home Rule in Ireland is in the main "worked "by a group of irreconcilable, disappointed politicians, who do not scruple to play upon the ignorance and bigotry of a mob. Thus for the wretched people who made the disgrace- ful attack upon Lord Pirrie and Lady Pirrie at Larne on Saturday last there can only be a feeling of contempt,mingled perhaps with pity. But a much stronger and more indignant feeling must surely be entertained of the action of the titled instigators of riot and' outrage, whose words and deeds had their actual and abominable effect in the attack at Larne on a distinguished Irishman, who is not a Catholic, whose splendid brain has built up the source of half the prosperity of Belfast, but who ventures—and this is the reason for the Orange ruffialiism just men- tioned—publicly to state his faith in the capacity of his fellow countrymen to manage their own affairs. Can political insanity go further?

div.head: NATIONAL INSURANCE.
div.p: NATIONAL INSURANCE.
OPENING OF LOCAL CAMPAIGN IN SUPPORT OF THE ACT.
MR. A. H. CROSFIELD REPLIES TO MR. WYNDHAM.

The first of a series of meetings to explain the pro- visions of the Na.ional Inurano3 Act was held in the Silver-street schools on Monday evening. The Progressive Lab iur League had promoted the meeting which was largely attended and very enthusiastic in its support of the measure. Mr. J. JARMAN presided and was accompanied on the platform by Mr. 11. Wilson (Liverpool) and Mr. Harry New. The following letter from Mr. A. 11. Crosfield to Mr. E. Wynne Junes (president of the League) was read :
39, Hyde Park Gate, S.W. February 12th, 1912.

Dear Mr. Wynne Jones, lam delighted to note that this evening the first of a series of ward meetingi will be held under the auspices of the Progressive Lib ,ur League- meetings which are bound to have great educational yalite in the town.

The record of work accomplished under our Progressive Government during the last half dozen years provides an ample bill of fare for Liberals. -May I just allude to two of those questions of paramount public importance upperm )st in most of our minds at the present time. I understand that during this series of meetings time will be given to considering in detail the great Insurance Act that was passed last autumn, and I am convinced that the more the complicated provisions of that Act are understood and considered, the more all thinking citizens will realise what an untold blessing it will be to the nation. When the first few months of contributions have been made, and after- wards when for a couple of years, those unfortunately in need of them have recived—just at the time when of course they are most urgently, and in some cases terribly in need of them—the benefits conferred under this Act, people will only wonder how they ever got along without it. And then I am sure a word or two will be said of the enormous advantages we in Britain enjoy under oar Free Trade system, alike from the point of view of th 3 great consuming public; fi orn that of the artisan and labouring class, who know the value of busy times and plentiful employment; from that of the manufacturer who is in a position to give it, thanks to the fact thot Free Trade enables

him at hom3 and blaraad to offer goods of first quality and at moderate prices; and lastly from that of the statesmen and politicians, who can pursue their calling without being driven from public life by the corrup- tion which in Protected countries sickens and disgusts many an honest man. In explaining the be leas, and let us not forget as the years run on, the in”-casing benefits of this great system of State Insurance, and expounding alike Part I. and Part 11. of the Act you will pat a stop to the gross misrepresentation of those who try ta make a little party capital—or a good deal of it —by exciting prejudice against the measure; and I venture to suggest that it will be just 83 necessary to expose some of the really extraordinary misstatements for which Tariff Reformers—in their desperate plight— make themselves responsible. May I take this opportunity to draw attention to one or two of them. When Mr. Wyndham was in Warrington the other day he said in the course of his speech "The (Labour) Exchanges were thronged with applicants and in the nine months from January to September of last year the number of applicants for a job and who got no job was 873,573. Was that condition continued in the next three mouths? He had not gat the figures but he knew that (luting the next three months of winter, unemployment was greater than it was in the summer, and if the ratio continued during the next quarter of the year of specious and false prosperity many more than 1,030,000 men-I,ooo,ooo—went to apply for the lowest form of employment at pitiful wages and could not obtain it.' Now the conclusion any one reading that statement would draw, and I venture to say the conclusion which the audience were intended to draw, was that something like 1,603,000 men would be applying for work at the Labour Exchanges last year, even work of the lowest character, without being able to obtain it. Well I have been looking into the official figures which the Board of Trade Labour Gazette gives us, and I venture to draw the attention of every one who either heard or read Mr. Wyndham's speech, to the actual facts of the case. Taking the figures for the whole country the Labour Gazette shows that out of all those who made application for employment through the Labour Exchanges, only 46,701 of the men and 8,563 of the woinen failed to get work,and as regards what Mr. Wyndam calls the lowest f win of employment, I find the list includes thousands of bakers, carpenters and joiners, printers and painters, decorators, vehicle makers, watchmakera, and several other classes of skilled tradesmen, who, to quote Mr. Wyndham came to the State " seeking employment" and—correcting his monstrous inaccuracy—found it. Mr. Wyndham also says in another part of his speech : They saw there (at the Dumping Exhibition), and always had seen everywhere goods made by foreigners—goods which we used. to make in England and which we could make still, but which our people were not allowed to make because they were sold in this country for less than the cost of production." Mr. Wyndham is apparently arguing that Tariff Reform would keep out goo is sold here at less than the cost of product:on, and my attention has been drawn to some remarks on the matter in the Tariff Reform League Monthly notes of last August : "It is not the aim of Tariff Reform to keep out foreign goods from this country. To do so would be merely to raise prices and produce no revenue " and to the remarks of Professor Ashley r.,f Birmingham the one stray British Professor of Economics who may fairly be called a Tariff Reformer, and who states in his book : "No low or even moderate duty will suffice to keep out foreign goods when they are being sold at any price to relieve' the domestic market." Here we have two examples; on the one hand of the hopeless confusion and contradiction in argument which you find among the tariff reformers themselves; on the,ether hand of the hopeless and indeed astound- ing inaccuracy of many of the statements which they make. With all best wishes for the success of and the greatest confidence in the usefulness of your meetings, believe are,

div.head: Very faithfully yours, CIIOSFIELD,
div.p: Very faithfully yours, CIIOSFIELD,

Mr. E. Wynne Jones, 510, Knutsford-road, Warrington. The CHAIRMAN Said he was rather sorry to read tha\ night that the Act was going to be called a Party measure. If the Liberal party got all the kicks, how- ever, it was only rignt they should have the halfpence as well. (Hear, hear.) There was one particular clause in that Bill which he heartily welcomed and that was the appointment of Heelih Committees in various localities. (Hear, hear.) They were going to get something done towarch tho sweeping away of slums. (Hear, hear.) That district in which they were met had the highest death rate in Warrington. What was the reason ? Why. some of the houses were unfit for habitation. When slum property existed as it did in Warrington, Ho( Town Council hi their endeavour to do away with ii were met by large claims above the ordinary value oi the property. It was ridiculous to have ta pay extreme sums of money for property that they wanted to pull i down. (Rear, hear.) On the other hand t was not right that the slum property should exist as it did. But under the Bill, where the sickness was above the normal, the Health Committee would have the right to confiscate the alum property, and the owner would have to meet the expense of the excessive sickness. (Hear, i bear.) It gave the people a voice n the settlement of an affair which they had not had in the past. (Applause.) There was a great deal of misrepresentation going about the country. In regard to the doctors' attitude on the present occasion, the people had helped a great deal in the upkeep of the hospitals, the training ground of the doctors,and people had been experimented on by the young students, and now the doctors were refusing to do something in return for the working men w'oo had been the means in EOM ways of giving them the experi- ence they bad obtained. (Rear, hear, and applause), Mr. WILSON said the Insurance Act meant a benefit both for the employer and employee. It made men fitter and better from their own standpoint and better from the employers' standpoint. (Hear, hear.) No man could help being sick, and it had meant in the post a loss of money to him in that respect. Things often went to the pawnshop to enable the housewife to keep the home going. When anything found its way into the pawn- shop, it was two to one against it ever coming out again. In future if a man was taken ill he would

_ ' receive 10s. wr week. One Peer .had said a What ia 10s. ?" and he had been answered by a Labour/nay with "It's 10s. more Haan nothing." (Hear, hear.) That would provide some of tin necessities of life. (Hear, hear.) The landlord had a perfect right to his rent. (Hear, hear.) Under the Act so long as a man was ill and was receiving benefit the landlord stood a better chance of getting his back rent than he did before the passing of the Act. If a man showed that he was willing to pay, all the better for the landlord. If on the other hand he did not d a his best, the landlord could put him in the County Court but he could not sell him up whilst he was ill. (Applause.) When a man was out of work through bad trade, which was no fault of his, it was no reason why the wife and childran should suffer. (Hear, hear.) The man would receive is. Gd. per week which would keep then front want and uhilst he went out to find work there was somethin g to keep the cupboard warm. (Applause.) The Insurance Act gave& start for the child and was a boon to everyone. (Hear, hear ) It gave to the worker the idea of the dignity of labour, besides numerous other benefits. (Hear, hear and applause). Questions were afterwards invited and were ably answered by Mr. Jarman who further explained the benefits which would accrue under the Act.

Mr. NEW, in a short address on the Act, said there bad been plenty of misconceptions by the Tory party, and many misrepresentations. After the Act had been working for twelve months it would explain itself. Out of the 141 millions of wage earners in the country there were only about five millions who had made provision for the times of distress. They would still have to be thrifty under the Bill and they would be in a better position to save. The beuefi:s to be derived would soon gain the favour and appreciation of every member of the community. It was tbe greatest joy of his life as a trade unionist to see all th 3 people coming into line and on the same footing as unionists, and enjoying better benefits than before. The object was to make every man self-supporting. (Hear, hear.) There were also sanatoria for consumptives. That in itself was one of the finest things the people of England could have. (Hear, hear.) The Bill would be welcomed on every hand when the people realised how beneficial it would be to them. (Hear, hear and applause).

div.head: MEETING AT THEWLIS-STREET SCHOBLS.
div.p: MEETING AT THEWLIS-STREET SCHOBLS.

An enthusiastic meeting under the auspices of the Warrington Liberal Ass )ciation was held in the Tbewlis-street schools on Wednesday evening. Mr A Tilling presided over a large attendance. Councillor Grindle, of Manchester, spoke for an hour on the Insurance Act and explained its provisions in a very lucid and interesting manner. Mr. Harry New also spoke. Several questions were asked and answered.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " Twelfth Night."
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " Twelfth Night."

It is doubtful whether Warrington theatre-goers have ever bef ire had the opp irtuaity of seeing in their own town a Shakespearian production on so complete a scale as Mr. Richard Flanagan's presenta- tion of" Twelfth Night" at the Royal Court Theatre this week. For many years Mr. Flanagan's annual revivals at the Queen's Theatre, Manchester, have enjoyed fame even beyond the borders of the county palatine, for he has been eminently successful in producing the works of the immortal bard on the most lavish scale, whilst sacrificing nothing of the purely artistic and poetic elements. Owing to a change of ownership, the Queen's Theatre has closed its doors and for the present Mr. Flanagan's theatrical enterprises in his own city are suspended. Manchester's loss, however, is proving the gain of smaller towns, for " Twelfth Night,"—one of the most popular of the whole series of revivals -is being taken on tour by the same company which achieved i such a triumph at the Queen's n 1910. It cannot be said that Warrington's lovers of Shakespeare have risen to the occasion, the audiences during the week not having ben nearly so large as the high class attraction warranted. However, the feeling of all ivho have attended is one of gratitude to the manage- ment and t Mr. Flanagan for giving them the opportunity of seeing this most delightful of English comedies, exquisitely mounted and brilliantly acted. The true spirit of boisterous, roystering fun is perfectly realized and the audience rocks with laughter at the inane conceits of Malvolio and the simple plot of his jolly, mischievous enemies to give his vanity a shock. There is not a single weak part in the cast. Mr. Ryder Boys, who revels in comedy, is the ring-leader of the mirth-makers as the bibulous, rubicund Sir Toby Belch. He enters into comic pranks with boyish gusto and that jovial, side-splitting laugh of his is infectious. Mr. Boys extracts the very maximum of life and merri- ment from the part and, quickly ingratiating himself with the audience, remains prime favourite until the close. As his curious ally, the hiccoughing Sir Andrew Aguecheek, Mr. Harold Neville is equally happy, and when the two are in their cups the audi- torium is in a roar. Miss Ethel Griffies impersonates Viola—one of the most charming of Shakespeare's heroines—with an irresistible grace and winsomeness, combined with a rare depth of feeling, that choice passage in which she confesses her love for Orsino being beautifully interpreted. Miss Una Rashleigh as Maria is the embodiment of roguishness awl gaiety, the naturalness and freedom of her portrayal appealing to all. Miss Ponsonby Hartshorn gives a careful and convincing study of the cold Olivia, and Mr Edward Cooper portrays the love-sick Duke. Orsino with befitting ardour. Mr. Wilfred Beckwith gains one of the great successes of the play as the foolishly vain Malvolio, and the scene in which he so readily fells into the trap prepared for him, is the most laughable in the play. Mr. Geirge Horrocks as Feste, the clown, puts in some capital foolery - not unmixed with wisdom - and sings very accept- ably. The scenery and effects are gorgeous and range from a thrilling representation of a ship wreck to the fine chureh tableau and the marriage of Viola and the Duke, the lattet scene being marked by great ecclesiastical pomp and ceremony and a wealth of colour. A notable feature is that the scenes are changed so expeditiously that there is no tedious waiting between the acts. An orchestra, under the very able conductorship of Mr. Yorke Sheffield, plays choice inciden'al music—most of it we believe,compos d. by Mr. Sheffield himself—which adds not a little to the enjoyment of the evening.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMUE.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMUE.

"Peggy," fair and gracious, and with all the brightness, beauty, and brilliance of the latest Gaiety Theatre (London) success, makes her first appearance in Warrington on Monday next at the Royal Court Theatre. Having had a most successful run in London, this fascinating musical play should prove an equal success in the provinces, and in mise-en-scene and company Mr. George Dance presents it in fully worthy manner. The staging is beautiful, the dresses

la;nificent, ..- in quality and in numbers. .(ith its spark- music, its brig it aud whimsical plot, quaint and ;inal dances, an 1 clever artistes, " Peggy" has all essentials of successful musical comedy—in fact, a sheer jag of joy," as our American cousins phrase Lt—and an entertainment not to be missed. A matinee ,f rem " will be giv,n on Saturday, February 24th, at 2 o'clock. The Box Office is now open, where seats should at once be secured for this great ' ion.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Saturday, Jane Hemmings, 5, Stanley-street, was charged with stealing a lady's grey tweed skirt, value 9s. 11d., the property of Messrs. Lord Bros. of 128, Bridge-street. The Chief Constable stated that the prisoner took the skirt to Mrs. Caslin at 26, Barbauld at., between seven and eight o'clock the previous night and asked for 48. for it. She, however, at first refused to purchase, but subsequently gave her 25.10 r it.—The case was adjourned for seven days. At the Police Court on Monday, Peter Kemmings was charged with stealing or receiving the skirt know- ing it to have been stolen.—The Chief Constable stated that the prisoner's wife was before the Court on Satur- day, charged with having stolen the s'Art. The woman went to her lodgings and saw her husband who told her to get "shut "ofit as soon as possible. She went out and sold the skirt for 2s. and gave him the money.— The case was adjourned nntil to-day (Saturday).

- EXCITING POLICE COURT SCENE. DEFENDANP DIVES OVER WITNESS BOX. Much excitement was created in the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday during the bearing of a case in which Andrew Barrow, labourer, 11, Atherton-street, was summoned by his wife for persistent cruelty. Mr. Steel, who appeared for the complainant, said she was living at 25' Powys-street along with her mother. The parties had been married seven years and they had no children. The cause of all the trouble was the violent temper of the defendant and the fact that his brother, who bad been convicted in that Court on various occasions, was desirous of bringing stolen property into the house. The defendant wanted him to do this but the wife would have nothing to do with it, and the consequence was that she had to suffer at his hands on many occasions. In October of last year, the defendant and complainant were working in Moseley, hut tke defendant was dis- charged on account of having threatened to throw the , manager in the canal. Defendant : It's a lie.

Continuing, Mr. Steel said the defendant came back to Warrington, and between October and the Ist of January, be went over to Mossley and endeavoured to get his wife back to Warrington. She returned, and on January 2nd they took some furniture into the house. On that day he got into a temper and threatened tl smash the furniture and also to strangle his wife. He seized her by the throat. Afterwards, Mr. Steel con- tinued, he took up a knife and Eaid he would " rip her open." Defendant turned to his wife in court in an appealing and excited tone said "It's a lie, is it not ?" Mr. Steel proceeded with his case and without word of warning, but with a gutt eral noise, the defendant in a very excited manner, sprang over the front of the box and fell very heavily to the floor where he remained tnntinnleFs until several officers rushed to him and picked him up, one of them gaving him water to drink. Defenciait protested and in an unconcerned manner said " It's all right, I'm ageeeable to anything gentlemen." This unexpected occurrence caused no little excite- ment and after consultation with the Clerk the Chair- man said : In view of what has just happened the magistrates have to commit defendant on a 14 days' order to the Workhouse, so that he can be med:cally examined. The case will be adjourned. Defendant was then removed from Court.
The Examiner, Saturday, February, 17, 1912.

ALLEGED THEFT OF CLOTHLVO.—Thomas Hough (10) and Eliza Ann Hough (13), 5, Stanley-street were charged with stealing from a stall in the market between February 7th and 10th articles of clothing value £2 10s. the property of Rachael Tasker ; Thomas Hough and Mary Bough, the parents of the children were charged with receiving the property knowing it to have been stolen. The Chief Constable said the stall bLd ben secured n Wednesday even'ng and it was dis- covered to have been broken into on the Saturday when the property was missed. The case was adjourned for seven days.
TUESDAY.—Before Councillor Roberts (in the chair) Councillor Jackson Holmes, Lieutenant-Colonel Edelsten, and Messrs. W. Richardson and T. Locker. . . .

HA wK ER's TIIEFT.—James Taylor, hawker, 45, Warburton-street, was charged with stealing on, the 27th September a qnantity of vegetables, of the value of £2 10s, the property of Samuel Sutcliffe. He was further charged with having on October 2nd run away from the Borough leaving his wife chargeable to the Union. Prisoner pleaded guilty. The Chief Constable stated that on the date in question prisoner was sent out with a donkey and cart to sell the vegetables to the value mentioned. The same night instead of returning he sent the donkey and cart back to the owner by another mem—He was sent to piison for two months, one on each charge.

TR URSDAY.—Before Mr. W. Roberts (in the chair), Mr A. J. Jolley and Dr. Naden. ALLEGED MARKET THEFTS.—Mary Elizabeth Cann, 331, Wellfleld-road, was charged with stealing from a stall in ,he market on Wednesday, a piece of bed ticking value Od., the property of Sophia Brown, and was further charged with stealing on Saturday a child's jersey and other articles of clothing, the property of Isaac Ilerscovitz, another stallholder in the market. It was stated that in the first case the prisoner went to Mrs. Brown's stall and went towards her with a piece of bed ticking as if she was going to purchase it. How- ever she put it under her shawl. This action was seen by two young ladies. Prisoner bad been arrested at her home and on the house being searched there were found no less than 104 pawn tickets. In tbe other case she had visited tbe stall of Mr Herscovitz and after she had gone he missed several articles of wearing apparel. Prisoner who denied having taken the articles was remanded for a week.

div.head: JUNIOR LIBERALS.
div.p: JUNIOR LIBERALS.
ENTERTAINED BY MR. A. H. CROSFIELD.
Striking Speech on Ho]

There has been a welcome accession of interest in the work of the Warrington Junior Liberal Associ- ation and every effort is being exerted to make it a powerful force in progressive politics. A large and enthusiastic membership has been enrolled and the association is shortly to hold a public meeting at which a prominent member of Parliament is expected to speak. On Saturday evening the members of the association, to the number of about eighty, were tbe guests cf their P resident, Mr.A. H Orosfield, at dinner at the Winmarleigh Cafe. The gathering was highly successful and enjoyable and should prove a happy augury for the future of the association Mr. A. H. Crosfield presided and was supported by Mr. C. E. Parker (president of the I.iberal Association), Mr. E. Lloyd Jones (chairman of the Junior Liberal Associa- tion), Mr. G. Toulmin (deputy-chairman), Mr. P. 11. Brown (hon. treasurer), Mr. H. New and others. After dinner, which was well served by the:Cafd Comcany, a short toast ilst, interspersed with musical] items, was gone through. Mr. Cry's} lELD, in submitting the health of " the King," said the eventful visit of the King and Queen to India must have a beneficial effect, which it would be difficult to exaggerate, upon the 300,000000 Orientals under our sway. While in some parts of the world constitutions were in the melting pot or in the making, while we saw revolution and instability in certain quarters, he believed that the stability which we enjoyed in old England was very greatly due to that fine form of limited monarchy, under which the golden link of the Crown joined the wonderful British Commonwealth together. (Applause). Mr. C. E. PACKER in the course of a brief address, ' said he recognized that there were great possibilities in the Junior Liberal Association. " Warrington needs you " he continued " Liberalism needs you, the country needs you and the Empire nEeds you. The Junior Liberals of Warrington can do a great deal for what we believe to be the true side of politics." (Applause.) Mr. Parker next called attention to a fine passage in Mr. Churchill's Belfast speech on Home Rule : How often have we been reminded of the handful of Irishmen who fought against us in the liner War? have we forgotten the brave Irishmen that never failed in their duty to the Queen and to the W i Army ? by, gentlemen, n these days, when Irish Catholics are assailed with so much ill-nature, are they never to be remembered, too ? I cannot help thinking of the scenes of which I was a witness—when the heights of the Tugela were stormed and when Ladysmith was at last relieved. (Cheers). On the crest of the hill, facing the fire of sixty guns, in a veritable whirlwind of explod- ing shells, stood the valiant Boers. Up the slopes marched unflinchingly the Dublin and Inniskilling Fusiliers. (Cheers). There was a struggle of heroes—of heroes ranged by fate and duty on opposite sides. What a tragedy! What a cruel pity that such noble breeds of men should be locked together in hateful carnage ! (Hear, hear). And now we have made friends with our enemies ; can we not make friends with our comrades too ? " We had reconciled the people of South Africa, con- tinued Mr. Parker, by showing our confidence in them and granting them self-government. Would not the same principle hold good in the case of our friends in Ireland.? (Applause.) The tariff reform question had lately been brought to the front by wh ,t the Conservatives regarded as an electioneering triumph, and they thought the Liberals were very much discSur- aged because of the

div.head: DUMPING EXHIBITION.
div.p: DUMPING EXHIBITION.

Personally he was very glad that the exhibition occurred, because such an enterprise attracted many people who had never previously given any attention to political subjects—not only amongst the working classes but other sections of the community as well. If they could only get people to look at the subject, even through tariff reform spectacles, he regarded it as one of the first steps in their intellectual development with regard to economic questions. At first sight they would probably come to the conclusion that the goods made by the foreigner were defrauding the British work- man of work. Many had to work themselves through that first form of elementary reasoning to the further and the truer. As they became familiar with the laws which governed the exchange of goods they would realise the advantage it was for every nation to make the things which it could produce best and with the least possible effort. Some difficulty arose because people confused work and its results. They seemed to think the chief end of man was to work. He (the speaker) did not like work—(laughter)—except for its results. If they took away the results, work became wearisome and they I should therefore aim at doing that work which produced the most results, the most comfort and the most welfare. The Free Trade system of the exchange of goods between nations—each country doing that class of work which it was best able to (to— asts by far the best. He trusted that the Junior Liberal Association would take up that question seriously, although it was a somewhat difficult and complicated one. We bad not yet done with the controversy. The Tories would have the advantege of the Liberals having been in power a good while and when any party held the reins of government, whatever Bills it passed trod on somebody's toes and made so many enemies. The danger was that, although the country was not convinced that tariff reform was a good thing, the Tories might possibly be returned on other questions' and, sinless progressives took active steps to prevent it, our country might take the back- ward course of following Protectionist couatries. In conclusion Mr. Parker promised that he would do every- thing in his power to help forward the Junior Liberal Association, but be urged them to bear in mind that the more self-dependent they were the healthier would their association be. (Applause). Mr. E. LLOYD-JONES proposed the toast of" The Junior Liberal Association,' and coupled with it the name of Mr. A. H. Crosfield. He asked the young men of the association to brush on one side the prsonalities of political life and consider calmly what place Liberalism occupied in national and international affairs. They were not Conservatives because they were NOT SATISFIED WITII THINGS AS THEY WERE,

Conservatism stood where all was well, where there was plenty and more than enough to spare, surrounded by all that was strong and the prevailing sir of all that was satisfying and pleasant. What had the so-called democratic Conservatism of to-day t) say to the great social questions of the day ? What had it to say to labour ? Nothing. It sought to leave things as they were and not to be disturbed. The balm of freedom must not be applied to the wounds of Ireland. Wales might cry for Disestablishment, but Conservatism said " No." Conservatism was a policy of

DISTRUST AND SUSPICION. It distrusted democracy, it suspected foreign nations, it was always in a condition of alarm about the Empire. Ile ventured to say, however, that there was no greater Imperial party in England to-day than the party led by Mr. Asquith. (Applause). The true Liberal would not think merely of what he had to loose but of what gain to the nation as a whole might result from the policy which he supported. Why were they not Socialists? Because that policy was not practicable and young men, above everybody else, wanted practical politics. They wanted things to be done and not merely to dream about them. 'They wanted things attempt4-d that could be accomplished. They wanted to deal with things that were wrong—and God knew they need not go out of Warrington to (Ind plenty to do in dealing with wrong, suffering and misery. They wanted to bring about reforms gradually and in a practical manner. Ifs acknowledged that it was almost impossible for a democratic progressive politician not to have the thoughts of Socialists running through his mind, but when he came to the bedrock of activity and wanted to see things actually done,he must turn away from the dreamy views of Socialists to the practical work of Liberalism. Liberalism was the true force of evolution in politics. It was young, vigorous, active, wide-awake, alert and conscious of an ideal and a purpose. There was no room for pessimism in the ranks of true Liberalism ; its whole spirit was optimistic. Liberalism was not a crusade against wealth,rehich was a blessing to society, but it was a crusade against wealth gained by grinding and sweating. Liberalism stood for justice between employer and employed and the present Government had done much to bring capital and labour together. Toryism had always oppressed andicrushed those who were at the bottom and had kept them from rising. It was playing that part to-day. The recent dumping exhibition appealed not to the intelligenca but to the worst instincts of the people. In conclusion Mr. Jones appealed to the members to create a healthy political atmosphere and to make it possible for their President to be returned once more for the ancient borough of Warrington. (Applause). The toast was honoured with enthusiasm.the company singing " For he's a jolly good Jellow," ,and giving hearty cheers for Mr. Crosfield.

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD'S SPEECH. Mr. CROSFIELD, who was greeted with enthusiasm on rising to respond, said he lid not think it was any exaggeration to say that Ltberaham in these days was the
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD'S SPEECH. Mr. CROSFIELD, who was greeted with enthusiasm on rising to respond, said he lid not think it was any exaggeration to say that Ltberaham in these days was the

EMBODIMENT OF PRACTICAL lIUMA'NITY. Ile would not seek to belittle whit Liberalism had done in the past for the State, for the Empire and for the individual Englishman—indeed if they looked back over the record of the pastleentury they would find that Liberalism had been spelling out the evolution of the British race. Referring to some of the outstanding events of the century, Mr. Crosfleld first alluded to the momentous measure of 1829 when the Protestants of England, who were in so great a majority, finally made up their minds that it was not fair play that the Catholics. of. England and Ireland should be debarred from sitting in Parliament. At that time considerable apprehension was felt, and many violent things were said. They had just the same

rate, of Great Britain and of the overwhelming majority of the English-speaking race, proud to own their loyalty to the Throne and Empire, yet marvelling that we should s long tolerate the present anti-English system of government in Ireland. His appeal to every thoughtful citizen was: Is it not anti- Liberalism of the very first water to strive to perpetuate this

STRONG SENSE OF DISAFFECTION which pervades the minds of 20.000.000 Irishmen, scattered in all parts of the world? Is it not anti- Imperial and contrary to our system of Government in the Empire as a whole to persist in a policy of that kind? The case from the Imperial standpoint was overwhelming. There wJa not one of our great self- governing colonies that was not in overwhelming numbers in supped of the principle of responsible self-government for a nation like the Irish. (Applause.) In America the chief difficulty that would interfere with an ever-closer degree of affinity and political kinship between that great section of the English- speaking race and ourselves would be the feeling that we, not on account of any recent policy but simply because of indulgence in stupid, ignorant prejudice, had finally made up our minds that, although we had not time in the House of Commons to attend to Irish questions,we must insist upon meddling with them,instead of throwing the responsibility for local self-government upon the Irish themselves. He had been greatly impressed with that aspect of the question during those five eventful years when he enjoyed the honour and privilege of representing them in the House of Commons. (Applause and a VOICE : "And will again.") " Well, I hope 80 " continued Mr. Crosfleld. " Very kindly and cordial references have been made to the personal question to-night, and all I can tell the junior Liberals is that I have now fought four general elections, and I went into every one of them with a cheerful spirit—(hear, hear)—and without any mis- givings. If it is the pleasure of my fellow-citizens in %Varrington to invite me to fight again I SHALL GO INTO THAT FIGHT —(loud applause) with no less cheerfulness and courage, arid I think my own cheerfulness is pretty well shared by the Junior Liberals. (Applause.) And indeed, those who are associated with a party with slch a noble record of work—work which has made the fame of English statesmen and the glory of our nation—have every reason to hold their heads high." (Applause). Turning to Mr. Lloyd Jones' remarks as to the practical nature of the Liberal programme, Alr. CROEFIELD said he would like to ask some of his Socialist friends in Warrington whether they believed in their hearts that the wholesale introduction of officialism, the TREMENDOUS EXTENT TO WHICH INDIVIDUAL LIBERTY

WOULD ItE INTERFERED WITII under an extreme form of Socialism, with all its nepotism and jobbery, was going to give them the millennium? You cannot" continued Mr. Droefield " get a millennium at present in this world of ours. Humanity is not a race of angels, and you cannot leap into any millenninm in that way. What you have to work and strive for is neither Socialism nor individualism, but the thoroughly qualified indi- vidualism which you see in our time and which, to an increasing extent, develops the principle of collectivism. I welcome its further extension in the future as I also welcome the fact that, for the blessing of Britain and the whole world, the better side of individualism may be retained with it." (Applause.) Having put in a plea for equality of opportunity, Mr. Croefield re-echoed Mr. Lloyd Jones' remarks as to the optimism which should pervade Liberalism to-day. If one looked at the evil and the fiendish cru4ty perpetrated in different parts of the world, it was enough to make any man turn pessimist, but the reason why Liberals maintained a convinced optimism was because they saw the power which self- government gate people to work out the steady and well ordered progress of the race. .In our own country we had had the practical work of the Children's Act to protect the lives of the little ones and the determined effort by the present Government to hold the scales fairly between capital and labour in a measure like the Trades Disputes Act. Equally important was the fact that money was to be raised for better education and housing and for every phase of social reform by the taxation of luxuries and wealth and by introducing for the first time in our history the principle that wealth which was socially created should contribute to social needs. (Applause.) He wondered that a man like

MR. BONAR LAW had the colossal bounce to offer to thinking Englishmen the choice between splendid work of that kind and his own invitation to go back to the days of the hungry forties. Air. Boner Law had asked the electors to choose between Conservatism, including the policy of Protection, and what he described as Lloyd-Georgism. "I know of nothing more moving and more stirring in the history of modern politics " continued Mr. CrosSeld " than the way in

which that gallant-spirited, humbly born man of Wales has risen to the great position which he holds to-day. (Applause.) Not one of us would wish to depreciate by an iota the immense debt which the democracy of the United Kingdom owes to Mr. Lloyd George. (Applause.) But. Mr. Bonar Law is not quite correct when he calls the Government programme • Lloyd Georgism.' Without hyperbole cr exaggera- tion it may be said that there has never been in the service of any monarch or of the people of this country, a Cabinet EO full of brain power, so packed with men of supreme and eminent ability as the Cabinet which holds office to-day. (Applause.) It is to the work of the Cabinet as a whole, under the leadership of one of the bravest and coolest men of judgment and decision who has ever been Prime Minister—(applause)—that we have to look for these splendid resalts which we are so willing, taking Mr. Boner Law at his word, to put into comparison with the policy which he offers in exchange, lie tells his own followers that unless they will swallow Protection they are going to split his party from top to bottom. I should like to ask Mr. Boner Law if he df es not think his party has already been rent and split by the Protectionist campaign ?" (Hear, hear). Mr. Crosfield next dwelt upon the" raging and tearing tariff reform propaganda" with which, he said, Mr. Harold Smith and many others were so infatuated. He had spoken of the concentrated fury with which the taxes on necessaries of life, generally beginning in a small way and growing rapidly year by year, were viewed by the democracies of Germany, France, Italy, Spain—even reactionary Spain was now making a move in the Free Trade direction—Portugal and the United States of America, and of the difficulty they found in getting rid of the accursed system once it got the people fairly in its grip. He would, however, like to call attention to the point of view of the manufacturers who were beginning to realize how tremendous a handicap was being placed upon the development of their export trade by tariffs. The following extract from an editorial in the "Exporter's Review," an influential trade j)urnal in the United States, was doubly significant : " If we are to maintain the growth of our foreign trade it must be by reaching foreign marl ets more and more with cur manufactured products. They must compete in such markets with those of other manufacturing countries and one of the necessities in promoting such trade is economising cost of prearicrion. Another thing is necessary in extending exports of manufactures, and that is encouraging imports of those things which can be bought abroad at better advantage than they can be produced at home. There is ?to getting round the fact that exports are paid for indirectly zeith imports, values being set off against each other, and balances being settled first or last in gold. To obstruct imports is to hinder exports, and to make imports costly to get is to reduce the amount of them received in proportion to the value parted with." " I wonder " continued Mr. Crosfleld " if there. is any thinking employee at Dalton Bank to-day who will not endorse that? Would it develop the export trade of that works to check the purchase of the semi-manufactured steel that comes in from abroad to-day? For a good many years I was closely connected with the export trade and knew what it was to meet German and American manufacturers all over the world. I have seen what low cost of production means when you are faced with the competition of countries whose standing expenses are increased through Protection. That any firm largely interested in the export trade should seek to throw away the priceless advantage of low cost of production is truly amazing. (Hear, hear.) If that is true of individual firms, what about any town which depends to a great extent upon its export trade ? Surely the proposal is equally ridiculous and pre- posterous from that point of view." (Hear, hear.") Mr. Crosfield next alluded to the growing demand for Free Trade in Germany and quoted a comment by a " Daily Mail " correspondent who, writing on the recent Socialist triumph in that country, stated that "the commercial Liberals want lessened duties, cheaper prices, reduced cost of administration, some prospect of better relations with their workmen." Mr. Crosfield proceeded to direct attention to the views of some of the most distinguished men who had been associated with the Conservative party in modern times. Lord Goschen, speaking in the House of Lords on June 15th, 1903, deelared " There was a time when there was some hope of a Free Breakfast Table, but under the present plan not only will there be no Free Breakfast Table, but no free dinner table, no free tea table, no free supper table. Every meal would have to be taxed, and those classes would gain nothing by the imposition of a food tax. . I CALL THAT A GAMBLE. IT IS GAMBLING WITH THE TOOD 05' THE PEOPLE." Lord George Hamilton (who resigned office rather than tolerate the effort to reintroduce Protection) told us :

" Wherever Protection has been established, the cost of living has increased, the purchasing power of wages has been curtailed, and great fortunes have been made by the few through the merciless fleecing of the consuming majority. Free Trade on the other hand has always tended to a wider diffusion of wealth and to continuous improvemest in the well-being of the masses. Fiscal Reform to me means the extension of the principle of Free Trade." Lord James of Hereford said : , • " I will never support a policy which has for its object to render rich men richer at the expense of men who cannot afford to lose a penny. " Mr. Chamberlain had the candour to admit that tariff reform would involve sacrifices but in justification he I pleaded that we were going to bind the Colonies more closely to the Mother Country. That was an extra- , ordinary contention in view of the fact that there would undoubtedly be very severe haggling and a great deal of none too friendly argument with the Colonies on the terms of our bargain with them. L3rd Ritchie put the point in a nutshell when he said : " I am opposed to the policy, to the principles of the policy (Mr. Chamberlain's). I believe they

will be deeply injurious t 3 this country, and do more to disunite than unite the Empire." - One of the by-prockuts of Protection was that it would vitiate English public life which, up to the present, had been the purest of any great democratio government of our time. Lord Hugh Cecil, speaking at Sheffield in October, 1933, thus dealt with that sinister aspect of the case : " Protection will lead to the corruption of ee„r public life, as it has led to corruption in the Hie of other countries ; and the purity of our publics life is the life blood of the Empire. If Conserva- tives go in for Protection, I will have nothing to do with such an apostate party. If you are deter- mined to go down the path of dishonour to Imperial ruin, T will wash my hands clean of ee great a crime." Mr. Harold Smith, M.P. seemed to think that the import of semi-manufactured goods from ab,oed checked employment in England. The very reverse happened to be the fact. If Mr. Smith would refer to the Board of Trade figures he would find that it wee perfectly remarkable how unemployment in this countrY diminished as our power of consuming semi-roanufac- tured and manufactured goods from abroad—which we needed for our convenience and not for the foreigner's —increased. The Duke of Devonshire at the Queen'e Hall on November 24th, 1903, thus stated the case "I believe that no greater fallacy was ever Pro' pounded than that prohibition or restriction of our imports from abroad would add to profitable employment at home. I say it would be a moderate. estimate to say that the Glasgow Budget wools, entail an annual loss to the consumer of at least 35 and possibly 50 millions or more. I hold that Free Trade all round would be best, but if we are unable to have that—and we are not likely to have that --- at all events in our time—l am of opinion that we shall only make matters worse and injure our selves if, in addition to the hostile tariffs against curselves, we build up walls all round to prohibit or restrict the importation of tbose goods, which for our advantage and our purposes, and not for the advantage or the purposes of foreign nations, We desire to take from them. It is not in the power of Mr. Chamberlain or au/ other man, to give security that if we take the first step in the direction of Protection we can stop there. All experience proves that Protectionist principles, when once adopted, tend to increase severity and intensity." Finally he would quote the views of Mr. Chamberlairl himself, as expresssd in 1885 : If you are going to tax the bread of the people you will tax every household in the land, and yoe will throw back the working classes of this countrY into the starration wages and destitution froui which Sir Robert Peel and Mr. Gladstone have

relieved them." Ile was content to leave the question with tho quotation, concluded Mr. Crosfield. Men might change, their views—and they bad a perfect right to do so good reason could be shown—but Board of Trade figures and the whole of the circumstances of modero times proved that Free Trade was just as much the life blood of this country as it had been at anytime since. sixty years ago, those great statesmen had the foresigbt' and wisdom to carry it. (Loud applause). Mr. G. Tort.miN, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Crosfleld for his hospitality, said n 1 msn was more highly respected by members of all political parties. Mr. J. BOOTIE seconded. - _

Mr. P. H. BROWN. in supporting, said it was amusing to find a follower of Lady Greenell declaring that the backone of the democracy of England was Junior Coo' servatism. (Laughter.) Until, within the last fort- night, the Junior Liberal Association began to renew its activities, they bad beard nothing about Junor Conservatism from the individual in question. He vvoo evidently shaking in his shoes, for he realized that the Junior Liberal Association represented a force whici,.! was going to be powerful in Warrington and which would help to send Mr. Harold Smith to the right - about. (Applause). The vote was heartily passed. During the evening humorous songs were ably give° by Messrs. Farrington, W Lowe, and it Delaney, and .0 duet by Messrs. Furnival and Wright. A dramatic recitation by Mr. Chedburn was particularly vrell received.

extreme form of bitterness that was manifested to-day, not from Ulster—never let them confuse Ulster with a tiny faction of Ulster—but from that little section, largely centred in Belfast. Heaven only knew what was going to happen if Catholic E uancipation were passed, but it was passed and the doleful prognostica- tions were not fulfilled. It did not make for initability or revolution, but for the very opposite. They had the same terrible nrophecies in 1832 when even some of the most eminent statesmen feared that if the great Reform Bill—the most substantial measure of self- government that Englishmen had received up to that time —were carried, we should not know " whether we were standing on our heals or on our heals." That Bill also became law, without any of the dire results which had been predicted. Next they bad great disturbances, amounting to rebellion, in Canada. Lord Durham, a wise Liberal-minded statesman, dealt with the racial problems of the dominion,in a bold and generous spirit, and if they read his despatches to England they would see how the spirit of Liberalism pervaded them. A fine landmark in our history was staked out at that time ; a3cl Liberalism, on which the British Commonwealth was founded, once more prevail Ed. Then they had that never-to-be-forgotten period associated with the efforts of Villiers, Bright and Cobden and subsequently the manly conversion of Sir Robert Peel—names almost sacred to us in these days—to secure that most far- reaching of reforms,which brought untold relief to men women and children, who were literally starving and to homes that were being ruined through the misery begotten of that infamous system of taxing the bread of the people. We did well to remember the tremendous struggle that it took to destroy the old system, bscause it had a bearing on the trend of events in Europe to-day. In nations which were supposed to be

ENJOYING THE BENEFITS OF PROTECTION the people were cursing the evil of the taxes on food, clothing and all the necessaries of life, and yet they were not able to remove them. Were we in England to put the shackles upon our indus- tries and shoulder the incubus of I'rot3ction when we saw other people of Europe struggling to get rid of them, but in vain, bee use of the increased power of vested and selfish interests which was always generated by Protection. Returning to his resume, Mr. Crostield touched upon the Disestablishment of the Church in Ireland in 1868. He pointed out that the bitter section of the Orange faction in the Belfast district indulged in the gloomy vaticinations of which they were so fond, and the extreme langtnge which had such a familiar ring about it in these days Their ' tactics, however, did not deter Britain from a wise and far-sighted act of statesmanship. And he ventured to say that, in spite of all the
DUST AND NOIsE, we were in no humour to allow a handful of men to over-rule the opinion of the vast majority of their own fellow-countrymen—the enlightened opinion, at any

The First Eleven met Manchester University et Fallowfield last week and were beaten 12-3. For once in a way the visitors had to make the journey with tee players and this greatly militated against their chance of putting up a fight against their powerful opponents. Manchester scored 7 times in the first half, the Latchford defence being very poor, end Travis scored for his team after a brilliant run through the back The play was much more even in the second half but the University scored 5 times and Travis scored 2 more goals for Latchford against big odds. Although the score was one-sided the game %%as a good one and the general stickwork, dribbling, and shooting of the University players was distinctly educative in the nice points of hock( y. 'the Second Elevens should have met at Latchford but owing to defective arrangements at Manchester the University Second string failed to put in an appearance at Latchford, which caused much disappointment.
