div.head: TARIFF 'REFORM."
div.p: TARIFF 'REFORM."

This topic has bulked so largely in Warrington of late--thanks to the " Dumperies " and other provoca tive agencies—that I may perhaps without undue diffidence cast two or three mites into the treasury to which so many potent, grave, and reverend seigniors have contributed freely tf their substance in the course of the last fortnight or three weeks. WHAT THE PIG SAID.

There is a good old story, with an unmistakably chestnutty flavour, which 1 might well hesitate to report here, but for an addition which I am enabled to make. When Mr. Ecroyd contested the Rossendale Division against Lord Hartington, the cause of Tariff " Reform" had the benefit of extraordinarily able advocacy. The story goes that, just before the result of the polling had been ascertained, a farmer in those parts was on his way to feed his pigs, when he accidently tripped over a large stone and partially overturned the bucket, so that half thd contents fell upon the ground and was lost. He proceeded with the remainder to the sty, the inhabitants of which were eagerly awaiting his arrival. As he approached, an old sow, taking a pathetic glance at the diminished allowance of food,exclaimed with rueful countenance : " Ecroyd's getten in than ? " Mr. Fothergill, the Lancashire political lecturer, with whom I had an interesting chat the other night, tells me that he once repeated the foregoing at an open-air meeting, upon which a scandalised Tariff Reformer in his audience et ied out—" Rh! Why, it never said such a thing." Better to leave it there of course ;otherwise the speaker might have rf t red upon the interrupter, " One thing thou lackest "—just as the Dickens' lover might upon those members of the Town Council who chose his master's centenary week of all others in which to play with one of his most familiar characters such fantastic tricks before high heaven as was calculated to make the angels weep.

div.head: PUBLIC SPEAKER'S QUALIFICATIONS.
div.p: PUBLIC SPEAKER'S QUALIFICATIONS.

As Professor Brander Matthews testifies in the "Boston Sunday Globe," an audience is generally will- ing to listen when it hears a man talking earnestly and sincerely, talking out of the fulness of his heart. It may not approve of his sentiments ; it may even be frankly hostile ; but it is respectful, and it is attentive. And it is never respectful, and rarely attentive, when it discovers that the speaker has no message, and that he is talking for the sake of talking, indulging in mere self-display—in fact, only "showing-off. Listeners are always tolerant to a man who has something to say ; and they are likely to be intolerant towards a man who is only trying to say something. HECKLING THE HECKLER.

So Mr. Fothergill (who is doubtless known to many Warrington Liberals as a thoroughly capable exponent of Free Trade principles) generally has a patient and respectful hearing even when addressing mixed audiences out-of-doors. The exception to this rule proved of a peculiarly exasperating character; indeed, the lecturer was so annoyed that he was at length pro- voked into momentary rudeness, yielding to a sudden impulse to refer to the fiery red nose of his persecutor. The latter was quiet for a while, but on the speaker mentioning Germany, to illustrate the point, the tor- mentor broke out again with—" Were you ever in I Germany? " "No," was the naturally reluctant reply; "have you ever been there?" On being answered in the affirmative (it turned out to be an untruth, by-the-way), Mr. Fothergill suggested that he I should heckle the heckler for a change ; and this is how he did it :—" Do you know how to tell when German sausage is made of cab-horse ? " The gudgeon rose to the bait, not only admitting his ignorance as to this, but by his manner almost causing it to be sup- posed that he was thirsting for the information. " Well, then," pursued the lecturer, "I'll tell you. Take a sausage, cut it into pieces, and lay these in a line, say an inch or so apart ; then take away the fore- most, and if the others move up, it's cab-horse ! " MIGHT HAVE SCENTED DANGER.

I have already shown—and everybody is bound to admit—that the blush nose (I had almost written the "Scarlet Pimplenel," but that were too atrocious) is not the exclusive property of the music-hall comedian, although it is so conspicuous a feature of many star turns ; and I am reminded of another tit- bit in which a red-nosed heckler cut but a sorry figure. A curate was addressing the crowd, and the interrupter persistently asked " Who was (hic) Lotsh wife ? Tha's warra wanter know. Who vvosh Lotsh wife ?" The speaker, noticing that the question proceeded from an irresponsible quarter. charitably ignored it for a while ; lint ultimately, like Mr. Fothergill, ventured upon a trifling speculation as to the amount that must have been expended in impart- ing so decided a hue to the interrupter's proboscis. " exclaimed the victim of the gibe," " thash where yer make a mishtake. It hashent cosht anything like it, 'cos I'm a moderate drinker, I am." "Then," commented the curate, "the meter evidently registers more than you consume." THEORY AND PRACTICE. The friend with whom I had had this conversation within the week as stated has no difficulty in exposing the hollowness and absurdity of the tariffists' pretence that the foreigner pays whatever tax is imposed on imports. I cannot now enter into the arguments, but if the fact be challenged I will return to the subject on some future occasion. I want just to mention the case of an acquaintance who has two eons, one in Rochdale and one in the United States. They are so similar in build that the one here at home invariably buys two suits when he needs only one, and, after wearing his brother's a little while, sends it to the latter, who thus obtains five suits for what in America would buy only two. The wool buyers of Rochdale regularly meet at the London wool sales, the buyer for a New York firm, who is professedly strong on Tariff Reform—a native of the county of broad acres, by-the-bye. Being very deaf, he recently showed one of the Rochdale men an instrument which enabled him to hear quite well; "and," he went on "the best of all is I got it here in London for £4, whereas in New York it would have cost me £6." His hearer, pretending to be horrified by this incon- sistency, said he had always understood that he was an upholder of the fiscal system that obtained on the other side of this Atlantic. "That's all right," said the other, "but you know I'm Yorkshire !"

div.head: „... ANTIQUARIAN CHAPTERS
div.p: „... ANTIQUARIAN CHAPTERS
THE ROMANCE OF THE BRIDGEWATER CANAL. LECTURE TO THE WARRINGTON SOCIETY. BY MR. iT-MOUNFIELD.

The publicity given by the act brought storms of rid icu de. Most particularly the idea of the aqueduct came in for censure. His most considerate friends felt that the Duke's love affair had softened his brain. For a brief moment his courage failed him, and he called in Smeaton, famous as the designer of lighthouses, for advice. Smeaton's advice upon the aqueduct was discouraging and emphatic; I have heard of castles in the air, but never before saw a picture of one."

THE FAMOUS AQUEDUCT. To Brindley's rough practical sense the aqueduct was easy. He proposed to build a stone bridge over the Irwell,forming upon it a clay channel in which the canal would run. If it were argued that the bridge would leak, Brindley knew the way to make it hold water. His plan was to puddle clay by pound- ingit and place it layer after layer for canal or river beds.
It says much for the Duke's perception that he followed Brindley and risked the whole costly scheme upon his judgment. . ..
THE "RIVER IN THE AIR."

Then came the years of toil that made the plan a reality. Brindley entered the Duke's employ at the princely salary of a guinea a week, and the work began. At the Worsley end they burrowed the cliffs for a full mile, and narrow boats, designed by Brindley, went direct to the colliers at their shaft. A stone bridge rose over the Irwell and soon " a river hung in the air," as the populace termed it, drew crowds of sightseers. Ten and a quarter miles of cutting with ten and a quarter miles of puddled clay, and they were ready to let in water that would make a silver streak in the landscape from Worsley to Manchester.

Poor Brindley in his excitement took to his bed at a Stretford Inn, and tried to rest his high-strung nerves. But all went well, and when the Manchester coal market fell at once to 31d. per cwt, everybody realized that a great and potent event had happened. It was the year 1761, and the Duke had now time to reflect and look ahead. The canal had cost a thousand guineas a mile, exclusive of buildings, aqueducts and the borings at Worsley. But the ten miles was only the first part of a large and peculiarly bold project. With fine perception he saw that the join- ing of Liverpool to Manchester would be a scheme of extraordinary value. THE COMMERCIAL SITUATION.

Here perhaps we had better pause a moment to take in the commercial situation. We are so accustomed to the (shuttle-like traffic that links the two big cities that we cannot realise their separation. Yet in the Duke's day not more than forty tons of merchandise per week passed between them, whether by road or water. The fact is that both stream and roads were well nigh impassable. A stage coach ran, which needed six or eight horses to drag it through. No waggon could face the journey, and by pack horse or boat the carriage for goods cost £2 a ton. _ _ _ _

It was in vain that nature had shaped and endowed Liverpool if the town were isolated by bad roads. How much the Duke may have foreseen of the future of Liverpool :we do not know, but he certainly saw that it was the natural port of Manchester, and that with a sufficient artery commerce would flow freely. To form this artery was his absorbing idea.

div.head: BRINDLEY'S EXTRAORDINARY SCHEME.
div.p: BRINDLEY'S EXTRAORDINARY SCHEME.

Again Brindley dazzled him. He rode over the ground upon his mare, and without any sort of accurate survey described his plan. A canal was to be cut upon the Cheshire side of the river to a point not far from Runcorn. From thence it was to be carried across the Mersey by an immense aqueduct, and a cutting made to a point close to what is now the Liverpool Landing Stage. The Mersey is 460 yards wide at the point at which Brindley proposed to carry his canal across it, but he saw no difficulty. Most astonishing of all, the canal was to be on one level and, save at the Liverpool dock, was to have no locks for the raising or lower- ing of the barges. One level sheet of water, reaching from the Liverpool landing stage to Manchester, carried twice across the Mersey and once across the Irwell. Such was the scheme. _ _ _

„ It was want of funds and not of courage that hindered this collossal undertaking, and when at the end of 1761 the Duke put forward a Parliamentary Bill, it was to confer powers for the making of a canal, not to Liverpool but to Runcorn.
I3RINDLEY AND THE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE.

This time there was decided opposition to the Duke's plans,and the next chapter in our romance shows Brindley setting out for London to convince a parliamentary com- mittee of the value of canals. He spent a guinea upon a pair of breeches, and, with lavish prodigality, two guineas upon a coat. The same pocket book shows six shillings spent upon a pair of shoes, and six days con- sumed in the jouryney. At London be made a bad beginning. Induced in a moment of weakness to go and see Garrick as Richard 111., he was worked to a frenzy by the acting, and fell ill for several days. But once upon his feet again, he took the stage himself in the making of a bit of real history. The Canal Bill was made a party question. The Duke as a Whig got Whig support. The " Toories, "as Brindley called them, were his foes. It is a pity that the proceedings of that Parliamentary Committee have not been preserved. Poor Brindley, notwithstanding the brilliance of his two guinea coat, must have impressed them strangely. But he himself had no misgivings, and he had gone to London to see the thing through.

div.head: HOW BRINDLEY DEMONSTRATED.
div.p: HOW BRINDLEY DEMONSTRATED.

_ Several good stories are told of the dis- cussions. One noble lord did not understand what an aqueduct was. Brindley, always slow of speech, asked that a large cheese be brought in. Cutting the cheese in two halves he made of them the two circular arches of a bridge, and showed how a hollow half tube could be carried across the arches. The committee required no further light upon the subject of aqueducts. Another member did not know what "puddling" was. Brindley gravely asked for clay and buckets. He showed that water would find its way through clay in its ordinary condition, but proceeded to pound and squeeze it in imitation of the process of puddling, and was able to show that it would

afterwards hold water without the least leakage. And the Committee proceeded to discuss puddling as though they had known it from infancy. When someone wanted to know what a "lock" was, he produced a piece of Chalk and sketched one upon the floor.

Brindley talked so much of canals that a noble Duke seemed to feel that he was reflecting upon the wisdom of God in making rivers. "And what Mr. Brindley " he said "do you suppose that rivers were made for." Like a flash came the reply "To feed canals with water."
There was no arguing with_Brindley. And
when after eiglit hours debate in the Commons the division was tlken the engineer was able to record in his pocket book

div.head: Ad a grate division of 127 for Duke 98 Nos
div.p: Ad a grate division of 127 for Duke 98 Nos
For te Duk 29 Me Jorete.

A few more weeks and the Parliamentary victory was won. But public opinion in Lancashire and Cheshire had yet to be moulded. The Manchester and Worsley scheme had never been taken seriously; but the brilliant success of Briedley's "river in the air" had set the country agog. The new canal interfered with everybody's interests; it spoiled everybody's view; it interfered with every river, brook and water supply and of Course it cut through the back garden which was the only solace of the widow and orphan. It is good to remember th At in Warrington there was a sound and enlightened opinion in favour of the Duke, and Mr. John Hart in the December of 1761 published a dignified yet spirited pamphlet addressed to the gentlemen and traders of Warrington. And now to the business. BRINDLEY GETS TO WORK.

Nine weeks in London upon such dull business was a sore trial to Brindley, and he rode back upon his mare glad to fling him- self into the task of cutting the 24 miles from Longford Bridge to Runcorn. The project, though simpler and less brilliant than the

div.head: DUKE OF BRIDGEW A.TER.
div.p: THE DUKE OF BRIDGEW A.TER.

original scheme, was—large enough to tax both genius and patience. The canal was to be of one level from Manchester to Runcorn. It was there to descend by a series of steps into the Mersey, from which point the boats were to navigate the open river to a dock which was to be made at Liverpool. Perhaps it would be tedious to give details of Brindley's difficulties. In the lowlands immense quantities of material were needed to level the valleys, and it seemed that not "all the king's horses and all the king's men" could every carry enough. But the engineer had his own ideas,and seemed happiest when other people had used the final word impossible.

INGENUITY EXTRAORDINARY. He arranged to make and fill the canal in sections. Where there were valleys or low- lands to be crossed he suspended large tubes in which a barge could float. Two of these were fixed with a space between. A special triple barge was designed, the centre one having trap doors beneath. This centre chamber was filled with soil at some point where soil was plentiful, and floated over the tubes so that by the opening of its trap doors the soil was dropped exactly where it was needed. "The King's horses and king's men" were not wanted for the carting of material, and the critics were humbled into silence.

" Brindley's brain is an unknown world," said Arthur Young, who visited the work- ings. So it was, but it was a very practical world. With no previous experience to help him he planned and carried through without mishap or serious error a work that even yet excites admiration. He contrived, too, that It should be a marvel of cheapness. He floated his workshops, and the smith, car- penter and mason followed the workings.

div.head: BRINDLEY'S DAILY DAYS.
div.p: BRINDLEY'S DAILY DAYS.

He himself counted bricks, made- surveys, acted as paymaster or boat builder, as the duty of the day required. Three successive days as described in his pocket book show him designing the big aqueduct across the Mersey and deciding upon its 66 feet span, corking boat bottoms and landing timber out of the river. Meanwhile he books his modest guinea a week and his entries for food give the cost of " ating and drinking "at 6d. a I day. _ -
To be Continued.

div.head: OUR INDEBTEDNESS.
div.p: OUR INDEBTEDNESS.

Our neighbourhood would be the poorer but for the kindly consideration of many of our local men and women, who, for the sake of others do not hesitate to speak out and give their personal experiences. " Nearly two years ago I was very bad with back- ache and rheumatism," says Mrs. E. Boardman,of 60, Garibaldi-street, Warrington. "Pains used to take me just over the kidneys so severely that I could not stoop to do anything, for if I bent my back it was almost impossible for me to get upright again. Often in bed, too, I could scarcely move. The rheumatism used to take me in the knee joints, ankles, and shoulders. - -

6 I am glad to say that I have been free of these troubles since I tried Doan's backache kidney pills. I found so much benefit from the first box that I-kept on using the medicine till I was cured. I only used four boxes altogether. " I have recommended several people to give the pills a trial, for they did me a world of good. (Signed) Elizabeth Boardman." MR. LLOYD GEORGE AND THE DOCTORS. Speaking at a meeting arranged by the Natienal Liberal Federation and the Liberal Insurance Com- mittee in the London Opera House on Monday, Mr. Lloyd George replied to a number of Tory misrepre- sentations of the Insurance Act. Referring afterwards to the attitude taken up by the medical profession, he warned the doctors that if they refused to work the Act medical dispensaries and institutions would spring up everywhere. The Insurance Commissioners possessed suspensory powers, and could arrange for the medical benefits to be handed over to the insured persons through the approved societies, and the doctors would be deprived of theodeguards Ilidch the Ad provided.

div.head: LIBERAL DINNER.
div.p: LIBERAL DINNER.
FIGHTING SPEECHES AT ST. AUSTIN'S WARD GATHERING.

Another of a successful series of dinners to the members cif the various Liberal Ward Committees took place on Saturday evening when the workers of St. Austin's Ward were entertained at the Winmarleigh Cafe by Aldermen Tinnion and Burton. Alderman Tinnion presided over a large assembly of members, and amongst these present were many gentlemen prominently identified with the Liberal cause in Warrington.

Alderman TINNION, in opening the proceedings, said the members of the St. Austin's Ward Committee had done good work in the past and he was glad to see their interest was still as great in that ward, which was only one portion of the Liberal organization in Warrington. It augured well for the future because they bad such a good body of men engaged in the work. They were, in that ward, going to give a better account of themselves than they had done in the past. The alderman strongly emphasised the desirability of having a Liberal Councillor to represent the ward,and referred to the needs of the great working class com- munity which now lived and had its employment in that part of the town. He looked forward to the time when St. Austin's Liberals would not only see to their own representation in the Council but give a lead to other wards and provide a strong fighting force when the general election cam. (Applause). . .

When the election of cfficers was under considera- tion Alderman TINNION said it was about 20 years since he first became oil° of the vice-chairmen of that ward. St. Austin's would always be able to claim his services but be would be pleased to give way to a better man as chairman and still do as much and all he could f r the interests of St. Austin's and the interests of Liberalism and the Progressive forces in Warrington. (Loud applause.) Alderman Tinnion was enthusiastically re-elected chairman.

The following officials of the No. 11 district were appointed and those who were re-elected were praised for their valuable services and made suitable responses : - Deputy-chairman, Mr Tilling ; sec retar y Mr T Farrington ; twelve representatives on the Executive Council, Messrs. .1 Elwell, Messrs J Corradine, B fl Gallamore, H Brimelow, G G Kenny, and W Bennett, secretary, chairman and vice-chair- man exofieio ; Representative Association Executive Council, Messrs T Farrington, J Corradine, J Elwell, N Parsons, S Hassell and It Brimelow ; representative on the Finance Committee, Mr Wilkes ; representative on General Council. Messrs Pepper, J Barrett, W Miles, J Davies, D Brown and C Pritchard. The following is a list of officials for No. 10 I district :—Chairman, Captain Roberts ; deputy- chairman, Mr Griffiths ; representative on Finance ICommittee, Mr Critchley ; secretary, Mr Wilkes ; representatives on the Executive, Messrs J Critchley, W Bibby, G Weaver, H White, and the Rev W Cooper. After the formal business the evening was spent in a sociable manner. Many interesting speeches were made, and songs were excellently given by Messrs T Humphries and 3 W W.llett. Mr Sam Aukland highly amused and pleased the audience with his witticisms and his clever manipulation of the concertina. The duties of accompanist were ably carried out by Mr T F Wallington. Alderman BURTON after referring to memories of the past which the gathering re-awakened, said the old fighting spirit exited to-day and that they were Just as anxious that they should return their own representatives both municipally and parliamentary as they were in times gone by. (Hear, hear.) Their opponents had brought MOTO influence to bear on the ward and other wards in the town than they used to do. That inffuence had made some changes. He thought there was a deter- mination amongst their men that they were not going to take it lying down, He thought the time had come when they would return their candidates to Parliament and the Town Council as they used to do. (Applause.) To his mind Tariff Reform was the same old dog, Protection, but was dressed up in various colours. It did not make any difference how they turned it out ; it was the same old dog and if it got loose it would bite someone, and they would smart very much from it. (Laughter.) He did not know there was a nation which had adopted it which was not smarting from the effects of Protection. Many people in foreign nations would be thankful to live in a country where they had Free Trade. (Hear, hear.) Mr. GEORGE WALKER said that unfortunately they- lost at the last general election and they were dis appointed. In the first place they were disappointed because the man the Conservatives put up against Mr. Crosfield was a stranger and they did not like to be beaten by a stranger. (Hear. hear.) He was a stranger who had no record—a man who basked in the reflected glory of his brother. (Hear, hear.) The Liberal Government had done much and Warrington should have a fair share in a policy that was going to ameliorate the conditions of the people. (Hear, hear.) In Mr. Crosfield they had a democratic representative who would have backed up the C+ weamea t. and they had every reason to be proud. It was said they had a lot of unrest in the labour world. They would have unrest, and he rejoiced in it to a certain extent because ashen people were quiet and contented things were apt to become monotonous. When they got them interested something would be done in some form or other. They wanted better ideals in life. He supposed some of them had the opportunity of visiting the Tariff Reform " show." A greater slur upon the German or anybody he never saw. If that was the class of article English labour had to Tear the thing was absurd. (Hear, bear.) It was the better class work that the Germans did that might be a competitor to the English labour. (Hear, bear.) He had had the opportunity of visiting several European countries and he had never seen a people who were better off than the English. When he recently returned from Germany he was amused to see in the papers that there was no distress there. They had their troubles like we had in England. They had their periodical depression. Fortunately, there they had a good deal of of agricultural as well as industrial labour which was one source of help in their troubles. In conclusion he urged them, in that Ward to " buck up" and got representation on the Town Council. He would ask them not to rest but to work with all their hearts and endeavour to alter the representation in the Town Council. Let Warrington also take its fair share in returning a member who was prepared to advance Liberal interests in the country. (Loud applause). Mr. C. E. PARKER, President of the Liberal Associa- tion, said the large attendance and the enthusiasm displayed must mean they were going to have more workers at the next election. He was sure the country and the Empire needed Liberalism-.-(Hear, bear)—progressive Liberalism. (Hear, hear.) They had a grand political programme in front of them and they must put their shoulders to the wheel and advance the principles they had at heart. (Hear, hear and applause.) The Rev. W. Coorsa said that when he came to Warrington he was little more than an invalid and when the 1010 election came he was just able to put in a few hours work. He saw so much that day that he macte up his mm o that if he got better health— which he was thankful to say had come—he would devote more time to the interests of Liberalism. (Applause,) For various reasons he wished to be closely allied with that movement. First of all because of the glorious programme of the party (Hear, hear). Of all the governments which had held' office in this country, none was equal to the present administration. Another reason was that their enemies resorted to such questionable tactics. Never had there been so much misrepresentation as in these days. Now, the 'Polies were floundering in the mud and vented their feelings in " mud slinging." Notwithstanding that, the Liberals held a meeting at Belfast. (Hear, hear and applause). In spite of all the erroneous things in the Press, the Party was going on with its programme. They should do as Mr. Parker had said, bring the principles of the present Government in touch with every day life. His next reason was a selfish one. A minister, to have a healthy ministry, ought to mix with something else besides 'church life. He wanted to get amongst them and rub shoulders, especially with the working men. He found that to concern oneself with the problems of every day life tended to humanise preaching. The church must have his first consideration and the Liberal cause would have the next call upon his services. (Applause.) They should all work together and take the splendid example of their leaders and they would not only change the representation of St. Austin's Ward but they would also change their i Parliamentary representation. (Applause). Councillor J. T. Isocsra (secretary of the Liberal Association;said he was pleased to be allied with their chairman who was one of the pillars of their party. He had trained him (the speaker) to become an enthusiastic Liberal, and he had put into his

div.head: "GOODALLS"
div.p: "GOODALLS"
roil
DECORATIONS CARPETS • CURTAINS FURNITURE
KING. STREET, MANCHESTER.

mind the thought that he owed a duty to the party to which he was proud to belong. (Applause.) Mr. J. G RIFFITIIS said the Liberals were not the party of large vested interests, but probably they had something better than those material things and that was they were the party with big hearts. (Hear, hear.) That large-heartedness just now was having very practical expression in the legislation which was being c trried through. In moving a vote of thanks to Aldermen Tinmm and Burton for their hospitality, the speaker said they were two old warriors in the fight of Liberalism in Warrington. (Applause.) Mr. J. Et WELL seconded.

• At this juncture Mr.A. H. CRO•FICI.1), who had addressed a meeting of the Junior Liberals just pre- viou,ly, entered the room, and was received with much enthusiasm. In a short speech he said they could look at all the achievements of the Liberal Party with pride and eatirlaction, and they could be hopeful for the future. (Hear, hear and applause). Alderman Trxmoi,-, in response, said there never was a time when it was more desirable for Liberals to do their utmost on behalf of the those who had so few opportunities of helping them- selves. If there ever was a time when they, the workers, should be banded together and work out their own salvation, the present was the time. They had a Government, in office, the members of which were a most brilliant set of men—(hear, hear)—whose sympathies were in the right direction. There never oas a Government of which he was so proud. (Hear, hear.) There never was an Opposition who were so absolutely bankrupt in policy. (Hear, hear.). In con- clusion he asked them with every confidence to do all they possibly could to further the interests of Liberalism in Warrington and when the opportunity came to return Mr. Crosfield to Parliament. That would be the greatest thanks they could give him and the Liberal party in Wa•rington. (Hear, hear and applause;.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
New Offices to be Rented.

The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, In the absence of the Cnairman (Mr. G. Mather), who, along with the Clerk (Mr. A. Bottomley) wss attending the Central Poor LAW Conference in London, Mr A J Jolley, presided. There were also present :—Miss Broadbent, Mrs Simpson, Mrs Collingwood, Revs T R Matthews and A M Mitchell, Messrs J Billing°, W Gill, A Brooks, W C Brooke, W Furness, J A Rushworth, Backhouse, J A Hughes, it W _Peacock (deputy clerk).
GUILD OF HELP. • - At a meeting of the House Committee it was decided that Mr. Rowlmnds, secretary of the Citizens' Guild•of Help, be permitted to interview the committee, but the date was not fixed.

NEW OFFICES. The Finance Committee considered the question of providing adequate accommodation in one building for the clerical staff, relieving officers, officers of the Rural District Council and the provision of board and com- mittee rooms for the Guardians and Rural District Council. It was recommended that the Local Govern- ment Board be asked to approve a proposal of the Guardians to rent the premises 19 and 21, King-street, on a lease for a term not exceeding 25 years, at a rental not exceeding £lO5 per annum, and if considered desir- able to obtain an option to purchase the premises at e figure to be now fixed at the expiration of the lease. It, was further recommended that the Registrar General be asked to sanction a proposal of the Guardians to provide accommodation at 19 and 21, King-street for the district registrar's office,

The CHAIRIAN in moving the adoption of the minutes, said it was within the knowledge of all the members of the Board that the accommodation in the offices had been very inadequate for a long time. The question of building offices had several times been con- sidered more or less definitely and each time it had been allowed to drop. The need for additional accommodation was so pressing that the matter could not be allowed to stand over indefinitely and accord- ingly the Finance Committee had been making some inquiries. The question of building offices for Union purposes and registration work was carefully considered ' by the committee as a question of principle and finally, by a majority of six to two, it was considered inexpedient to proceed with any building scheme. The capital outlay would be of such a heavy nature that it was thought scarcely justifiable to recommend that line of action at present. An offer was made to the Board, through the Finance Committee, of the premises 19 and 21 King-street. They had been inspected by the committee and appeared to be very suitable. They were central in situation, large, and could, at a trifling cost, be well adapted to serve for a number of years for the business of the Union and of the registrar to be properly and efficiently performed. The terms suggested were eminently reasonable, and, in its final form, the recommendation came from the committee without dissent. Mr. FURNESS seconded.

_ ..... The Rev. A. M. I\llTeitgu. asked whether the Chair- man and any members of the Rural District Council had inspected the premises. Was it with their approval that the purchase was being made? Mr. JOLLEY Absolutely. Not the chairman, bat the vice-chairman, inspvcted the premises and the Finance Committee comprises three members of the Rural District Council.

The Rev. A. M. NIITCIIELL We are all thoroughly agreed that there is a great and pressing need. I sup- pose this is the very best that can be done. May I ask who is the owner of the property ? Mr. JOLLEY : I believe it belongs to the trustees of a Roman Catholic College—Ampleforth College,l under- stand. lam not perfectly certain about it, but I know it is a body of trustees connected with the Roman Church._

The Rev. A. M. 11frrc1rEn : It is a question of wisdom or otherwise. I don't think we ought to pledge ourselves without being p3rfectly clear. The CHAIRMAN : I think it will be pretty safe. It has gone through the Finance Committee ; it is now before you, and tvro higher authorities in London have to be satisfied.

Mr. BactmousE thought that In view of the fact that the Board of Guardians and Rural District Council contemplated joint offices, they ought to go in for a building scheme and thus obtain the best possible design for the purposes in question. The new offices would be in a most depressing locality and he believed that if the Guardians went out of their way to find a worse situation in Warrington, they could not do it. The CHAIRMAN said that after the somewhv.t drastic) remarks of the Chairman of the Rural District Council it would be well to point out that the members of the Finance Committee visited the premises and were satisfied that they were airy, well-lighted, commodious and convenient. There was a large open spice at the back.
The minutes were approved. - ALTERATioNs AT THE WORKTIOINE.
...... The Local Government Board wrote authorising the Guardians to make alterations at the Workhouse at a cost not exceeding £l,BO and to borrow that amount.

THE GROWTH OF ROMAM CATHOLICISM. Cardinal Bourne, presiding over the annual dinner of the Catholic Association in London on Monday, said the Archbishop of Canterbury had referred to the number of non-Catholio pupils educated in Catholic convents. That was not because the nuns sought these pupils, but because non-Catholic parents sought convent schools. Despite the archbishop's statements regard- ing the stationary position of the Catholic Church, he (Cardinal Bourne) believed the Church was steadily increasing. The number of the churches and the clergy was three times greater now than sixty years ago. The Duke of Norfolk and Lord Denbigh also spoke, the latter saying that Catholics had to tight a spirit of irreligion and indifference.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Dale of Fife's Funeral—Apart from the State opening of Parliament, the King and Queen have been seen out very little since their return from India, and all Court fixtures are more or less in abeyance until after the funeral of the late Duke of Fife. For the same reason Lady Londonderry and Mr. Asquith abandoned the receptions it is customary for party hostesses to hold on the eve of the opening of Parlia- ment. The cruiser Powerful with the remains of the late Duke of Fife on board, is expected to arrive the end of next week. The family vault of the Fife family is at Banff, to which town the late Duke not long since handed over Duff House but the Princess Royal is understood to desire that the funeral should take place at Mar. The late Duke was said to be one of the six men who owned a sixth of Scotland, but although he had in latter years disposed of a good eh al of his landed property,he still had a rent roll of not less than .£50,C00 a year. His death will cause some changes en Upper Deeside, but the Princess Royal and her daughters will very probably continue to make Mar Lodge their principal country residence. There were to have been great celebrations there in May,in honour of the coming of age of Princess Alexandra—now Duchess of Fife— but all the projected festivities will of course be abandoned.

A Society Wedding.—The marriage of the Marquis of Stafford and Lady Eileen Butler is to take place on April 11th. It will be one of the leading society events of the London reason, and will unite two of the most prominent families in Scotland and Ireland. The bride-elect is the daughter of the Earl and Countess of Lanesborough and was one of Queen Mary's six train- bearers at the Coronation ceremony last year. She is one of the prettiest girls in Society, and is two years younger than the Marquis, who is in his 23rd year. As the elder son of the Duke of Sutherland, the Marquis of Stafford is heir to one of Scollsnd's most ancient titles, and in the ordinary course, will one day be the biggest landowner in the kingdom. As head of the Leveson-Gower, he will succeed not only to the dukedom and several mansions, but to about 1,358,000 ecres in England and Scotland, and probably to large estates in Canada.

The Price of Wealth and Fame.—That famcus violinist Knbelik, perhaps the most, famous technician on his instrument that the world has as yet beard, has been able to win for himself the two things that most people count dear—wealth and fame. Yet, he is apparently not happy. He has found as many a man before him has found, that the price of these things is too high. Beycnd the huge hmount of time that has to he spent in the drudgery of practise to preserve such a technique as Kubelik has, he has been called upon to leave his wife and family and spend lonely huurs in arduous travel in order to give the long list of concerts that brought him £20,000 and fame, and be is tired of it all. Can we wonder that he has made up his mind to content himself for the future with thirty concerts a year r' It is some consolation to those who are blest with only normal powers, that they are at least left that which the greatest and most talented often have to do without—the enjoyments of borne and family. British Drama.—Drury-lane Theatre in London, which celebrates its centenary this year, will always be memorable for the leading part, it has played in the development of British drama. It is Drury-lane the fourth, two of its predecessors having been destroyed by fire. The second Drury-lane was of Wren's building, and Pepys records in his diary, many visits to that theatre. In the Merry Monarch's time, performances used to begin at 3 o'clock in the afternoon and as there were no reserved seats, people of quality used to send their servants to occupy the desirable places until they arrived. The retainers then retired to the " footmans' gallery" kept free for them. Pepys, who may be regarded as an authority on such matters,recorded that it was at the Clare Market Theatre in 1661 be first saw a woman come upon the stage. Previously all female parts had been taken by boys or young men, but King Charles 11. had seen the professional actress on the Continental stage, and he no doubt suggested the change, on his return from his enforccd sojourn over the water.

Spring Flowers.—lt is pleasant to see the spring flowers again. Already they brighten the shops, and are being offered in the streets by the flower girls, The narcissi come mostly from the Scilly Islands, which know only three seasons, spring, summer and autumn, and owing to an exceptionally mild and favour- able reason, the flowers are very early and fine. They are picked whilst in the green bud, and the blossoms open in glass-houses under the influence of damp heat. They are then packed and shipped to Penzance, from whence they are conveyed by special trains to London and the Midland and and Northern industrial centres.

The January Fur Sales.—An altogether unexpected feature of the January Fur Sales was the advance in pricez, which is the more surprising, as until the recent cold snap set in, the season had proved unsatisfactory to merchants and manufacturers alike. The sales are an indication of the trend of fashions in fur, and es Musquash was in great demand, and sold at nearly fifty per cent, in advance on October prices, a continued popularity for the pelt may be expected. Australian opossum too, which has been so successfully dyed this season, advanced considerably in price. Skuns met with little favour, when it was revived a few months ago, but judging by the demand for it and the high prices realised at the sales it will have a vogue next autumn. Chinchilla is always fashionable, for it is one of the loveliest of furs, but unfortunately for its admirers, with small dress allowances it is always expensive, nor can it be said to wear well. Mole which has been so extensively worn this winter met with little demand, and unlike the other furs realised lower prices than in October last. Beaver on the contrary sold remarkably well. It has been out of favour for some years, but will be seen again next Beason. The " Little Ilat."—The little hat that is close fitting and comfortable is indispensable in both country and town, when the wintry and early spring winds blow, and every week milliners introduce new models, in these popular styles. Oue new model has the brim carried to the back, where instead of being joined in the usual way, the elongated ends are crossed, covered with velvet or satin shaped like wings, and made to stand erect at the back where they form the only trimming. This shape has a turned back brim all round, which comes well over the ears and almost covers the hair behind. The crown is wide but low, and is almost hidden by the brim and its wing-like ends. It is a very becoming shape, and as it is merely covered with velvet, comes within the scope of the home milliner. Another small model has two wings— its only trimming—and these are placed on either side of the crown, but one is placed much higher than the other. Hats of the jam-pot variety are still much worn. Often these have draped velvet crowns,and when trimmed with thistle-down plumage are decidedly attractive. Yet another new model, with draped crown and turned-up brim,is reminiscent of a heavy type of hat that had a vogue in the seventies.

div.head: AN ALPINE EPISODE.
div.p: AN ALPINE EPISODE.

In 1866 two great professors of Zurich—one of physiology, and the other of chemistry—prepared themselves for an avccnt of the Fauthorn, one of the Bernese Alps which rises 6,417 feet above the Lake M journey they Mentz. For seventeen hours before the they took nothing in the way of solid food but .cakes composed of ordinary ingredients tr,th the addition of dried fruit, for the sake of its grape sugar. At 5.30 a.m, they began the ascent, choosing the steepest paths from the little village of Iseltwald, on the Lake of•Brientz. By 1.90 p.m. the journey was accom- plished without fatigue, and from that hour until seven an the evening the travellers rested at the top of the mountain. During the whole of that limo— 31 hours— they took no other food than the cake, and sufferd no inconvenience thereby. Quite a treatise could be written on the episode, but suffice it to point out the enormous, nay marvellous, power of grape sugar. It is to be had in plentiful quantities in Currants. Modern Currant bread corresponds to the cake which , sustained the mountaineers, only it is better and more potent. In other words, bread with the Currants added is fortified bread. Furthermore it is most palatable and attractive. The natural moisture of the fruit keeps the bread fresh and sweet. Do not forget that Currants contain nearly SO per cent, pure nutri- ment. There is no food comparable with the Currant as value for money. If you want to have power and endurance sufficient to climb mountains—eat Currants

Spiiken in the quiet insistent Voice of thee man who had come back into his life at this crisis, he hated them with a bitterness that surprised even himself. "Let's stick to business," he said abruptly. "What is your price? and please be quick, because / have other matters to attend to."

A flush of anger ran up into Steinway's face. "I understand. You don't wish inc to draw you back into the old circle of friend- ship when we all stood to fail or succeed, and we were all equal then—yes, even the great Clifford Hawke took his turn by the camp fire and did his share of the work !"

He broke off to laugh sneeringly. "However, I'll do as. you wish', and stick to the business in hand. Let me see, you want my price for keeping that little secret, don't you? Let me think, how much it is really worth; it's difficult to put a price upon it at a moment's notice." _

"Yet you had no difficulty in trading on it as a means of securing an interview with me!" was the swift retort, "so you see I don't quite believe that you have not already arranged your price in your mind." "And what if I have? Surely you as a man of business appreciate an-one who puts a certain value on something he has for sale? My dear Clifford—l mean Hawke—l have ray price, but you will be rather surprised when you hear what it is." Hawke's brows met in an ominous frown. "I am prepared to pay a certain price," he said curtly, "that, and no more "What do you call a 'certain ' price?" Steinway asked. "In return for a written promise that you will not attempt to see me or molest me in future I will give you two thousand ponnds," was the slow reply, "not a farthing more!" A sudden smile dawned in the other's eyes. "I'm sorry, but that's not my price. You see, two thousand pounds would not last long. It doesn't reoresent much capital, and again, I am an extravagant sort of chap, and my long self-denial would make me spend the money too freely. I'm afraid I must refuse your offer." "Three thousand is the limit," Hawke rapped out; "take it or leave it—not a red cent more will you get from me!" The Australian's eyes flashed. "And, by Heaven, poverty - stricken devil as I am, not a red cent would I take! I ac- cepted the other paltry fiver because I was starving, and I knew you would not miss it, but now I can just hang on and make my own terms! "

"What are they? " "That you as secretary of the Amalgaitated Copper Trust can easily give me an oppor- tunity of earning my own living! " was Stein. way's answer, given in quiet, cool tones. "I don't want vnur ugitry .nrien I want a, chance of building up a new life for myself es you have, and perhaps of becoming another success in finance as you have! And you are the man to help me do that, and that is my price! " For a moment rage choked Hawke's speech. He felt an insane longing to take the man before him and throttle his audacious demand in his throat. He had expected blackmail— and was prepared to meet it—but this price that' Steinway had set up was impoesible, ridiculous, mad! "Come! " he said harshly, "I've not the time for jests of this sort. I refuse such a request." Steinway rose..

"Then we need not waste any more time discussing it. Remember you hadyour chance, and you've chucked it away. As his tall, thin figure stood silhouetted against the pale blue curtain that formed a portiere between the archway that divided the room from an inner one, Clifford Hawke's eyes rested on him with hatred. This man actually dared to pit his brain against his! He dared to think that he could fight him, that he was the type of man to be bullied into accepting any terms he laid down!

" Stop !" he said in a low, suppressed voice. "You really mean that money won't buy you?" "I really mean that the only price I accept for my silence concerning an interesting little episode is that I am taken into your office and given a billet. Failing that---" He paused s;snificantly, and shrugged his shoulders. "Failing th*, yctt say what you know," Clifford Hawk % snarled. "Have you con- sidered that you might not be believed, my dear Steinway? Your. word against mine, you know." "Your word 11 RiT.dt my proof," was the sharp retort, 'slid you know how many enemies you t.sve waiting to see you fall. You are best mud; as to whether you can face the besides, according to a Society rag, I see you contemplate mar- riage.' The veins eltiid out like cords on Clifford Hawke's brow. He was cornered, and the knowledge nt de him writhe. If glances had had the is.mix to kill he would have slain Paul Steinv.,y 'Obese% nd then, but with a great effort he swatters zd 'is rage and tried to speak with some o Is;.• old self-control. "We will ro' discuss at subject, if you please," he said slowly; "and since you will agree to no ol lor terms than your own, I will do as you tJk--only it will be the worst venture you evi,t' unciertook in all your life." Paul Steinwriq ?.yoia flashed with triumph. "I'll risk that! You made a. pile in the City, why shouldn't If I'm not afraid. I've a brain of my own, though it may not be so keen as yours." Then he went on slowly, "Vou'll try no bluff games on me, Hawke/ This is going to be a fair and square deal?" Clifford Hawke nodded. His eyes had grown sombre, and the red light in them glowed like dying embers. "It will be a deal," he replied grimly, "a deal in which the best man wins!"

div.head: SYNOPSIS.
div.p: SYNOPSIS.

CLIFFORD HAWKE, financier and secretary of the Amalga- mated Copper Company, is about to set the seal on his anibition. At the age of forty he has the consent of the managing director of the same company to propose mar- •riage to his only daughter, Stella Traine, a beautiful girl. Though scarcely sure of herself she accepts him. Hawke returns to his chambers, and receives a letter left during his absence. Though it comes from a former friend, Paul Steinway, Hawke is by no means pleased; evidently this man knows too much of the financier's former days. At the door of a house to which Hawke has driven Stella Train', in his motor, a girl ill the crowd faints. Stella asks Hawke to lift her up, but instead he sends for a se:vant. A young Re I.t guest comes to the fainting woman's rescue and carries her into the house. Later Stella and the artist —Jaspar Tennant—discuss what shall be done for the poor wornan—Lotty Bond—and this leads to an invita- tion for Stella to visit the artist's studio. In a conversation with his hostess—Lady Mary Stainer—Tennant refers to the subject which is his principal aim in life—the avenging of his bister on the man who deserted her and their child. _

Is',bet ?rant, a" poorrelation 'of Stella Trainee, who is in love with Clifford Hawke, is sitting in the park. Her attention is directed to a man whose eyes gleam with hate, and who is evidently intently watching for some person. As he walks past her an unpostoil letter falls from his pocket, which Iso,iel picks up with the intention of re- turning. The address of Clifford Hawke upon It causes her to change her plans, and once in her room she reads the letter. It contains the secret of Clifford Ilawke's past In fulfilment of her promise. Stella visits Jasper letinant's studio, in company with Lady Mary Stai-er. They are joined by Hawke and Isobel, the former in a vile temper because he has learnt on the way that the girl is in posses- sion of his secret. A picture of which Lotty Bond is the model also draws Tennant Into disclosures which make Hawke tremble and wonder how much he suspects or knows. While the financier is contemplating how best to crush these two, a third antagonist awaits him at his house—Paul Steinway.

div.head: CHAPTER VI. PAUL STEINWAY DICTATES.
div.p: CHAPTER VI. PAUL STEINWAY DICTATES.

There was a tense silence, broken only by the'sharp breathing of one man, and the hur- ried restless movements of the other as he caught and folded a paper on the table. At last Clifford Hawke spoke, He first gave a low amused laugh. "Really, Steinway, you are very dramatic. Have you been on the stage since we last met, or have you inherited .a natural gift? However, since you are here now you had better sit down and• have a chat. You inter- est me very much." The expression on Paul Steinway's face changed from rage to one of suspicion. "It's no use your corning any games of bluff on me, Hawke; let's understand each other from the beginning. You know what I know—and I'm not going to pretend to forget it." • "Precisely," was the reply; "but why de- claim? I certainly did not care about renew- ing my acquaintance with you, my dear Stein- way—not on account of the little bit of infor- mation you happen to possess concerning what you are pleased to call my 'past life,' but because I have dropped all connection with the days that belong to my boyhood. I have begun a new life, built up a new career, and to succeed a man should make new friends."

"Which you seem to have done pretty well," was the sneer. "Anyway, I'm one of those 'friends,' Hawke, as you prefez to be called now, who has no intention of being dropped again. It's taken me years to save the money to get my fare, steerage at that, from Australia, and I have come into your hie to stop this time." A smile flickered across Clifford Hawke's dark face.

"May I inquire how you propose to stay? You know I am a powerful man now, and though I don't care for the idea of being hard on a man who's had my friendship in the past, I'm not the type of man to brook petty blackmail. I only mention this," he added, "as a reminder that I am not to be drawn."

"I called to sae you the other day and left a note," Steinway said slowly ."I discovered you in an odd way. I took a pair of boots to be soled, and when I called for them the man wrapped them up in a sheet of newspaper. I had nothing to read that night in my lodg- ing over by Waterloo, and I started to glance at that old scrap of paper, and there I read the life story in short paragraphs of certain men who are making their fortune in the City, aNd each one had a small photo by the side of his autobiography. I knew you at once, man, in spite of the years and the changed name. I knew that Fate had brought you across my path. It was too good a chance to be lost. I went to the free li- brary the next day, looked up a directory, and found your address and called with a note."

"In which you threatened me," Hawke laughed contemptuously. "A novel way of reopening an old acquaintance, my dear Steinway." "No threat was intended—then," he said sullenly. "I only asked for help—for a loan from one who had once been A pal—and to whom I had once acted as a friend—and the only reply I got was a dirty fiver, and the door slung in my face." "You spent the fiver, I presume?" was the quiet reply. "Yes, I did. You'd have spent it too, if you had been on your uppers, came the re- tort) "but in my. second letter .I said "

"tour seconeletter! What do you mean?" Hawke said sharply. "I got no second letter from you." "I wrote you a letter—not a long one—and told you that I held a secret you would find to your advantage to have kept from the rest of the world, and I asked you to see me, or I would speak." "I never got it," Hawke said. "You fool, to write a letter like that and then to lose it."

A bewildered expression crept into Stein- way's face. "I could have sworn that I had posted it!" he said sullenly. "I wrote it the other day and sat in -the Park. I—l am sure I posted it." "And I am equally sure you did not," was the curt reply. "You must remember that I am not the type of fool who lies about thing's when the truth serves me best. Where did you drop this precious letter of yours mak- iltg me the prey of any other blackmailing creature _who finds it?"

"If I didn't post it then I don't know what became of it," Steinway answered. "Any- way I thought I had. I'm not likely to want anyone else to share my secret!" Clifford Hawke was silent. It was bad enough that Paul Steinway should have come across his path, but still worse that a threatening letter addressed to him should have been lost in London! It was more im- perative than ever that no breath of scan- dal should touch his name—for the sake of the woman who was to be his wife. Ile knew that she respected him, perhaps ad- mired him—but one suspicion of dishonour- able conduct, even in the past that belonged to the days of his youth, and she would send him from her. She was proud, and made of such integrity herself that even a dishonest thought would be repugnant to her. No, at any cost he must keep Stella from ever know- ing anything of those days. lie turned to Steinway suddenly. A change had crept over him which the other man had been quick to notice. It was al- most as though he had at first hesitated to deal with him, but now the first shock was over he gripped the matter with all the force of his strong personality. "Look here! you ve got a price!" he said curtly. "In my experience of men there's not been one who hadn't—or women either for the matter of that. Tell me yours. Mind, I'm not intending to submit to any form of blackmail—ofily a damned coward would do that, and I'm not built on those Hum But if you want to sell your silence, put your price on it, and if it's fairly reason. able I'll pay." The other broke into a short laugh. "Spoken like the man of former days! on always let people know your mind pretty freely even in the old Tarragoola days. There always was a certain refreshing candour about you that made us look up to you!" Hawke made an impatient gesture. Those ram iniarPtlCo* bored and irritated him.

div.head: CHAPTER VII. A MAD CONFESSION.
div.p: CHAPTER VII. A MAD CONFESSION.

The light was waning in Jasper Tennant's studio. He had been working hard, putting into the picture on the easel all the concen- trated essence of that feverish energy that had gripped him since he had met Stella l'raine. At last he flung down his pallet and looked at the girl who had been silently regarding his movements for some time. "Finished for to-day, Lottie !" he said cheerfully "are Volt firoilP" She shook her head, and smiled. No, Mr. Tennant, I like being here, it's all so restful, so—so—" she paused for a word, "so different from everything else." He looked at the pretty fragile face with kindly eyes. The pale brown hair and forget- me-not blue eyes had a special claim on his sympathy because of their resemblance to that long-dead sister whose life had been i wrapped n mystery for so long. He was glad, for her sake, that he had been able to help this girl. "You'll soon grow tired of it, Lottie," he said slowly. "And I darcsay something far better will turn up for you to do. I saw that young lady the other day—the one who was so interested in you, you know—and she asked me about you. Perhaps she will call on you soon." The girl's face flushed warmly. "She is very good," she murmured. "I can't think why everyone is so good to me ; I seem to have found such good friends just when I was desperate with the need of one. That day," she went on quickly, "I had been dismissed from the place where I worked in a shop off the Tottenham-court-road, be- cause I was always fainting, and I didn't know where to turn. I walked about wonder- ing what I should do, and how I should pay the six shillings rent a week for my room, and then some wonderful good fortune sent me to you! " With trembling lips she added, "I "an never, never be grateful enough." "That's all nonsense: my child," he an- swered briskly. "I might answer that some wonderful fortune sent you to me; you see I have been able to go on with my picture now that I have found you, so it Cuts both ways." She shook her head with a sigh. Tennant looked at her with interested eyes. In her shabby old dress and worn leather shoes she was peculiarly attractive. There was a simplicity and delicacy about her that made him curious. There was nothing of the cockney about her, none of that pert readiness and cynical acquaintance with `gutterdom" that had been the characteristic of his former models. She was like a flower that had been plucked from a garden and, flung into the gutter. _ . _

"When did your mother die, Lottie? " he asked, after a pause. "When I was fifteen. We lived just out of London then, at Brixton, and mother used to do sewing, she did nothing else. She was al- ways sad, always sweet," the soft young voice went on. "and then one day I came home and found her dead."
"Poor girl! " Tennant murmured, "and your father died when you were younger, I suppose." She nodded.
"Yes-. ifoili-er never mentioned him—never. Only once she told me that he had broken her heart."

"Never' mind! The past is past, and now you have good friends who will see that you don't have any cause to go about fainting any more," Tennant said cheerfully. "When my picture is finished we must think of something else, only don't wovy—just look ahead! " As he spoke he put his hand on her shoulder and gave it a brotherly pat. She was so much younger than he was that it did not occur to him that the vivid blush that stained her pale cheeks was caused by his friendly act, or that in the girlish eyes lifted to his there was the dawning light of a woman's adoration.

But -another figure that suddenly appeared on the threshold of the studio, and saw that familiar attitude, recognised what the man failed to see, and when Jaspar Tennant, with an exclamation of pleased surprise, turned. to greet her, he wondered at the coldnese that had fallen over the lovely proud face. • "Miss Traine I what good wind blows you here? Is Lady Mary downstairs?" She shook her head, and a faint colour stained her cheeks.

"No, I was driving past, and I thought that I would leave a message, and then your old housekeeper said you had your little model here, 6o I changed my mind and came up." She glanced at Lottie, who had been look- ing at her with large awestruck eyes. Never, in all her life had the girl beheld such a dream of loveliness ,as thin tall, graceful girl in her clinging white gown and large picture hat. Lottie's eyes drank in with passionate admiration the vision of wealth and beauty. They saw the knot of malmaisons tucked into the belt, caught the gleam of a diamond brace- let on a white gloved wrist, and her nostrils were assailed by the faint perfume of some rare costly scent. Stella, as though conscious of the girl's silent admiration, smiled, and the coldoces left her face as snow melte be- neath the warm sun.

"So you are better, and able to sit to Mr. Tennant?" she said quietly. "I have been wanting to see you, but my time has been so dreadfully occupied that I have never yet found time. Can you come to me one day?" she wn.t. on "Come on Watinpschw and have tea with me, and we will have a 'nice talk. Mr. Tennant will tell you my address."

And then, when Latie had faltered out her fluttering thanks and disappeared, a sud- den silence fell between Stella and Tennant. "You said you had intended leaving a mes- sage for me," he said abruptly. "Wu it an important one? Can I do anything for you? I know it is absurd of me to offer my ser- vices," he laughed, "but anything I can do you may rely upon my doing with all my heart." "You are very kind," she replied, flushing, "but it was nothing important, Mr. Tennant. I was passing the studio and I thought I would run in and tell you myself that I was sorry that I should be engaged on Tuesday, and hoped you would forgive my not seeing you." "I understand," he said in a quiet tone. "I shall not call, then, Miss Traine ; you were right to say it was nothing important, just a broken engagement," he laughed bitterly, "that's all." "You are wrong to think that," she began hastily. "I am sorry—more sorry than I can say—but I cannot explain why I have asked you not to call—and if you are as generous as I think you are, Mr. Tennant, you won't ask me." Then before he could interrupt, she went on, "I am going to be married to Mr. Hawke in five weeks time, and of course I shall be very busy—with my trousseau." "Married in five weeks' time," he repeated. "Isn't that—sudden?"

"Yes, but my father and Mr. Hawke wish it," she said wearily, "and after all, what does it matter when I am married—next month or next year?" Her words, unguarded and spoken on the spur of the moment—the moment when a ar ••1 fora:rate to 101fLV 11 11,1.1. f—sent the blood

to his veinnn a flood of -surpthed joy. This marriage with the rich and powerful City man was not a love match—she had given her hand where her heart was not—and now was she regretting it? Little glances and phrases came back to him. She was not happy. This beautiful girl, whose love should crown any man's life, was eating her proud heart out through a sense of honour. . .

He took a step towards her. They were alone in the studio. The sinking rays of the sun caught a coil of her russet hair and burnished it into a band of gold. Never again might such an opportunity occur when they would be alone. "Miss Traine," he said hoarsely, "you are unhappy in this engagement—oh, you can't deny it 1" be went on passionately, as she raised a proud, angry face to him, "it is too late to pretend to me. You are unhappy, I repeat it—and you must break this engage- ment off!"

"Really, Mr. Tennant," she laughed, after a moment's angry surprise, "you are presum- ing too far in your idea of how far an acquaintance should go in dictating to any- one upon quite private matters. Please will you see me downstairs now?" she added in a trembling voice. "I am late as it is." His outstretched hand fell by his side. "Forgive me," he said humbly, "I had no right, I know. I am barely an acquaintance even, but your happiness is more to me than your opinion of me even! And I hate to see you unhappy! Oh, of course, I am 'imper- tinent' and presuming,' " he said, with a dreary laugh, 'but I can't help it—l love you She looked at him, with wide frightened eyes; the colour now stained her lovely face, and she flung out her hands uncertainly. "You—love me! How—how dare you tell me such a thing, Mr. Tennant !" He laughed recklessly and caught her hands in his.

"Because I am mad as well as impertinent and everything else. Because now I shall never see you again I will take this one and last opportunity to tell you the truth—that I love you. The very moment I saw you at Lady Mary's that day I knew that I lifted my eyes to a star that I could never hope to reach, but which no power on earth could prevent me from worshipping. There, now you know the truth," he finished, "there is nothing more to say." "But it is not finished," she panted, "there is more to say—there is--" She stopped suddenly. The door had oPened noiselessly, and Clifford Hawke's voice, cool and ominously self-controlled, said quietly: "Mr. Tennant is right. The comedy of friendship is finished, Stella. I will not com- ment, on Mr. Pennant's idea of • honour in making love to another man's future wife, but I can prevent him from repeating his offence by forbidding him ever to speak to you again!" "I must say one thing!" Tennant broke in quickly, and that is that Miss Trains was forbidding me to see her again, and I ac- cept her decree where I would not yours!" Hawke opened his mouth to speak, then turned his back on him with a contemptuous laugh. "Come. Stella. are you ready? or de you wish to speak to thie man again r She lifted her pale face to his and lookEd at him with dull eyes. "I am ready," she said quietly, and the next moment she had swept past him without glancing again at the tall figure near the window. Clifford Hawke followed her, a cynical smile on his lips. When he was alone Taspar Tennant broke into a bitter laugh. "I have lost her now—my madness has put an end to all pretence of friendship. In future I have nothing before me except work —hard, undying work to keep my mind from dwelling on what might have been. He turned and walked into the inner room. It was the room in which Clifford Hawke must have listened to his conversation with Stella. Ile looked round carelessly. Then moved by a sudden impulse, he went to his desk and opened it. Ire had intended show- ing her the letters and papers relating to his dead sister's life and marriage. She had taken an interest in the story, and he had promised to tell it to her. But now that was over. Suddenly he uttered an exclamation. The place—a secret drawer at the back of the desk, where he kept those precious docu- ments relating to that secret marriage—was empty. "Stolen!" he exclaimed. "Stolen —by whom?"

The death occurred on Saturday of Mr. Henry Soho Meld, J.P., of Whitworth, near Rochdale, whose family have maintained unbroken association with Whitworth since the middle of the seventeenth century. The deceased gentlemen, who was aged sixty-eight, had held every public office in the district except that of churchwarden. One son is the vicar of Whitworth, and another a curate.

Lymm. MAY QUEEN.-A meeting is to be held in the village next week to discuss the question of once more holding the old time May Queen Festival. CoNG REG ATIONAL CHRISTIAN SERVICE BAND.—A good number of young people attendad this meeting on Monday evening last, Mr A iLeath3r addressed the meeting from the passage of scripture " Ye are my witnesses."A very effective solo " I am thine :0 Lord." was rendered by Mrs Cyril Lewis Mr S 3 dney Miller presided. The meeting concluded with several short prayers from the mem! ers.
LY MM TERRITORIALS. ANNUAL DINNER AND PRESENTATICN OF PRIZES.

The annual dinner of the Lcmin detachment of the sth (Earl of Chester's) Battalion of the Cheshire Regiment was held in the Drill Hall. on Saturday even- ing. Among these present were : Lieutenant G It Hartley (enairman), Major England (Thelwall), and Sergeants II Holt, George llolt, W Daniels, H Carson and ex-Sergeants C E Ardern, Hugh Kirk, W Kirk and J A Thomason. Lieutenant Hartley said they were very anxious t) increase their numbers. (Hear, bear.) A short time ago the numbers dwindled to 23, but now he was glad to say they had over 50 men, and if they con- tinm d to increase they might have the use of the Drill Hall as in days of the old Volunteers. (Applause.) The idea seemed to have got about Lymm that the Terfi- torials were almost non-existent. Certainly it bad been very uphill work, but he could tell them that the Territorial movement bad come to stay. (Applause). He would like the men to help by getting recruits. Major Groves wrote: "I am leaving for the Continent

div.head: PRIVATE ARTHUR THOMASON,.
div.p: PRIVATE ARTHUR THOMASON,.
Of the Lynam detachment of the sth (Earl of Chester's) Battalion Cheshire Regiment, not only the best shot among the remits in the battalion but in the whole of the Cheshire Btigade.

Had I been able to be present I had hoped to express personally my congratulations to you and the non- commissioned officers of the detachment for the success you have met with in raising it to its present strength, and if you will only cantinue your efforts, I feel sure that they will be rewarded by again having a full company at Lymm in the near future. Should such a satisfactory result be brought about, I feel that I am warranted in guaranteeing the detachment a head- quarters secured entirely to themselves, either on the present premises or elsewhere." (Applause.) Lieutenent Hartley, continuing, said he would like to have a full company in Lymm and he was sure they would all like to see it. (Applause.) If , they all put their shoulders to the wheel they would I get the men' but it rested a deal with the men them- selves. With regard to the shooting, one of the recruits, Private Arthur Thomason, was an excellent shot. He was one of the keenest men they had ever had in Lymm —(applause)—aia.d had the best sclre not only of any recruit in the battalion but in the Cheshire Brigade. (Applause.)—itlajor England, of the East Lancashire A.S. Co., presented the prizes.—Sergeant-Instructor Moore appealed to those present to bring in their friends to join the detachment, reminding them of Colonel Saner's remarks v. hen inspecting the men in Lymm, that "he had never seen a smarter lot at drill." He was glad to have the honour of training Private A. Thomason, whose shooting was excellent. (Applause.) The other prize winners for shooting were Sergeant G. Holt and Privates EL Clare and T. Percival.—Some good songs were given by Privates Hog Hillier, A. Taylor, Douglas Kirk, and Mr. Vaughan. Mr. Bowen kindly acted as accompanist.

div.head: LYMAI LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. ANNUAL TEA AND SOCIAL.
div.p: LYMAI LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. ANNUAL TEA AND SOCIAL.

The event of the week as far as Lymm is concerned has been the annual Liberal tea and soiree, which was held in the Drill Hall on Wednesday evening, and con- sisted of a knife and fork tea, concert, and dance. The room had been decorated with strings of bunting and flags, whilst the platform had been tastefully beautified by the aid of plants, though the ladies appeared to have concentrated their decorative abilities on the tables, which, whether viewed artistically, or from a practical stand point, presented an unusually attractive appearance Though promoted by the Liberal Association, politics appeared to have been for once relegated to the back- ground, and there was little evidence of the turmoil of party strife amongst the 400 persons who sat down to tea, and who for the time being appeared to have little thought for anything beyond the business in hand. The arrangements for the tea were in the capable bands of , the Ladies' Committee, assisted by a splendid body of young helpers whose -,mtiring efforts to fulfil the desires of the diners called forth many eulogistic remarks. Tea over, willing handa soon cleared the tables, and shortly after 7.30 p.m. the concert programme was commenced. Mr. Mather efficiently performed the duties of chair- man, introducing himself in a short racy speech in which he thanked the audience for their presence, extendi g a hearty welcome to persons of all parties and hoped that the evening would afford everyone unalloyed enjoyment. Miss Margaret Collins gas() the next item in the form of a song entitled" My dear soul," which, judging by the applause, was well received. Mr Arthur Leyland came next with the popular song "Young Tom O'Devon" the able rendering of which brought in its train as an encore " A son of the desert am I." Mr Norman Blackett, elocutionist, followed this by a recital of " Billy Hodge." That he was a master of his art was only too apparent when towards the chasing scene of the race which he depicted, he had even the youngest member of his audience spellbound. his imitation of the aged student in his encore, too was very well done and caused much amusement to the audience. Miss Collins sang " When mandolines are ringing " in such a captivating style that she was requested to and kindly gave an encore. Mr Arthur Leyland's singing of Three for Jack " gave quite a rollicking tcne to the meeting and prepared the audience for Mr. Norman Blactett's next recital " The obstructive hat." He obligingly gave an encore "No thank you Tom." Mr T s 1 Eastharn accompanied with his usual skill. In the course of the evening Mr F Milne, of Bowdon, in the opening remarks of his address alluded to the death of the late Mr. John Alfred Swanwick, and testified in glowing terms to the excellent work he did in Lyram in connection with the Liberal party. Expressing his delight at being privileged to be present at such a gathering he said how proud he was to know that Lyrum th 3 °Len called Tory stronghold was at heart faithful to the Liberal cause, and urged the party supporters to " Press forward and be true." Making e reference to the dancing which was soon to follow ha said the Tories had danced but their effect was a poor, dull, dirge-like affair." We have the vision of a very bright future, and it rests with us to do our share to help the Liberal party." After the applause had subsided, he dwelt briefly on the policy of the party. He said that Home Bule was coming, as was also Welsh Disestablishment. Being a Churchman himself he did not wish to see harm come to the Church, but he most certainly advocated religious equality in Wales. Electoral reform's were also on the way. The present Government " he said " are deserving of our thanks for all their good efforts, and especially Mr Lloyd Georg for his great Insurance Bill." Ile touched upon the working finances, and benefits of the latter measure, and added that the present Government had given Old Age Pensions, and proved true to its pledges He stated that he had been hoping to have been able to give the name of the future Liberal candidate at this meeting but regretted that he was unfortunately unable to do so. After expressing his sympathy with the present member in his illness, he called for the best united efforts of all present to uphold the Liberal Party and so get a victory at the next election and let there be a Liberal member for this Division once more (Applause). Mr. J. D. B. Smith proposed a vote of thanks to the speaker, drairman, ladies and all who had helped to make the soiree such a great success. This was carried with great enthusiasm. The room was soon prepared for the dancing which commenced at 9.15 p.m. and was carried forward with great vigour by the younger persons present, though even some of the elder folk could' not allow their once youthful spirits to be dormant, for they too were noticed to have a fling now and again. Mr. George Undervvood's orchestra provided the music and Mr. Bell acted as M.C.

div.p: Winwick.

DEATH OF MR. THOMAS SMITII.—An old resident of Winwick, Mr. Thomas Smith, of Arbury View, passed away on Tuesday. Deceased was 62 years of age, and bed suffered for a long time from cancer, which was he cause of his death.

div.head: Stockton Heath.
div.p: Stockton Heath.

SocrA.L.—On Monday evening the workers of St Thomas's Band of Hope enjoyed a social evening in the Parish Room. Games of various kinds were heartily joined in and refreshments and fruit verved at intervals. Songs were given by Mr. Baguley. At the close Mr. Hallows thanked all the workers for their kind co-operation and help.
