div.p: Higher Walton.

THE LATE MR. JOSEPH TAYLOR.—The funeral of the late Mr Joseph Taylor, hay and corn dealer at Higher Walton for about 30 years, took place at St. John's Church in the presence of many relatives and old friends on Sunday. The Rev LJ T Darwall officiated. The psalm and two hymns were sung by the choir. Mrs Darwall was at the organ,and as the cortege entered the the church, played" 0 rest in the Lord." Mr Taylor, who was 82 years of age, died on tLe Bth February at the residence of his son-in-law, Mr G H Phillips, Hallflads-road, Warrington.

div.head: Moore.
div.p: Moore.

WHIST DRIVE.—A very successful parochial whist drive was held on Tuesday in the Milner Church Institute when about a hundred lovers of the game sat down. In the interval excellent refreshments were served in the adjoining billiard room. The first prize winners, lady and gentleman, were Miss Baguley of Norton and Mr S Whitlow of Preston Brook. WESLEY GUILD.—On Wednesday evening Mr Arthur Ward, of Padgate, gave a literary paper on " Oliver Goldsmith, his Life and Works "which was very much enjoyed by all present. Mr Ward is a keen literary student and always handles his subject in a masterly way and succeeds in keeping the interest of his bearers from first to last. An interesting point in connection with Goldsmith was his unbounded generosity even to the point of going into debt himself, in order to do it. A very hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Ward was pro- posed by Mr Lawton and seconded by Mr G Edwards.

div.head: Great Sankey.
div.p: Great Sankey.

NEWTON DIVISION LABOUR PARTY.—ThO above organisation held another most successful %%hist dtive and dance in the Sankey schools on Saturday evening last, about 80 being present. The arrangements were in the capable hands of the Entertaining Committee of the Building Fund scheme, and they are to be congratulated on thair efficient management. Special mention should be made of the untiring efforts of Mrs Haslam and Mrs Gill who were in charge of the refreshments and Miss Cooke who supplied the streamers for the decoration of the school. The IM.C.'s for the whist drive and dance were Mr Gill and Mr H Shaw. The prize winners were :—Ladies, Miss E West (Runcorn), and Miss N Gottlden gentlemen, Mr ['astern and Mr T Ditchfleld (Clock Face). The Brothers Misses J and F Hall supplied the music. The proceedings commenced at 8 p in. and about 1.30 a.m. all wended their way home after spending one of the pleasant evenings of the winter.

div.head: Penketli.
div.p: Penketli.

LABOUR PARTY.—The Local Labour Party were fortunate in getting Mrs. Simpson (of the Warrington Board of Guardians) to speak to them at their fortnightly meeting held on Wednesday evening in the Wesleyan Sunday School. The speaker took for her subject some of her experiences as a Guardian and gave many interesting impressions of the work. After a warm discussion Mrs. Simpson was heartily thanked. Mrs Cooke (President of Women's Labour League) was in the chair. DEATH- OF AN OLD RESIDENT.—There passed away suddenly on Wednesday morning one who was highly where respected, in the person of Mr P Aldcroft, at the advanced age of 80 years. Be had resided in the neigh- bourhood of Penketh, chiefly at Marsh Crossing, Fiddler's Ferry, for about 39 years. He was for over 20 years a platelayer for the L. and N.-W. Railway Co., and amongst his fellow-workers he was extremely popular. He was a native of Altrinchatn, but spent some 33 years in the Isle of Man. He was pensioned off by the Railway Company about four years ago. The funeral takes place to-day (Saturday) at Sankey Cemetery.

Padgate. WESLEY GUILD.-At the weekly meeting of the Guild Mr. Elliot delighted the members with a charming paper on " Books "Mr. Birchall presided. Speaking on " What to read" the lecturer gave those present good advice by urging them to make a point of reading the works of the great masters of English literature. Under the heading "How to read ' Mr. Elliot recommended the making of notes, and reading, during the same period, books of a different interest and character. On the subject of " Why we should read " the speaker commented on the foolishness of reading except for recreation and improvements. A vote of thanks proposed by Mr Duckworth and seconded by Mr E Andrews was accorded to Mr Elliot.

- - VISIT OF MR. JOHN DUXBURY,—The third entertain- ment of s series of five, in aid of the reduction of the debt on the new Wesleyan School premises was provided on Thursday by Mr. Duxbury the well-known professor of elocution of Manchester. In the afternoon Mr. Duxhury gave a recital "The story of Joseph." The old Bible story was placed before the audience in quite a new and attractive manner and many were the favour- able comments made by those present. In the evening "Jean Vol jean" was given For two solid hours Mr. Duxbury entranced his hearers by what appeared to us a faultlesg performance. Voice, gesture, and pronunciation were admirably controlled. Nothing was Broiled by (what is common to many amateur performers) exaggeration. The marvel is that so much of Victor Hugo's masterpiece could be so intelligibly condensed, as to be well understood by those who had not read the work. If anything more could have been introduced we should have liked to have had included the memorable and terrible death of Javert. How that sleuth hound of the police was finally conquered by the forgiveness and love of Jean Voljean, whom he bad repeatedly persecuted and terribly punished, wculd have made, in the capable hands of the eminent elocutionist, a most effective and dramatic episode. However, the wonder is not that so many fine passages and scenes were omitted, but that it was possible to include so much. Once or twice some of those present, not knowing the work applauded at an awkward moment, but on the whole the tense silence was more elcquent of rapt appreciation than the applause. We respect and hope there may be quite a raid upon the booksellers of our town for copies of • Les Miserables." They are cheap enough in all conscience and surely the audience of Thursday last, will supplement the recital by a careful reading of Hugo's principal works. WHIST DRIVE AND DANCE —A well-attended whist drive and dance took place on Thursday evening in the Church of England schoolroom under the auspices of the Primrose League. For the third time in succession Mrs. Whitlow was successful in obtaining the first prize in the drive,Mrs Robinson taking second honours. Messsrs R W Cousins and C Woods were the sue cessful gentlemen in the competition. The prizes were dis- tributed by Mrs C Turner end Mr P Royston was M.C. The Misses Hughes, Ball and Brandreth were the vocalists ins short concert arranged by Mrs Lightburn who also accompanied. lhe chair was °coupled b y Mr Mather. For the dance the duty of M.C. was capably filled by Mr James Critehley, while 111 Ir W Wainwright accompanied with his usual ability.

Photographic Society. Messrs Johnson and Sons, of "Scaloids" fame were vei y ably represented st the Society's Tuesday meeting by Mr. Curtis. After giving a shott history of this century-old London firm, and incidentally mentioning that £2OOO worth of gold per month is disolved by them for photographic materials ohne, he approached his subject of the " After Treatment of negatives." Every point was illustrated by experi- ments, whole plate negatives were cut in two and after one half had been reduced, or intensified, the two parts were handed round for comparison, and loud praises were called forth by the result. The dem- onstrator then treatea on the varnishing of plates, and the simplicity of the process was so definitely proved that several members are already converts to the idea, which ought to be far more generally carried into practice. Lastly Mr. Curtis dealt with retouching. His references all through the lecture to his firms pro- ductions were so humorous that all idea of " puff or advertisetrent seemed out of the question, and the wish was heartily endorsed at the close that he will be able to represent Messrs Johnson again next year. Twenty five were present.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
YOUNG LOVERS' TRAGEDY.

A sad story was unfolded to Mr. Coroner Ridgeway at Runcorn on Monday, at an inquest on Richard Brown James, of 40, Bentinck-street, Runcorn, who was drowned in the Weaver Canal at Weston on Sunday evening. The lad's father said he was not quite seven- teen years old. Sarah Evamv, a young girl, living with her aunt in Portland-street, Runcorn, said she had known James for three years. He met her out of chapel on Sunday night. They went for a walk round Weston, and lost their way. They took a road leading through Weston Soapory. It was very dark, and soon after they had passed through the works gates she thought she saw saw something shining. She said to James, " Isn't that water ?" He replied, "No ; it's the main road at last." The next thing she knew was that they were both in the water. " I was floating,' said witness, who was deeply distressed. " I got hold of a stone, I let go, but my foot csught in a stone in the bank, and I g'bt out." In reply to the foreman, witness said she and the deceased were holding each other's hands, and they fell in together. George Thomas Molyneux, of Weston, said be was going to work when Miss Evans ran to him and told him what had happened. He got a boathook—the canal was from six to ten feet—but could see nothing. The body was recovered in an hour. The night watchman at the works said the road lead- ing through the soapery to the towing path was a good deal used, especially by canal boat people. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death," and expressed sympathy with the bereaved.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday. Mr Spruce presided over a good attendance of members. Miss Bessie Dutton had written on behalf of the Ladies Visiting Committee asking for permission to bold the annual tea and old folks treat on the 22nd Inst. The desire was expressed that as many of the members of the Board as possible attend the function.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF CHAPLAIN.
div.p: THE APPOINTMENT OF CHAPLAIN.

TILE POSITION OF NONCONFORMISTS. Mr. Norman moved the following resolution : "That recognising the fact that there are Workhouse inmates not belonging to the Church of England this Board recommends that the restriction to appoint as chaplains Anglican clergyman only be removed and that all Poor Law Guardians be empowered to appoint Nonconformist and Roman Catholic chaplains also. And that this resolution be forwarded to the Local Government Board. _ _ _

After having submitted this Mr. Norman said he thought the resolution spoke for itself. It was simply advocating the policy that they as a Board had accapted. The only difference in appointing Nonconformists chaplains was that they had to call them visitors and they were not dignified with the name of chaplain. He wanted equality on all grounds—(hear,hear)—and it was simply on those grounds that he had put the resolution. Mr. Woodward said he was in sympathy with the principle of the resolution. Ho thought that when they approached the question of the chaplaincy of any public institution, all sections otreligions life of the country should have equal privileges. However, he did not object to the appointment of an Anglican chaplain. (Hear, hear). Mr. T. Wood in supporting the resolution, said he thought the present conditions of things was a standing libel on the Church of England. Nowadays the War Office appointed Nonconformist and Roman Catholic Chaplains to the Army and Navy. They evidently recognised that Nonconformists and Roman Catholics did as much for the country as:members of the Anglican Church. The only thing they could assume was that there were no Nonconformists or Roman Catholics in the Workhouse. It was a standing libel on the Church of England. The motion was passed unanimously. - RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday. Mr. T. Wright presided.
THE FRODSTIAM COMPLAINT.

The London and North-Western Railway Company wrote with regard to the Frodsham alleged nuisance that Messrs. Heywood and Massie hakappointed one of their staff to do the unloading work at Frodsbam Station and the traffic was being regulated as far as possible. The firm were taking delivery of the bones on the day of arrival, and should it happen by any chance that they could not clear the whole of the waggons the latter were taken away in the evening and brought back in the morning, so that everything possible was done to avoid causing a nuisance. It appeared that matters were being pushed to the extreme as there had not been any bone traffic at Frodsham Station for a considerable time, of which anyone could possibly make any complaint. The Council might rest assured of the combined efforts of Messrs Heywood and Massie and of the Railway Company to avoid causing a nuisance to anyone. Mr Woodward said to the inhabitants of Frodsham it was very important indeed. In looking after the interests of the people of the district it was not their intention as a Council to in any way minimise a trade in the neighbourhood of Frodsham. At the same time it was incumbent upon that Council when anything that might be injurious to health was happening, to do their best for the interests of the people. Was it possible that the traffic could be continued and no smell arise ? They were informedlthat it was possible to treat the bones in such a manner that they would not smell so much without having a deteriorating effect on them. I It was decided to leave the question in abeyance a mcnth and see if the smell nuisance was abated.

MOORE SEWERA OE. The Local Government Board wrote stating flat they had under consideration the report made by their Inspector (Mr. Drury) after the inquiry held by him with reference to the application of the Rural District Council for sanction to borrow £2,300 for purposes of sewerage And sewage disposal for the township of Moore. The Board were advised that the proposed sites for the sewage disposal works were rather small and they directed him to suggest that the Council should, if possible, arrange for a larger area. The Board suggested a number of additional works which it was thought ought to be undertaken in connection with the scheme and asked for amended plans and a revised estimate of the cost. It was decided that the Moore Sewerage Committee be requested to submit amended plans. ISOLATION HOSPITAL.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
DISTRICT NURSING AT ST. HELENS.

At the yearly meeting of the St. Helens Distrio Nursing Association on Tuesday, Miss Sinclair (hon. secretary), presented the report which showed that on the whole the work of the year had been rather less heavy, as, though there were more cases in March than in any previous month, in June and August there was less work than usual. One thousand, four hundred and thirty-three cases had been reported and bad occasioned 41,914 visits. Of the cases, 1,024 had recovered, 25 were relieved, 150 patients had died, 72 teen removed to hospital, 14 remeved from the books for various causes, ani 148 still remained on the books. The balance sheet, presented by Mrs. W. Pilkington showed that the receipts, including the balance from last year, amounted to £792, and the expenditure to £6BO, leaving a balance to the good of £ll2. The report was adopted, and the whole of the officials were re-elected. Colonel Pilkington, who presided, said no unwilling- ness had been shown on the part of the workpeople of the town to subscribe to the funds, but he understood there was some objection, which in his idol was ground- less. Ile hoped the work of the association would proceed as satisfactorily as it had done in the past and that the example of Messrs. NuttalPs" workmen, who contributed /20 a year, might be emulated by the work- men in the town.
CHARITY BALL.

The Charity Ball of the Roman Cath Aics was held at St. Heler Ft Town Hall on Wednesday night. There was a large attendance, and this seventy-fifth yearly function proved a great success both socially and financially. The arrangements were carried out by an influential cemmittee of which Mr. G. Stringfellow was chairman, Councillor Woodcock treasurer, and Mr. Joseph Sephton Eecretary. Music was provided by Mr. W. Dennettis band.
SERIOUSNESS OF WHOOPING-COUGH. DOCTOR ON PEOPLE'S CARELESSNESS.

Alderman Dr. Bates presided at the St. Helens Health Committee on Wednesday, when Dr. Buchan reported that the death-rate for the past three weeks had been 20.6, against 87 last year. Of the 117 deaths, forty-two had been children under five years of age. Whooping-cough had caused eleven deaths, and bron- chitis and pneumonia thirty-six. Mr. Fox :said whooping-cough "ought to be a notifi- able disease, and the parents ought to pay strict attention to dealing with it. Dr. Buchan said there was considerable looseness about the way people treated the matter. Patients ought to be isolated,but that was rarely done. Circulars had been given to all school children to tfike home, but they could not overtake all the ignorance and careless- ness there was on the matter. The Chairman said they could have large warning notices printed and posted in the town. Dr. Buchan said that in connection with the new St. Helens Act they asked for powers to make whooping- c Dugh notifiable, but could not get them. Dr. Jackson said that, unfortunately, whooping-cough was looked upon as one of the diseases of childhood, which every child had to go through. But the disease left a child with tendencies to all sorts of bronchial and chest complaints. It was fearfully infective, and if one person in a house had it, all the others would,unless very great care was used. He had seen men of seventy suffering from whooping-cough, but people did not credit it. Dr. Buchan reported that during January whooping.

Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Church.

The members of the choir spent a very pleasant even- ing on Saturday, on the occasion of their annual tea and social. Great credit is due to Mrs J Webb who had the arrangements for the tea in hand. After tea a very pleasant evening was spent in games and conversation. Light refreshments were partaken of. The literary evening of the Wesley Guild was held on Monday and took the form of a "Magazine" evening, the contents of which are Bent in by Guild members and friends, some of the articles being original and some from other sources. The magazine was compiled by (Mr C It Muir) who has nJt only the honour of being the editor of the magazine, but also the pleasure of reading its contents to a very attentive audience. This is the fifth yearly issue, all five of the magazines being in good preservation. The articles this year included one from the Connexional Secretary (Rev W 1.3 Fitzgerald). The contributions "A nest in the Gymnasium,"" A Choir's adventures at Rhyl "and "Notes on the society class" were much appreciated.

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ASSOCIATION

N.A. CENTRE. The weather being ideal on Saturday last enticed from twenty-five to thirty anglers out on the Sunday, several making for the Gowy with good intentions. However they did not catch their prey !easily. The best that was done was the creeling of three roach, the largest being 150 z. The water was of a reddish brown which made it almost impossible for the fish to see the telt. Several members took the 10.15 a.m. to Preston Brook and walked along the Acton Bridge length, their report being that they never saw the canal look better in the last three years. The society has put two specials up for competition in this length for eel. This at least will give membera encouragement to give the water a fair trial. The natives round about Acton Bridge had fair catches of eels after the ice boat had broken up the ice, one in particular taking at least four eels. The anglers who visited the Dutton Flashes end Little Leigh Pool were very much dissappointed to find them covered with ice one loch and a half in thickness. They had to break places to throw in their bait and it was only the sun, that made a gallant display towards 3 p.m., that kept them at their task until train time, sport being of the worst kind after trying every bait they had brought along. The General Meeting took place at the club house (Gladstone Arms) on Monday and was one of the most interesting meetings held for several years both in dealing with the rules of the society and finance, there being no less than £4 5s given by members towards special prizes for the present year. It was resolved that the officials' match, which takes place on the third Sunday in August, shall come up for discussion on the night the prizes are given out for the opening match. The society then will be better able to let the members know how they stand with finance. This will give them an idea of what sum to grant to the match. It was also moved that the entrance fee for the opening match be Is 3d. The Secretary has had news from the Crewe centre Secretary that the place is Billings Green and not Village Green as was stated some weeks back, and that the length is free from pollu- tion and very good results have been obtained. The following prizes will be competed for this coming season :—Seven sets at 8s ; a set bream, chub, roach, trout, dace, perch, gudgeon ; total, £2 16s. Specials, Ist, 2nd, 3rd, roach from Worton, Bs, 4s, 3s, Ist 2nd and 3rd ; eels from Acton Bridge 65,45, Ist ; pike (close season) ss, Ist ; Flounder, (close season) .is., Ist and 2nd ; Daddy Ruffe (open water). ss, 2s Gd, Ist ; roaoh (Norton juveniles), 53, Ist ; gudgeon (Norton juveniles), ss, Ist ; roach in July, 2s lid, Ist ; roach, August, 2s, Ist ; roach, Sep- tember, 2s, (from Norton), Ist ; six roach caught one week end from 12 noon Saturday till Sunday evening, open waters, ss, Ist ; novice not in prizes at opening match, 3s,lst ; novice not in prizes at annual match Si, this making the prize list for the season the magnifi- cent sum of £7 is. In all cases, Ist means heaviest weigh at end of season. Travelling cards have not arrived up to writing. Members wishing to use them this week end please call at club house on Saturday evening any time after 7.30. Assistant Secretary will be present with them if they arrive in time. Old cards cannot be used. A. S.

div.head: " Poverty and Christianity."
div.p: " Poverty and Christianity."

Preaching at the evening service at the Colborne- street Baptist Chapel on Sunday, the Rev. H. Ogden took for his subject "Poverty and Christianity." He said that it was wisely ordained by Providence that Christ should be born in a home of industry and of toil. It was too rarely in the worlds history that rich I men knew how to sympathise with the misery and want of the poor. One rejoiced that amongst the aristocracy of the earth there should be the Earl of Shaftesbury who was as noble in nature as his title and ever studied to relieve the miseries and poverty of the poor. The question had been asked " could a man be a Christian on Li per week ?" The Master as the text said" Had nowhere to lay his head." That was 20s. less than a £1 per week and yet no-one would suggest that He did not do as a true Christian should. Surely in the purpose of Providence it was meant that man should have a wider life, no matter how poor be was. There was a way for all to have the Word of God spoken to them. INSTANT REL.IEF

div.head: Mr. E. A. White as Humorist.
div.p: Mr. E. A. White as Humorist.

Sir—How am I to get out of the position in which you endeavour to put me in last Saturday's " Examiner?" If I question the accuracy of the report of my remat ks, it will be a new way, but cot original. If I apologize,l shall again lack originality. If I say that your ieading of my remarks can only arise from wilful misconstruction or a limited intelli- gence, I shall be rude. Nothing remains but for me to try and to live it down. Don't you think it is rather rude to say that I prse as somewhat of a humorist? Won't y,-,u apologize, or at least say it was a printer's error? -Yours &c., E. AUBREY WIIIIE.

div.head: Women's Clubs on Licensed Premises.
div.p: Women's Clubs on Licensed Premises.

Sir,—Would you kindly allow me apace to con- gratulate the Licensing Bench, Mr. M. Nicholls, Chief Constable, and all concerned, upon awakening from their.sleepiness to realise their duty, in stamping out the "abominable evil" that has been going on over 30 years in our midst. Imagine some 300 or 400 members attached to one house—the wife or mother of as many homes. Can we wonder why we have such an appaling state of affairs, numberless "undesirables" manufactured yearly, and " dumped " upon us by our own local " trade ? " We cannot estimate the blessings the magistrates have rendered to thcusands of helpless children and workingmen's homes by their action. As you rightly remarked in your leader, it will require strict surveillance to prevent the evil E till smouldering. Cannot the clergy cf all churches and others interested in the welfare of our town fellow up he movement ?—Yours,
A SUFFERER.

Brewster Sessions and Drunkenness in Warrington. Sir,—The Chief Constable has a pain presented his annual report with its sad tale of drink. As a town we still retain the unenviable position of being the second most diunken town out of ten of a similar size in the North. It is true the report stated that there was a decrease of three cases of chunkenness on the previous year, but the year 1910 showed an increase of 99 cases of dtunkenness as against the year 1909, consequently we have not got back to the normal condition of the more sober towns. After last year's startling increase in drunkenness we should have thought that the brewers who own all the licenced houses with few exceptions, would have instituted a searching inquiry and have cleared out those servants who were unable to discover when their customers had passed into the danger zone, for I believe it is !mphatically stated by the trade that the drunkard is the greatest menace to their business. However it such inquiry was instituted the results to say the least, have been disappointing as the Chief Constables report states that 477 Males and 101 females, total 581 were prcceeded against for dlunkenness in 1911, or 91 more than in 1909. Wake up Warrington, and try to realize the enormous amonnt of wretchedness; misery and suffering this debauchery brings into the homes of the people, and if the trade will not under- take to correct this glazing evil, then we must ask if the churches will not realize their plain dnty, and determine by all possible means to discover the source of this terrible scourge and deal with it in an effectual manner.—Yours, &c,
SOBRIETY.

div.head: Iron and Steel Trade.
div.p: The Iron and Steel Trade.
Mr. Harold Smith's " Usual Carelessness."

Sir,—ln reply to Mr. Harold Smith's statement at the Dump Exhibition that 'only a few years ago we were the leading nation in the manufactures of iron and steel goods. tut now we had dropped to third place, which seemed to please Free Traders." We admit (not any decline in cur trade, for that has advanced by leaps during recent years) our failure to maintain the premier position. This was not the result of Free Trade but was the direct outcome of the enormous development of steel manufacture. In Germany this was traceable to the discovery in 1379 of the basic process by two young chemists, Thomas and Gilchrist, whereby the vast quantities of phospheric ore Germany possessed, until then unworkable, could be utilised for the purpose of making steel. If Mr. Harold Smith will examine the German returns he will find that nine-tenths of the product of their furnaces is by the basic Bessemer and basic open hearth process. In America the development was due to her vast national resources in coal and iron ore, her large requirements for railway construction, &c. In 1805 about 18,000,000 tons of ore were sufficient for the world's needs for one year, now nearly 150,000,000 tone are required. We are therefore not surprised that a small country like Great Britain should have to lose the premier position as an iron and steel pro- ducing country to one like America, about 49 times greater in area and twice the population. As Free Traders we have never claimed that all cur success as a manufacturing nation was due to that policy, bat we claim it is the best in the interests of the great bulk of cur people. Mr. Harold Smith, with his usual carelessness, made a mis-statement when he said the returns took no cognizance whatever of quantities. If be studies the returns be will find both values and quantities given. One impertant factor in cur trade is the bearing imports have upon exports. I find that in nearly every instance over a fairly long series of years when imports are high exports are high also. That in the iron and steel trade, the proportion of imports to exports remains a fairly constant quantity, imports ranging from one-fourth to one-fifth of the amount of our exports. Another mig-statement of Mr. Harold Smith's is that the character of cur exports are raw and semi-manu- factored and that exports of more highly finished articles are declining. This is manifestly false. Instead of exporting less and less finished goods we exported lastitear £10,518,207 more than in 1910. He also said we imported something like £15,000,000 less of raw material this yearlban last. The figure is £13,012,911. But if be refers to the quantities he will find that fully half of this is accounted for in the drop in the price of rubber. It is absurd to gauge the prcsperity or otherwise of our trade on the returns of one section for one year. With the exception of 1910, the year 1911 was a record one for imports of raw material, imports of all classes combined, and exports also eclipsed all previous records. Thanking you in anticipation, yours faithfully, J. ELWELL.

div.head: SALE OF A CHIP-SHOP.
div.p: SALE OF A CHIP-SHOP.
Alleged Misrepresentation.

At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday,before his Honour Judge Stanger, Samuel Hawkins sued W Chadwick, of 9, Mason-street for damages for mis- representation on the sale of a fish and chip potato business, carried on at 114, Winwick-road, Warrington. Mr Steel appeared for the plaintiff and Mr Browne appeared for the defendant. Mr. Steel stated that in consequence of seeing an advertisement in a local paper on the 23rd September with regard to the sale of a fish and chip potato busi- ness complainant and his wife called on the defendant the same evening. It was explained that the plaintiff had had an accident and that he was looking for a business that would keep him. The defendant stated that he business had kept them and that they had saved money. When asked what the profits per week were the defendant said they were E 2 5a in winter and .C 2 lOs in summer. Out of this sum they hild to pay Bs. per week for rent. The defendant gave as his reason for selling the business that he had had his old situation offered to him and he was desirous ot taking it. Arrangements ware made for the purchase of the business for £23. The money had been paid but it had been ascertained that instead of the profits showing the amount stated by the defendant they had not averaged more than 245. per week. Evidence was given on both sides relative to the value of the business, land the case was subsequently adjourned to March 7th.

div.head: LETTER FROM MR. F. STOTT.
div.p: LETTER FROM MR. F. STOTT.
LICENSING POLL IN NEW ZEALAND.

Concurrently with the election cf Parliamentary representatives the licensing poll took place in New Zealand. Under the Act of 1910, every person (male and female), who was born in the Brit' sh Empire, or Others who had been naturalised in New Zealand, and had resided for twelve months in the Dcminion, was entitled to vote. Exceptional interest was taken in this question aud, in many districts, the interest in the licensing poll was greater than was taken in the election of Parliamentary representaiives. It may to of interest to your readers, to explain the differerce between the old and the present Licensing Acts. At previous elections the questions submitted to the electors were :

a f I vote for continuance of licences. t I vote for no licences being granted. b f I vote for no reduction of liceneei. I vote for a reduction of licenses. Each Parliamentary constituet cy was created a separate licensing district, which, in my opinion, owing to the small areas affected, was one of the weak places in the cld Act, and is also in the present Act. Take Wellington City as an instance. The City is divided into five Parliamentary districts, and at the elections in 1908 two diatricts carried no licence. The result as that in many instances the hotels were closed on one side of a street, and were left undis- turbed on the other side. This meakrit st is more apparent in the cities than in the constituencies cover- a large area. REDUCTION OF LICENCES.

The question cf reduction was far from satisfactory and has now been omitted. Whet° reduction was carried no proportion of licercts to be eliminated was sprcified, and it depended entirely on the coustitution of the licensing authority, whether the :eduction should be one, or fifty per cent.

div.head: PRESENT ACT.
div.p: THE PRESENT ACT.
The Act of 1910 eliminated the question of reduction and the two lames voted upon at the recent election were :

\ I vote for licences being continued. 41) I vote for no licences being granted. (b, I tote against National prohibition. I vote for National prohibition. When the Bill was before the House, the intention of Parliament was to count all votes for and against local no-license, as votes for, and against national prohibition. To this the no-licence party offered a strong prcArst, with the result that the Government decided to take separate votes on the two issues, with ballot papers of two distinct colours. THE THREE-FIFTHS HANDICAP. To carry local no-licence, or national prohibition, sixty per cent, of those voting must be in favour of it. When the Bill was being discussed, there was a strong agitation in favour of reducing the handicap to fifty- five-sixtieths. The importance of this alteration will be recognised when it is known that if the concession had been granted to the no-licence party, national prohibition would have been carried at this the first attempt. Fifty-six per cent of the voters were in favour cf national prohibition, and the result has been an unpleasant surprise for the brewers and their allies.

LOCAL NO-LICENCE POLL. The poll for local no•licence was d:sappointing, for no new districts went " dry." On the other hand, none of the no-licence districts carried restoration, but in one or two instances the votes for restoration were higher than the votes for continuance were in 1008. The importance of making the questions of local and national no-licence separate issues, will therefore be seen by the different results. In two no-licence districts restoration wculd have been carried on a bare majority vote. THE ROMAN CATHOLIC VOTE.

The opinion is expressed in some quaiters, that National prohibition would have been carried, but for the action of Archbishop Redwood (Roman Catholic) who on the eve of the poll issued an injunction to his followers, asking them to vote against National Pi ohibition on the grounds that, if prohibition was carried, the next stop of the yrohibitiouists would be to stop the importation or wines and spirits for sacramental purposes and thereby interfere with, if not to actually prohibit the observance of Mass. This reason was a most trivial one, for the prohibitionists have repeatedly declared, that it is not their desire to try and prohibit the importation of wines and spirits intended for sacramental and medicinal purposes.

"BUNG'S" TACTICS. The campaign of the brewers and their supporters in their opposition to prohibition, reminded me of the agitation against the Licensing Bill some years ago in England. If anything, their tactics here were even more unscrupulous than those employed at home. The Press was used to a large extent by the inser- tion of advertisements in such a way that only the most careful readers would detect that they were not actual news columns, for which the editorial staff were responsible for having written. Posters and handbills were circulated by the hundred thousand, and the electors were warned against voting prohibi- tion on the grounds that it would mean a serious loss of revenue, and the workers would be heavily taxed to make good the loss; that unemployment would become a chronic feature, that the business of the Dominion would become stagnant (which is true as Tar as the drink business is concerned) if prohibition was carried. However, the future from the brewers' point of view is far from bright.—Yours FRED STOTT.
Roseneath, Wellington, New Zealand. January 3rd, 1912.

div.head: ESPERANTO SOCIAL. The Mayor and International Peace.
div.p: ESPERANTO SOCIAL. The Mayor and International Peace.

The last of the three socials held during the season in connection with she Warrington Esperanto Society took place in the Club rooms on Wednesday evening. There was a good attendance including the Mayor and Mayoress, Mr A Nil d, Dr Harold Joseph, Miss Taylor, Mr J Fulton Smith, Mr and Mrs Rhodes Marriott (Manchester), Mr Robert Jackson, Miss F J West, contingents of Esperantists from Chester, Liverpool, Widnes, and St. Helens and others. A successful whist drive was conducted and dancing was indulged in to music supplied by Mr. J. Caldwell. After refreshments had been partaken of the inter- national anthem the " Espero' was sung by all the membe,s present. Mr. John McCarthy gave a recitation on Esperanto and Mr. Rhodes Marriott made a short speech in the language, that those present might be able to form some judgement both as to its powers of expression and its musical sound. The federation ode "Al la Esperantistsro " was sung to the tune of " bleu of Harlech," rad Mr. F. J. West gave a good inter- pretation of " The Village Blacksmith" put into Esperanto by himself. At an interval in the proceedings tne Rev. It. B. Prircavesi as the recently re-elected president of the Warrington Esperanto Club gave an address of welcome to the visitors. It was pleasing for him in the name of the local club to welcome their many friends both locally and those who had come from other towns round about. It was a sign of sympathy on their parts towards the movement. The inclination of most people towards the movement was one of apathy if not antipathy. That was the great enemy they seemed to have to fight in Warrington. The people did not rise until they were addressed personally. He was glad to think those present came from a spirit not negative but positive. Of the movement, it was progressing favourably. Persons now who wished to travel, by writing to their National Esperanto Association could obtain the names of Esperanto Consuls in the majority of the great towns and cities of Europe. Consuls who were ready to give up their time gratis and make the stay of the Esperantist as enjoyable as possible. In conclu- sion he said he would be very pleased to think,that now the public's sympathy had been enlisted the public would rise and join the movement. (Applause). The MAvon, in a abort speech said, that for some time past he had been interested in the movement. He had been impressed that night by the language both as to its sound and also its adaptability and qualifica- tions for singing purposes. The effect had been most pleasing, the easy manner in which people could com- municate with each other had also struck him. He was persuaded that if the movement was taken up in the spirit with which it was intended to spread a net work through the different nations, it would be one of the greatest ventures for the abolition of war. The language looked difficult to learn whereas it was not. Those who had taken it up had assured him of that. Ile wished the movement every success in the town. (Applause).

ISS I. JENKS (" Nita,") MIL W. TYNAN (" Alfredo.")
"THE MOUNTEBANKS."
OPERATIC SOCIETY.

Bold brigands, coy, light-hearted peasant maids and ingenious mountebanks hold possession of the Parr Hall platform this week and right merrily do they entertain the audiences attracted to the annual per- formances of the Crosfield Amateur Operatic Society. It is in no spirit of formality that we congratulate these enterprising amateurs upon the addition of another conspicuous success to their bright record. They have every reason to be proud of their latest incursion into operatic realms, for their production of "The Mountebanks " is in some respects superior to anything previously attempted. When one considers the necessarily restricted field from which the society draws its talent, the results obtained are more than creditable they are remarkably good It is not often that provincial audiences have the opportunity of seeing "The Mountebanks'and the choice of this work was suffi- cient to arouse a considerable degree of interest in the performances. It possesses the advantage of being well within the powers of a well-equipped amateur organization and does not call for much of that highly emotional element which it is so difficuit for the budding aspirant to simulate with conviction. The general atmosphere of the opera is a delightful abandon and griety and here again the amateur, unless well conehe I, generally finds it difficult to appear natural and at ease. Thanks to the excellent supervision of Mr. Charles D. Law, who was responsible fur the dramatic side of the enterprise, ths members of the society—speaking collectively—had banished all stilted or self-conscious tendencies and appeared to revel in the incidents of the evening. Of the plot it need only be said thet, having emanated from Sir W. S Gilbert's fertile brain,it is—Gilbertian ! There is a most entertaining secret society of robbers who have a perpetual vendetta against dukes and duchesses and try to live up to their inspiring motto " Heroism without risk." But their exploits would be comparatively tame without the intervention of Pietro, the proprietor of the troupe of 3.1 tuntebanks, and his wonderful potion. It is the latter which causes all the com- plications, for by taking a draught of the mysterious mixture, people immediately become what they pre- tend to be —with results Coat are highly diverting. 'lhe music by Cellier, is very light—some of it captivatingly so—but there are few melodies which really haunt the ear or produce any lasting impres- sion. The orchestration,toreis not of striking interest. Nevertheless.the general effect is bright and sparkling and, in the hands of competent enthusiasts, the opera gces with a cheerful awing throughout. Although the audience at the ()peeing performance on Wednesday evening was not so large as might reasonably have been expected, it soon became appre- ciative—and that in an eminently cordial way, the applause which greeted all the principal numbers being unmistakably hearty, but not more so than was deserved. The beautiful stage p:ctures ie which pretty rural scenic settings, many-coloured costumes, effective grouping of characters and animation of movement were richly blended, excited great admira- tion. Particularly striking was the second scene—the exterior of the monastery by moonlight. Most of the principals had achieved distinction in previous operas, and their r e-appearcnce was welcomed. An admirable discrimination was exercised in the allocation of the various pia., with the result that each was adequately sustained. Miss C. Hastings added to her laurels as the tantalising Teresa, the village beauty. In the first act she was vivaciousness personified, and bewitched the young peasant Alfredo by her fascinating coyness and the cruelly light way in which she parried his advances. But what a change in the second act when, through the operation of the magic philtre, she began t. love Alfredo with an ardour akin to distraction, and was transformed from the most irresponsible into the most serious of maidens. Miss Hostings succeeded in realizing these contrasting moods with vivid effect and the refine- ment of her portrayal won general commendation. Her sweet and flexible voice was heard to distinct advantage in the sprightly " my opinion," and the plaintive " Where's my duck-a-deary," the latter being invested with a semi-tragic air in keeping with the suddenly changed outlook. Mr. W. Tynan gave u ' very praiseworthy portrayal of Alfredo —by turns the importunate lover and the amiable duke comforting himself well and, having overcome a little stiffness in the earlier stages, thoroughly entering into the spirit of the part. His voice, though light, is of very p'ea-ant quality and he sang with taste and expression. Miss C. Rigby, who made such a promising debut last year, achieved another signal success as the loving but much-detested Hltrice. Confident and self. possessed, she made the most of her opportunities without ex iggeratine, and her singing was excellent in tone and enunciation. Mr. E. Walker was a fear- some looking but hmaevolently inclined leader of the Tamorrae, the outlaw hand, and filled the part most satisfactorily. From the histrionic standpoint, the portrayal was an advance on any of his previous appearances in opera—he displayed greater freedom and dash, with a complete realization of the humorous possibilities of the character—whilst his principal song "high, Jerry Ho ! " was given in breezy style and proved popular. Mr. J. E. Newns afforded further evfdeoce of his versatility by a capital study of Pietro. Last year he was the miserable, avaricious miser; now he was the voluble, irrepressible proprietor of the Mountebanks, always ready to devise neer means of cajoling coins from the crowd. The facility with which be was able
MR. H. GRIFFITHS (" Risotto.") MISS C. HASTINGS (" Teresa.")
SOCCESSFOL PERFORMANCFS BY THE CROSFIELD AMATEUR

to take up such an entirely different type of character- isation was extraordinary and he must be credited with a large share of the honours of the production. lie was never at a loss for the right word or gesture but we thought he might with advantage have put more realism into his alarm at the prospect of the company drinking the mysterious wine. Act 2 made greater demands upon Mr. Newns, for he had to display the agonising symptoms of slow poisoning, but he was quite equal to the novel and trying task. Miss I. Jenks was a charming Nita, the dancing girl,and the pretty dance with which she introduced herself was very gracefully performed. She also sang sweetly and acted in an attractive and unaffected way, the piqttant passages with her solemn-faced companion ' creating considerable merriment. Mr. A. Davis, who I scored a decided success last year as the bailie's clerk, did even better as Bartolo, the clown with tragical aspirations, a mournful countenance and a sepulchural voice. How he managed to preserve such a woe-begone demeanour was something to marvel at and when he essayed a "new lea ding " of Hamlet the mirth of the audience was unbounded. Never was there a better instance of a part fitting its perLrmer like the provertial glove. The fun waxed fast and furious when Nita and Bartolo were transformed into automata, the stiff clock-work movements and stony stare showing how carefully they had been trained to represent these wonderfully " life-like " yet not alto- gether human figures. The duet "If our action's stiff I and crude "was cleverly done and received the waimest applause of the evening. A notable first appearance in a principal part was made by Miss M. Blackburn,who displayed uncommon aptitude and was a complete success as Minestra —first one of the happiest of brides and later, after the fateful draught, a tottering old woman. Miss Blackburn is a very acceptable vocalist and all her worth, whether sung or spoken, could be I heard with distincteess in all parts of the house. Mr. H. Griffiths did exceedingly well as Risotto. He has gained in confidence educe last year, and sang and acted brightly and with more finish. Mr. T. Lawton was a j )vial, rotund innkeeper and other parts were capably sustained by the following :—Giorgo, Mr. H. Foden ; Luigi, Mr. S. Bowyer ; Peppo, Mr. C. Dagnall ; page, Master James Callan. Of the con- certed numbers, one which delighted the assembly immensely was the trio " When gentlemen are eaten up with jealously," with its tick, tick accompaniment, in which Bartolo, Nita and Pietro were most success- fully associated. The chorus did its work with commendable whole- heartedness, the singing being crisp and the blend of voices good. Some little misunderstanding °centred lin taking up the finale of the second act, but matters were quickly righted and the curtain was rung down on a scene of beautiful movement to the strains of a hearty, rollicking chorus. Particularly pleasing was the waltz chores, "An boar, 'twill rapidly pass," with its delightful rhythm and fascinating action. The orchestration is not on very ambitious or exact- ing linea, and gave the instrumentalists small oppor- tunity to distinguish themselves. However, they devoted themselves to the work with care and discretion, the music being neatly and tastefully played. If anything the desire to subordinate the orchestra to the voices was carried to extremes—at times almost to the point of suppression, with the result that in some of the numbers the pianoforte appeared to have practically undisputed possession. This, of curse, enabled the soloists to make them- selves heard without undue effort, but there was a loss in general effect. Mr. A. Trow, who undertook the arduous duties of conductor, is to be congratulated upon the tact and skill with which he directed his forces and upon the happy results of what must have been long and painstaking preparation. To the producer. Mr. Charles D. Law, a special meed of praise is due for the smoothness with which everything passed off. As dramatic coach he had worked wonders and the zest with which the company threw themselves into the busy' action of the opera did him infinite credit.

Acknowledgment must a'so be made of a host of willing helper., prominent amongst whom were : Captain G. H. Crosfield, president • Mr. B. S. Townroe, director and treasurer; Mr. G. Hall, hon. secretary ; Mr. G. B. Dean, stage manager: Mr. J. Taylor, business manager ; Mrs. Law and Mrs. Bickford, makers-up. There was a larger audience on Thursday, and the performance, which passed off without the slightest hitch, was received with splendid enthusiasm. Last evening was a special military night when officers from Orford Barracks and the Territorial battalion attended in good fol ce. The performance had also the patronage of bir Gilbert and Lady Greenall, Mr. Harold Smith, M P., and Mr. A. H. Croefleld. There should be a crowded house for the concluding performance this evening. The proceeds will be divided between those three admirable institutiors - the Infirmary, the District Nursing Association and the Citizens' Guild of Help.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

There was a good meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society on &today. Mr 11 Osborne presided, and spoke upon Diligence." Mr Drewitt gave the address upon " Friends in love." Friendly actions were often seen, sometimes misunderstood, sometimes were not sincere ; but a true-hearted, whole-hearted, constant friendship was always done in love, not fur what could be received in return. It was more blessed to give than to receive. The Bible was full of examples of affection, love and constant devotion. The Chairman read the lesson and Mr. Payton presided at the organ. The Secretary said he had received a message from the new President of the Lancashire Federation,which he would read to them next Saturday. The New Church.

The Reading Meetings in connection w:th the New Church Mission are being continued at Atkinson's Cafe each Monde; evening. They are conducted alternately by the Revs. J. Howarth (of Bolton) and W. H. Claxton (of Elearsley.) The subject of study and discussion is the work by Emanuel Swedenborg, entitled " The Heavenly DoctriLe of:Ahe New Jerusalem." Considerable progress has been made since the reading of this work was commenced in October last. On February 5,11 the Rev. J. Howarth explained the sections relating to " Merit " and " Repentance " and the "Remission of Sins," and on February 12 the Rev. W. H. Claxton dealt with the latter portion of the section on " Repentance" and the important chapter on " Regeneration." The interest is well maintained. It is hoped a further series of lectures may shortly be gh en.

St. John's Presbyterian Church. On Sunday evening Rev. W. Reid preached from I. Corinthians sill., 13 " The greatest of these is love." He spoke of the contention that had arisen in the Corinthian Church as to the relative importance of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which had come to be looked upon as personal distinctions. Their value was dwelt upon, and it was shown that St. Paul, having them himself in large measure, could afford to make the declaration that the possession of them all could not compensate for the lack of what he termed the greatest of gifts, love. The preacher went forward to define this to show how only it can, and why it should be obtained. Its eternal nature bespoke for it the greatest of values. When faith having served its day bad vanished into sight, and hope emptied itself into realisation, love would shine the brighter and never be replaced by anything greater than itself.

Cockhedge Mission, Brick-street. A very successful concert was given at the above mission on Monday evening last by Mrs. Ziba Armitage's sewing class, in support of the new building scheme. The programme consisted of a floe tableau entitled " Madame Palaver's Waxwork Exhibition," which was greatly appreciated by a large audience, sorae very quaint old-time figures being shown, and as each was introduced to the audience by a brief description from Madame Palaver (Mrs. Hewitt) they sang, recited, or acted their part, according to the character represented. This was followed by a national tableau by children,and concluded with songs and recitatios by Mesdames Pennington, Whitby, Holmes, and Mills. Mr J Phennis, in moving a vote of thanks to these ladies for their efforts on behalf of the new building (which will realise about £3), exhibited the plans and outlined the progress of the Building Committee's work. Mrs P Edelsten occupied the chair.

div.head: Church Anniversary at Legh-street.
div.p: Church Anniversary at Legh-street.

Toe Primitive Methodist Church at Legh-street celebrated its anniversary on Sunday. The preacher for the occasion was the Rev. M. IL Chapman of Leeds, who was minister here some years ago. The services of the day were of a remarkably high order and many of the hearers will not easily forget the forceful and practical utterances of the preacher. In the afternoon, the choir gave a musical service under the leadership of Mr. A. Spruce, Mr. T. Tanner officiating at the organ. The soloists were_ Airs. A. E. Hoyle and Messrs. S. J. Hamilton and N." Cook, jun., the chair being occupied by Mr. J. T. Rowland. On the Monday evening the Rev. M. H. Chapman lectured upon " The Church and Social Service." Mr. Chapman proved to be master of his subject, and impressed his hearers with the fact that there is much for the Church to accomplish before it has fulfilled its high calling. Mr. .J. Broadhurst was in the chair. A rots of thanks was moved by Mr. J. Griffiths and seconded by Mr. A. E. Hoyle, B.A. In reponding, the lecturer spoke of his happy associations with the church in the past, and of the joy he had experienced in renewing old acquaintanceships, Baptist Meeting at Latchford. In connection with the Warrington and Mid- Cheshire Sub-District of the Lancashire and Cheshire Association of Baptist Churches,a series of meetings of a highly successful character were held at the Baptist Church, Latchford, on Thursday of last week. The first meeting was at four o'clock when a sermon was preached by Bev. T E Ruth, Southport. The preacher took his subject the Christian worker in his co-partnership with God and with Jesus Christ in the carrying on to its completion the work commenced by the Creator as recorded in the earlier pages of the book of Genesis. He carried his hearers through the years of the old dispensation showing them how God's faithful ones bad taken their share in the Divine plan,and how in later days, those who identified themselves with Christ in His earthly ministry and all those in the ages follow- ing, had fulfilled their part of the great yet still uncompleted plan commenced "In the beginning." At the close of this service tea was provided and partaken of by a company of about GO. In the evening a public meeting was presided over by Mr. Bradford, president, who,efter a brief but thought- ful address called upon the Rev. A. Lewis, Wigan, to address, the meeting. Mr. Lewis, who has paid several visits to the churches in this neighbourhood, was accorded a very warm reception, and delivered a very stirring and helpful address, dealing with several characteristics of the suonessful Christiin Church, pecially commendinF the cultivation in the church life of " Sprituelity; " Horneliness," " Joyousness," " Prayerfulness " and " Activity." After the singing of an anthem" There is a green hill," by the choir, Rev. A. E. Robinson of Manchester addressed the meeting. This was the first visit paid by Mr. Robinson, but he so captivated his audience by his telling message, that he has won his welcome for any future visit be may Fay- Mr. Robinson spoke as to the type of men required ; they must be dependable " men, they must be distinguished for their " willing- ness " and to ensure success they must be that class of men who are not to be deterred by any obstacles but must " keep on keeping on " all the time, only leaving off when called to higher service, when those who had been impressed by their example would begin where they left off. Following upon this the choir rendered another anthem and although not gathered in full force proved themselves to to a choir of no mean abilty. The last speaker was Rev. H. Ogden of Golborne- street and there seemed to have been a very happy arrangement with regard to the speakers and their messages ; for whilst those going before had dealt with the Church and the men who constitute the Church, it remained for Sir. Ogden to describe the work that lay to hand. This he did in a vivid manner, having called upon those who ranked themselves amongst the workers 'to be up end doing. The work of social reform he urged to be the (work of the church, and he claimed for a stronger attitude and more definite action regarding so many of the things thet tended for unrighteousness, and made it harder for a man or a woman to live a clean pure life than one that was not clean and pure. In SO far as the Church failed to see these things, and to put her whole energies into the struggle for uplifting the people morally, socially and spiritually, she failed to justify her calling, and his appeal to his hearers was that each one would see his own individual responsibility, and rise up to do his share in the great divine plan of redemption.
the Furnishing Problem —Solved.—
Hugh Price Hughes. Lecture to the Members of the Wesley Gull

The annual guild festival in connection with Of! Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church was held Sunday ea; Monday last. The Rev. W. J Tunbridge, of Birkenhesa delivered two interesting and educational sermons ofx Sunday. In the afternoon the guild choir rendered the cantata "Jesus at Bethany " with much taste, under ty alfe conductorship of Mr. W. Ilipkiss. Mr. J. V" Hayward, J.P., occupied the chair. Mr. W. Pearce waa at the organ. At the close of the ordinary service ea Sunday evening a guild devotional meeting was held' There was a good attendance on Monday evenlog when Mr. Tunbridge gave his popular lecture on " Huila Price Hughes." Mr. R. COBBETT presided, and referred to his 1-5. years' association with the Wesley Guild. They hea,T a great deal nowadays of the word " Organise." would be good for them to organise their lives on 9 higher and better scale than had hitherto been the case. Mr. TUNBRIDGE, who was accorded a laarty welcome, said the Rev, Hugh Price Hughes was at once th° central figure of modern Methodism. In regard to scholarships he would not say that Hushes equalled some men who bad been connected with that body c'r even that he was the greatest preacher or orator. What he claimed of him was that no man had understood Bad stamped his own personality on Methodism as he had done. John Wesley was the man in the earlier days of the Methodists but what he did at the begining Hughes had done for the latter part. Some men were born before their time or after their time, but Hughes Wa9 one of those who had come just at the right moment. He was wanted and he knew it, and with a great force of character and a strong zeal for righteousness he carried out what was his aim from the beginning- Anything that was engaging the attention of the peof!la had his fullest consideration. He was always a social reformer, a preacher of the Gospel and 8 Nonconformist Statesman. Hugl‘es had change& the entire outlook of Methodism and what a change it was. He taught them that it vrss not only their duty to Pray,lbut to enter the ballot bolt. to take part in the work of social reform. They were to face important social problems during th 3 nest years. A solution was going to be found with the members of the Church, or without them, but than' would never have Christian laws unless Christian mea, made them,and they could never have a better Englaeo if there was a reluctance on the part of the people to discharge their public duties. They had a duty not only to themselves, hut to the community. The wal in which they could give a demonstration that they loved God was by loving the brethren and engaging in the service of their f silo cv.s• Hughes showed the importance of the work of the 130' for the Church ; women also found a new place la Methodism, and he taught them all to be of service ta Christ in the expounding of the Gospel by the power of intellect. Hughes finished his work, and a great work it was, and having finished it, God called him home. The rev. gentleman was accorded a hearty vote of thanks at the close of his lecture. Thanks were also accorded to Mr. Timms and those who had taken part n the services on Sunday.

Holy Trinity Church. Complete success attended the congregational 'social in connection with Holy Trinity Church, which WO held on Thursday evening in the Museum-street Echool: room. There was a large gathering of parishioners sec' friends and the proceedings were highly enjoyable. The' first portion of the programme took the form of a concert. The following artistes were responsible for the various enjoyable items which were all well received: —Songs by Mr J A Westcott (who had arranged the musical portion of the programme), Mrs Booth and I Miss Lockerbie,quartettes by Messrs Westcott, Taylor, Smith and Wright,and humorous tit-bits by Mr Grounds. Miss Longdin and Mr Richards accompanied. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton presided and delivered a short address on parochial and other Church questiols. were served and subsequently dancing was indulged ie. A successful whist drive was also held the winners 01 which were :—Ladies : 1, Mrs Worthington ; 2, 1kih3.,4 A Place • consolation, Mr 3 Redhead. Gentlemen : Mr Walsh ; consolation, Mr Gill. The prises were re seuted by Mrs Gill- The dance music was supplied py Mr Lomas.

Warrington and District Cricket League. The annual meeting of the Warrington and District Cricket League, was held on Tuesday evening at the Roan Cow Inn, Bridge Foot, Mr. J. W. Travis presid- ing. The report of the treasurer, Mr. C. hackney, showed that the receipts amounted to 1S 10s. Sci, and the expenditure .£l6 13s. (a, leaving a balance in hand of .1:1 his. 2d. The secretary, Mr. J. Woodheadi intimated that he had received notice of the intention. of one or two clubs not to join the league for the coming season. In order to strengthen the position of the league it was decided to extend the radius for membership to junior clubs within eight miles fropo• Warrinaton. Colonel J. Reid Walker was again elected president, and the following officials were appointed, chairman, Mr. J. W. Travis; treasurer: Mr. C. Hackney; secretary, Mr. C. E. Hawthorn, assistant secretary, Mr. 11. Daintith. A hearty vot.c of thanks was accorded Mr. Jas. Wcodhead for his past services as secretary of the League.

Ile is in his seventy-eighth year, • STOP SMOKING. The South Carnarvonshire Calvinistic Methodists monthly meting at Pentretelin, Portmadoc,on Monday, adopted unanimously a resolution by the Rev. Amon Jones, Chwilog, that the members of the denomination should use their influence to bring about total abstinence from tobacco. Ile remarked that many mernbets who grudged nominal contributions to their chapel funds thought little of squandering shillings weekly on tobacco. Alderman J. T. Jones, seconding,said it was disgrace- ful to sea deacons and ministers of the Gospel smoking in stations and public streets. It was high time to stamp out that objectionable practice.
